title: New Jersey and Florida Men Sentenced to Prison for Involvement in Multimillion-Dollar Bank Fraud and Identity Theft Scheme
body: Press Release New Jersey and Florida Men Sentenced to Prison for Involvement in Multimillion-Dollar Bank Fraud and Identity Theft Scheme Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Alabama MOBILE, AL – Two defendants were sentenced to 192 months and 140 months in federal prison, respectively, for their roles in a sophisticated, multimillion-dollar bank fraud and identity theft scheme that operated across the United States for nearly a decade. According to court documents, Vernon A. McCreath, 39, of Jersey City, New Jersey, and Mikhail C. McCreath, 35, of Miami, Florida, pleaded guilty to participating in a complex scheme involving bank fraud, identity theft, mail theft, and check counterfeiting. From September 2015 through September 2025, the defendants and their coconspirators stole mail, counterfeited checks and money orders, and used stolen identities to open bank accounts and conduct fraudulent financial transactions nationwide. To carry out the scheme, the defendants and their associates obtained stolen checks and money orders, used victims' personally identifiable information (PII) to open fraudulent bank accounts, manufactured forged identification documents, and counterfeited hundreds of financial instruments. The conspirators then negotiated those instruments at financial institutions throughout the United States, including within the Southern District of Alabama. Victims included religious organizations, small businesses, charitable organizations, and public school systems, among others. In April 2025, law enforcement agents executed a search warrant at the residence of one of the defendants' primary coconspirators, Demetrius J. Manassa, in the Atlanta, Georgia, area. During the search, agents recovered dozens of stolen and counterfeit checks and money orders, fraudulent identification documents, stolen mail, check-counterfeiting equipment, printers, blank check stock, a loaded Glock pistol, and ammunition. Latent fingerprint analysis linked Vernon A. McCreath to stolen postal money orders recovered during the search. Agents also examined cellular telephones belonging to Manassa, uncovering hundreds of Telegram messages exchanged with the defendants and other coconspirators in furtherance of the scheme. The messages contained stolen PII, information used to create fraudulent identification documents, images of stolen checks and mail, and videos showing participants with large amounts of cash believed to be proceeds from the fraud. Investigators also identified Mikhail C. McCreath's fingerprint in an image depicting a fraudulent deposit of approximately $1.3 million that was transmitted through Telegram. One of Vernon A. McCreath's Telegram usernames was "IDoBankFraudd." Chief U.S. District Judge Jeffrey U. Beaverstock sentenced Vernon A. McCreath to 192 months' imprisonment and Mikhail C. McCreath to 140 months' imprisonment. The Court also ordered the defendants to pay $687,259.04 in restitution to the victims of their crimes. Following their release from prison, both defendants will serve five-year terms of supervised release. As conditions of supervision, they will be subject to drug testing, financial monitoring, and restrictions on obtaining new lines of credit. For their roles in the scheme, the court previously sentenced several coconspirators as follows: Demetrius J. Manassa (180 months); Shaquan L. Manassa (60 months); Jarrod A. Ross (84 months); Khashawn D. Sidberry (90 months); and Terran E. Walker (60 months). Other coconspirators, including Patrick E. Williams and Jahvon H. Mosquito, will be sentenced at a later date. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service and the U.S. Department of Labor, Office of Inspector General investigated the case. The U.S. Secret Service, the Baldwin County Sheriff’s Office, the Florida Highway Patrol, the Glen Rock Police Department (New Jersey), and the South Fulton Police Department (Georgia) substantially assisted the investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Justin Roller prosecuted the case on behalf of the United States. Updated November 6, 2026 Topics Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - Alabama, Southern
retained_feed_body: MOBILE, AL – Two defendants were sentenced to 192 months and 140 months in federal prison, respectively, for their roles in a sophisticated, multimillion-dollar bank fraud and identity theft scheme that operated across the United States for nearly a decade.

title: Former Commercial Real Estate Vice President Sentenced To 11 Years In Prison For Defrauding His Employer Of Over $9.5 Million
body: Press Release Former Commercial Real Estate Vice President Sentenced To 11 Years In Prison For Defrauding His Employer Of Over $9.5 Million Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of New York Attorney for the United States, Acting under Authority Conferred by 28 U.S.C. § 515, Sean S. Buckley, announced that JARED SOLOMON, a former vice president of leasing at the commercial real estate company Vornado Realty Trust, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Loretta A. Preska to 11 years in prison for wire fraud, aggravated identity theft, and bank fraud in connection with a 14-year scheme to defraud his former employer of more than $9.5 million, forge the signatures of real people, and lie to banks.  SOLOMON was convicted in April 2026 following a one-week jury trial and remanded following his conviction. “For fourteen years, Jared Solomon abused the trust his employer placed in him, inventing brokers and stealing more than $9.5 million for services that were never performed,” said Attorney for the United States Sean S. Buckley.  “This individual, as shown, took advantage of his position and used victims’ personally identifiable information.  This will not be tolerated on any level.” According to the Indictment, statements made in public court proceedings and filings, and the evidence at trial: Beginning in 2009, SOLOMON, a Vornado leasing agent who later became a vice president of leasing, created fake commercial real estate broker companies.  Over approximately the next 14 years, SOLOMON lied to Vornado by claiming that brokers were owed broker fees or construction reimbursement expenses on commercial real estate deals on which he worked.  In fact, no such work had been performed, and the payments were sent to bank accounts in the names of the fake businesses, which SOLOMON controlled.  In total, SOLOMON caused Vornado to make 17 payments totaling over $9.5 million. To carry out and conceal the scheme, SOLOMON created fictitious personas and email accounts and used a temporary phone number and a newly purchased cellphone to pose as representatives of the fake companies. He forged the signatures of real people on the fake agreements he submitted to his employer and provided a fraudulent business certificate to a bank to open a business bank account.  SOLOMON spent the fraud proceeds on a $4.55 million house in Purchase, New York; a $3.6 million apartment on the Upper East Side of Manhattan; a country club membership; and a Porsche, among many other luxury expenses.  He also provided false information and a doctored bank statement to a mortgage lender to obtain an $850,000 mortgage loan. *                *                * In addition to the prison sentence, SOLOMON, 49, of New York, New York, was sentenced to three years of supervised release, was ordered to forfeit over $9 million in fraud proceeds and his interest in the two luxury homes that he purchased with those proceeds, and was ordered to pay restitution. Mr. Buckley praised the outstanding investigative work of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. This case is being handled by the Office’s General Crimes Unit.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Z. Margulies, Rita K. Maxwell, Joe Zabel, and Daniel C. Richenthal are in charge of the prosecution, with assistance from Paralegal Specialists Saadhana Jakka and Olivia Sebade. Contact Nicholas Biase, Shelby Wratchford (212) 637-2600 Updated November 6, 2026 Component USAO - New York, Southern Press Release Number: 26-319

title: Tallahassee Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Distribution of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Tallahassee Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Distribution of Child Pornography Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Tallahassee, Florida – Zachary Phillip Larson, 29, of Tallahassee, Florida, has been sentenced to six and a half years’ federal imprisonment for one count of the distribution of child pornography. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida announced the sentence. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “The distribution of child sexual abuse material has the effect of re-victimizing the innocent kids who have been exploited each and every time those horrific images and videos are shared. Ensuring this defendant spends years behind federal bars for his heinous crime delivers justice for the countless victims in this case, and should warn other offenders of a similar fate that awaits them if they commit these offenses in my district.” In 2024, the Tallahassee Police Department received tips generated by the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children that the defendant had uploaded multiple videos containing child pornography to a social media platform. Law enforcement obtained search warrants for the defendant’s social media account and his cellphone, which contained 12,522 images of child sexual abuse material, including the multiple videos that the defendant uploaded to the social media platform. “Those who exploit children and distribute child sexual abuse material will be held accountable for their actions,” said FBI Jacksonville Special Agent in Charge Jason Carley. “Through strong partnerships with our local, state and federal law enforcement partners, the FBI will continue working relentlessly to identify offenders and protect children. To those who think they can get away with targeting children: justice will find you.” The case was jointly investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Tallahassee Police Department. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Christie S. Utt. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys' Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit Justice.gov/PSC . title: Three Pensacola Men Face Federal Fentanyl Distribution Conspiracy Charges
body: Press Release Three Pensacola Men Face Federal Fentanyl Distribution Conspiracy Charges Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Pensacola, Florida – Douglas Lewis, Jr., 49; Kenneth Savage, 47; and Emmit Crum, 48; of Pensacola, Florida, have been arrested on federal charges related to a multi-year conspiracy to distribute fentanyl, using telephone facilities to carry out the drug conspiracy, and maintaining a drug premises. John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida, announced the charges. The three defendants were arrested during an operational takedown involving the search and seizure of evidence from multiple Escambia County residences. Also arrested on federal drug charges were Tiffany Oppelt, 36, and Britny Davis, 36, of Pensacola. As revealed in court during a preliminary hearing, law enforcement seized close to two pounds of fentanyl, multiple firearms and vehicles, and over $100,000 in United States currency during the course of the search warrant executions. The criminal conduct involved significant amounts of fentanyl being distributed throughout Escambia County over more than a year. The three men appeared this week before United States Magistrate Judge Zachary C. Bolitho at the United States Courthouse in Pensacola, Florida, for their detention hearings. They were ordered to be held in the custody of the United States Marshals Service pending further judicial proceedings. This case is being investigated by the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Escambia County Sheriff’s Office, Santa Rosa County Sheriff’s Office, Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office, Walton County Sheriff’s Office, the Pensacola Police Department, Florida Highway Patrol, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the U.S. Marshals Service, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney David L. Goldberg. A federal criminal complaint is merely an allegation that a defendant has committed a violation of federal criminal law and is not evidence of guilt. All defendants are presumed innocent and entitled to a fair trial, during which it will be the government’s burden to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt at trial. This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. title: Rosebud Man Convicted in Federal Court  of Assault With a Dangerous Weapon
body: Press Release Rosebud Man Convicted in Federal Court  of Assault With a Dangerous Weapon Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of South Dakota PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced that a jury has convicted Ervin Burning Breast, Jr., age 31, of Rosebud, South Dakota, of two counts of Assault with a Dangerous Weapon following a two-day jury trial in federal district court in Pierre, South Dakota. The verdict was returned on November 4, 2026. Each charge carries a maximum penalty of ten years in custody and/or a $250,000 fine, three years of supervised release, and a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. Burning Breast, Jr. was indicted by a federal grand jury in March 2026. The convictions stem from an incident that took place on December 24, 2025, in the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation.  At trial, the evidence established Burning Breast approached a group of individuals outside of a residence in Rosebud.  He was armed with a knife and swung the knife at two individuals within the group, with the intent to do bodily harm.  Neither victim was injured. This matter was prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian Country be prosecuted in Federal court as opposed to State court. This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Abby VanDenBerg prosecuted the case. A presentence investigation was ordered and a sentencing date has yet to be set. The defendant was remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service. title: Fort Walton Beach Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Fraud Crimes
body: Press Release Fort Walton Beach Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Fraud Crimes Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Pensacola, Florida – Marcus Bernard Clark, 30, of Fort Walton Beach, Florida, was sentenced to two and a half years in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to fraudulent possession of fifteen or more unauthorized access devices and aggravated identity theft. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution was made possible thanks to the excellent investigative work of the Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office, and now this fraudster will spend time in federal prison. Those who seek to enrich themselves by preying upon and defrauding others should be warned that my office will ensure they see the inside of a federal prison cell.” Court documents reflect that in September and October 2022, the defendant worked at a Wendy’s restaurant in Destin, Florida. During a judicially authorized extraction of the defendant’s cell phone related to another criminal case, law enforcement discovered over 200 photographs and some short videos of different individuals’ credit and debit cards. Investigators determined the photographs were taken at a Wendy’s fast food restaurant while the defendant was working. None of the victims gave permission to the defendant to photograph their bank cards containing their names and card numbers. “Those who prey on others by stealing their personal and financial information should know that we will always take these crimes very seriously,” said Okaloosa Sheriff Eric Aden. “Our investigators and our counterparts are totally committed to pursuing offenders and making sure they’re held accountable.” The case was investigated by the Okaloosa County Sheriff’s Office. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Jessica S. Etherton. title: Tallahassee Man Pleads Guilty to Interstate Stalking
body: Press Release Tallahassee Man Pleads Guilty to Interstate Stalking Friday, November 6, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Tallahassee, Florida – Matthew D. Weger, 33, of Tallahassee, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to interstate stalking. The plea was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution ensures this defendant will be held accountable for the numerous criminal threats he made toward the victim over the course of several months. My office will not hesitate to aggressively prosecute anyone whose behavior exceeds the limits of constitutionally protected speech and crosses the line into criminal threats.” Court documents reveal that law enforcement received a tip from an individual regarding concerns about threatening statements the defendant made against law enforcement officers. Law enforcement interviewed the individual and learned that the defendant had been stalking the individual from at least December 14, 2023, through June 25, 2024. The defendant had left threatening messages and voicemails, including threats to kill. The defendant refused to stop calling and messaging. The individual eventually blocked the defendant’s number, but the defendant was still able to leave voicemails. The defendant also sent threatening messages to the individual through Cash App as messages which accompanied online payments. In total, the defendant sent approximately $2,000 in $1.00 increments. Each payment was accompanied by a threatening message. Weger faces up to 5 years’ imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for February 5, 2027, at 1:00 pm before United States District Judge T. Kent Wetherell, II in Tallahassee, Florida. The case involved a joint investigation by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms & Explosives, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Tallahassee Police Department. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant United States Eric Welch. body:
ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026 Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date PRESS RELEASE ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026 6 November 2026 The aggregate of total assets of EU-headquartered credit institutions increased by 5.18%, from €33.27 trillion in June 2025 to €34.99 trillion in June 2026 During the same period, EU credit institutions’ aggregate non-performing loans ratio [ 1 ] increased by 0.03 percentage points year on year to stand at 1.99% in June 2026 EU credit institutions’ aggregate return on equity [ 2 ] was 5.31% in June 2026 and their Common Equity Tier 1 ratio [ 3 ] was 16.43% Chart 1 Total assets of credit institutions headquartered in the EU (EUR billions) Source: ECB Note: Data for all reference periods relate to the EU27. Data on the aggregate of total assets of credit institutions headquartered in the EU Chart 2 Non-performing loans ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU (EUR billions; percentages) Source: ECB Note: Data for all reference periods relate to the EU27. Data on the aggregate non-performing loans ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU Chart 3 Return on equity of credit institutions headquartered in the EU in June 2026 Source: ECB Note: Data for all reference periods relate to the EU27. Data on the aggregate return on equity of credit institutions headquartered in the EU Chart 4 Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU in June 2026 (percentages) Source: ECB Note: Data for all reference periods relate to the EU27. Data on the aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 ratio of credit institutions headquartered in the EU The European Central Bank (ECB) has published consolidated banking data as at end-June 2026 , a dataset for the EU banking system compiled on a group consolidated basis. The quarterly data provide information required to analyse the EU banking sector and comprise a subset of the information that is available in the year-end dataset. The data cover 336 banking groups and 2283 stand-alone credit institutions and non-EU controlled subsidiaries and branches operating in the EU, accounting for nearly 100% of the EU banking sector’s balance sheet. They include an extensive range of indicators on profitability and efficiency, balance sheet composition, liquidity and funding, asset quality, asset encumbrance, capital adequacy and solvency. Aggregates and indicators are published for the reporting population. Reporters generally apply International Financial Reporting Standards and the European Banking Authority’s Implementing Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting. However, some small and medium-sized reporters may apply national accounting standards. Accordingly, aggregates and indicators may include some data that are based on national accounting standards, depending on the availability of the underlying items. In addition to data as of end-June 2026, the published figures also include a few revisions to past data . For media queries, please contact Benoit Deeg , tel.: +491721683704. Notes These consolidated banking data are available in the ECB Data Portal . More information about the methodology used to compile the data is available on the ECB's website . Hyperlinks in the main body of the press release lead to data that may change with subsequent releases as a result of revisions. Defined as the ratio of non-performing loans to total loans. Cash balances at central banks and other demand deposits are included. Defined as the ratio of total profit (loss) for the first six months of 2026 (non-annualised) to total equity. Profitability indicators are not annualised. Defined as the ratio of Common Equity Tier 1 capital to the total risk exposure amount. title: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
body: Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents November 5, 2026 by Hannah Coutand 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power. What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity. The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU. Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU. Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests: Perplexity : Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system. DeepInfra : Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested. ClickHouse : Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard. DuckLabs : Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline. Daytona : Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86. Modal : Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU . title: Treasury Targets Global Scam Networks and the Corporate Infrastructure That Enables Them
body: November 5, 2026 WASHINGTON — Today, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned four individuals and 41 entities that support the business network of Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO) previously sanctioned by the United States for its role in cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking.  Additionally, OFAC designated a Malaysian individual who defrauded U.S. victims by managing a network of Africa-based scammers. “Cyber scam syndicates continue to steal billions of dollars from American victims while relying on sophisticated international business networks to launder their illicit proceeds,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent . “Treasury remains committed to dismantling every layer of these organizations—from their leadership to the corporate structures and financial facilitators that enable them to operate with impunity.” Today’s action builds on OFAC’s October 14, 2025 and June 23, 2026 designations targeting Prince Group leadership, affiliated companies, and financial facilitators. Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have generated billions of dollars in illicit proceeds through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online fraud that have victimized Americans and individuals around the world.  Many of these operations have been linked to scam compounds in Southeast Asia that rely on trafficked and coerced workers, while criminal proceeds are laundered through complex networks of offshore companies and financial facilitators.  The newly designated individuals and entities have helped sustain Prince Group TCO’s illicit global operations after the October 2025 and June 2026 designations by managing offshore corporate structures, concealing beneficial ownership, facilitating commercial activities, and providing administrative and financial services to senior Prince Group TCO executives.  Individuals targeted today have participated in activities to evade previous sanctions targeting the Prince Group TCO, including the transfer of property and owning of companies with or on behalf of previously designated Prince Group TCO leaders.  Today’s action further targets the corporate and financial infrastructure that has enabled Prince Group TCO leaders to conceal assets, evade prior sanctions, and maintain access to the international financial system. These actions are in furtherance of President Trump’s Executive Order (E.O.) 14390 of March 6, 2026, “Combating Cybercrime, Fraud, and Predatory Schemes Against American Citizens,” which orders the U.S. government to unleash every available tool to stop foreign-backed criminal networks that exploit vulnerable Americans through cybercrime, cyber-enabled fraud, and extortion.  OFAC is designating 45 targets pursuant to E.O. 13581 (“Blocking Property of Transnational Criminal Organizations”), as amended by E.O. 13863 (“E.O. 13581, as amended”), and one target pursuant to E.O. 13694 (“Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities”), as further amended by E.O. 13757, E.O. 14144, and E.O. 14306 (“E.O. 13694, as further amended”). These actions are in coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s New York and Honolulu Field Offices, Department of Justice’s Scam Center Strike Force, and the U.S. Attorney’s office for the District of Alaska.  OFAC also appreciates the cooperation of the British Virgin Islands Financial Investigation Agency (BVI FIA) and the United Kingdom’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO), whose timely assistance and information sharing were instrumental in supporting this sanctions action. TARGETING THOSE WHO EXPLOIT AMERICANS THROUGH FRAUD Prince Group TCO-affiliated actors have targeted victims in the United States and around the world through sophisticated cyber-enabled fraud schemes, including digital asset investment scams, romance scams, and other online financial fraud.  These schemes rely on deception and social engineering to persuade victims to transfer funds or digital assets to criminally controlled accounts, generating billions of dollars in illicit proceeds. Many of these operations are carried out from large-scale scam compounds in Southeast Asia, where trafficked and coerced workers are forced to perpetrate online fraud against victims across the globe.  Criminal proceeds are subsequently laundered through an international network of shell companies, offshore holding companies, financial facilitators, and digital asset transactions, allowing transnational criminal organizations to conceal the origin of illicit funds and integrate them into the legitimate financial system. Today’s action builds on Treasury’s ongoing efforts to dismantle not only the leadership of these criminal enterprises, but also the overseas corporate infrastructure and professional facilitators that enable them to target American victims, move illicit proceeds across jurisdictions, and evade law enforcement.  The Prince Group TCO has developed an extensive network of companies spanning multiple jurisdictions to support its commercial interests and conceal assets connected to its criminal enterprise.  Rather than operating through a single corporate structure, senior Prince Group TCO executives have relied on layers of offshore holding companies, foreign entities, nominee directors, and corporate service providers to maintain control over assets while obscuring beneficial ownership.  Today’s designations target key components of that network, including companies and individuals that have facilitated corporate administration, managed offshore entities, and provided business services to senior Prince Group TCO officials.  These facilitators have played an important role in enabling the Prince Group TCO to access the international financial system and preserve the appearance of legitimate commercial activity. DISMANTLING THE PRINCE GROUP’S CORPORATE INFRASTRUCTURE Qiu Yong is a key Prince Group TCO member who controls multiple BVI and Hong Kong companies on behalf of Prince Group TCO, and who has served as an employee of a company controlled by Prince Group TCO’s leader, Chen Zhi.  Chen Zhi was designated on October 14, 2025. Qiu Yong holds passports from multiple jurisdictions, including Cambodia, St. Lucia, and Türkiye, and is the beneficial owner of multiple BVI-based companies that control a network of Hong Kong companies involved in money lending and other business ventures. Hong Kong-based companies Premium Financial Limited (Premium Financial) and Solar Scape Financial Limited (Solar Scape Financial) are money lending companies ultimately owned by Qiu Yong through BVI-registered Sun Speed Holdings Limited (Sun Speed Holdings) and Solar Scape Limited (Solar Scape), respectively.  Hong Kong-based Direct Astute HK Limited (Direct Astute HK) is ultimately owned by Qiu Yong via BVI-registered Direct Astute Limited (Direct Astute).  Hong Kong-based Glad Vast Limited (Glad Vast), Glad Sparkle Limited (Glad Sparkle), and Glad Harvest Limited (Glad Harvest) are linked to the wine industry and are ultimately owned by Qiu Yong through BVI-registered Glad Glory Limited (Glad Glory). Per Hong Kong media reporting, Qiu was involved in the distribution and sale of wine across Hong Kong and Macao, illustrating Prince Group TCO’s reach into ostensibly legitimate businesses.  Qiu is also the beneficial owner of BVI-registered shelf companies Victory Flora Limited (Victora Flora), Win Applause Limited (Win Applause), Celestial Drive Limited (Celestial Drive), and Sino Sagacious Limited (Sino Sagacious). Hong Kong-based Zhao Mengyao , a.k.a. Amy Zhao, is Qiu Yong’s personal assistant and serves as company secretary and co-director of multiple Hong Kong-based companies ultimately controlled by Qiu Yong.  Zhao Mengyao and Qiu Yong are both shareholders of Hong Kong-based Mighty Divine Trust Hong Kong Limited (Mighty Divine Trust), a company directed by Zhou Yun, an individual previously identified by OFAC as a financial assistant and wealth manager for Prince Group TCO leader Chen Zhi.  Mighty Divine Trust and Zhou Yun were both designated on October 14, 2025. Qiu Yong is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Prince Group TCO.  Premium Financial, Solar Scape Financial, Sun Speed Holdings, Solar Scape, Direct Astute HK, Direct Astute, Glad Vast, Glad Sparkle, Glad Harvest, Glad Glory, Victora Flora, Win Applause, Celestial Drive, and Sino Sagacious are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Qiu Yong.   Zhao Mengyao is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Qiu Yong. OFAC is also targeting two individuals who are holding property for, or co-directing companies with, Prince Group TCO executive Chen Bo, who was designated on June 23, 2026. This includes Chen Bo’s wife, Cambodian national He Yujing , and Cambodian Prince Group TCO associate Visal Pang . Since OFAC’s action in October 2025, Chen Bo has transferred ownership of his Tokyo mansion to He Yujing, who also owns the Cambodian company Super Light Speed Kh Technology Co., Ltd .  Cambodia-based Visal Pang controls eleven Cambodian companies, several of which he co-directs with Chen Bo: Cambodia First Unite Construction Group (CFU Group) Co., Ltd., First Unite International Logistics Co., Ltd., First Unite Networks Entertainment Co., Ltd., First Unite Property Co., Ltd., First Unite Decoration (Cambodia) Co., Ltd., Cambodian First Unite Construction Machinery Co., Ltd., Linkedus Technology Co., Ltd., Cambo Duty Free Merchandise Co., Ltd., Marco Polo Hotel Co., Ltd., U-Life Go Now Co., Ltd. , and U-Life Kh Super App Co., Ltd. Visal Pang was also designated by the United Kingdom on March 26, 2026. Chen Bo remains in control of eleven Cambodian companies: Asian Welfare Lotteries Co., Ltd. , CB General Insurance PLC. , Cambodian Resource Energy Development Co., Ltd. , Cambodian Unite Wei Ye Investment Co. , DT Zhi Zao, Co., Ltd. , First Aquatic Industrial Co., Ltd. , Mo Net Beauty Co., Ltd. , Prince International Airlines Co., Ltd. , Richeng Property Developer Co., Ltd. , Tian Xu International Technology Plc. , and ZHX Printing Equipment Cambodia Co., Ltd . He Yujing is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of Prince Group TCO.  Super Light Speed Kh Technology Co., Ltd is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, He Yujing. Visal Pang is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of Prince Group TCO.  Cambodia First Unite Construction Group (CFU Group) Co., Ltd., First Unite International Logistics Co., Ltd., First Unite Networks Entertainment Co., Ltd., First Unite Property Co., Ltd., First Unite Decoration (Cambodia) Co., Ltd., Cambodian First Unite Construction Machinery Co., Ltd., Linkedus Technology Co., Ltd., Cambo Duty Free Merchandise Co., Ltd., Marco Polo Hotel Co., Ltd., U-Life Go Now Co., Ltd., and U-Life Kh Super App Co., Ltd. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Visal Pang. Asian Welfare Lotteries Co., Ltd., CB General Insurance PLC., Cambodian Resource Energy Development Co., Ltd., Cambodian Unite Wei Ye Investment Co., DT Zhi Zao, Co., Ltd., First Aquatic Industrial Co., Ltd., Mo Net Beauty Co., Ltd., Prince International Airlines Co., Ltd., Richeng Property Developer Co., Ltd., Tian Xu International Technology Plc., and ZHX Printing Equipment Cambodia Co., Ltd. are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Chen Bo. On June 23, 2026, OFAC designated Prince Group TCO associate Dai An, a high-level leader in the Prince Group TCO.  Dai is the majority owner of Singapore-based Chen Hua Holdings Pte Ltd (Chen Hua Holdings) and serves as director for Mauritius-based Meritwise Group Public Ltd (Meritwise Group) and Malaysia-based Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd (Greenmeadows). Chen Hua Holdings, Meritwise Group, and Greenmeadows are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to have acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Dai An. Singapore-based Greenbay Multi Media Pte Ltd (Greenbay Multi Media) is 100 percent owned by OFAC-designated Prince Group TCO executive Thet Li.  Thet Li was designated by OFAC on October 14, 2025. Greenbay Multi Media is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13581, as amended, for being owned or controlled by, or to have acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Thet Li. SANCTIONS AGAINST FACILITATOR OF MADAGASCAR-BASED SCAM NETWORK Chui Kok Wa (Chui) led an extensive network of scammers located in Madagascar that targeted Americans with scams, including defrauding Americans of digital assets.  The scammers led by Chui exploited cyber-enabled technologies, including cryptocurrencies and digital systems and technologies, to defraud numerous Americans of over $400,000 equivalent, thereby materially contributing to the cybercrime and scam center threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economic health of the United States.  Chui’s network garnered sympathy from vulnerable victims in order to misappropriate their funds for the private financial gain of his network. OFAC is designating Chui Kok Wa pursuant to E.O. 13694, as further amended, for being responsible for or complicit in, or having engaged in, directly or indirectly, cyber-enabled activities originating from, or directed by persons located, in whole or in substantial part, outside the United States that are reasonably likely to result in, or have materially contributed to, a threat to the national security, foreign policy, or economic health or financial stability of the United States, and that have the purpose of or involve causing a misappropriation of funds or economic resources, intellectual property, proprietary or business confidential information, personal identifiers, or financial information for commercial or competitive advantage or private financial gain. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  Unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions by U.S.  persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of designated or otherwise blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis.  OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  In addition, financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities involving designated or otherwise blocked persons. The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing or conspiring to cause U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000. The power and integrity of OFAC sanctions derive not only from OFAC’s ability to designate and add persons to the SDN List, but also from its willingness to remove persons from the SDN List consistent with the law.  The ultimate goal of sanctions is not to punish, but to bring about a positive change in behavior.  For information concerning the process for seeking removal from an OFAC list, including the SDN List, or to submit a request, please refer to OFAC’s guidance on Filing a Petition for Removal from an OFAC List . Click here for more information on the individuals and entities designated today. To report internet crime to the FBI, click here. ###

title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents See how developers are combining AI agents with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build simulation applications, test physical behavior and guide improvements. November 5, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

body: Investing in Wyoming’s infrastructure, energy and workforce Nov 05, 2026 | x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We’re building our first data center in Wyoming, representing a $17 billion investment in the Cowboy State. Steve Walter VP, Global Infrastructure and Energy Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Your browser does not support the audio element.
