Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Bank rate increased to 4% - November 2026 Monetary Policy Summary and Minutes The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee is responsible for making decisions about Bank Rate. Related links Related links Our latest decision explained Monetary Policy Report - November 2026 Current Bank Rate 4% Next due: 17 December 2026 Monetary Policy Summary and minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee meeting on 4 November 2026 ( PDF 0.2MB) PDF Close dialog Published on  
        05 November 2026 Monetary Policy Summary, November 2026 At its meeting ending on 4 November 2026, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%. The conflict in the Middle East is now in its ninth month. Global energy prices have continued to rise from an already elevated level. UK CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September. It is now expected to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year. It is then projected to fall as the impact of rising energy prices on 12-month inflation rates fades, and still restrictive monetary policy bears down on inflation. While the direct effects of higher energy prices are clear, and will continue to feed into firm and household energy bills, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages. However, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. Activity data in recent months have generally been stronger than expected, adding to the case for modestly tighter monetary policy. Monetary policy is not on a pre-set path. The Committee will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of underlying pay, pricing behaviour, and slack. The Committee will adjust Bank Rate as necessary to ensure CPI inflation returns to the 2% target in the medium term. Minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee meeting ending on 4 November 2026 1: Before turning to its immediate policy decision, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) discussed key economic developments and its judgements around them, as well as its views on monetary policy strategy. The latest data and analysis underpinning these topics were set out in the accompanying November 2026 Monetary Policy Report . The Committee’s discussions 2: The impact of protracted conflicts overseas on global energy prices remained the main source of uncertainty for the UK inflation outlook. The path for inflation was being shaped by the scale and duration of the energy and other global supply shocks, their knock-on impact on medium-term inflation through potential indirect and second-round effects, and the outlook for domestic activity and spare capacity. Monetary policy could not influence global energy prices, but was being set to ensure that the economic adjustment to them occurred in a way that achieved the 2% inflation target sustainably. The Committee would particularly need to guard against second-round effects that created inflation persistence, while considering any trade-off with weakness in economic activity. 3: Energy prices had remained sensitive to geopolitical news, and there had been significant further rises in spot and futures prices. The front-month Brent crude oil futures contract and the UK front-month natural gas futures contract averaged $108 per barrel and 216 pence per therm, respectively, over the 15 UK working days ending 27 October. These were 38% and 81% higher than at the time of the July Monetary Policy Report, and 5% and 27% above the respective 2026 Q4 futures-price assumptions in the July Report adverse scenario. Although a credible and sustained de-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East could lead prices to fall, continued periodic conflict, wider regional escalation or further damage to refining capacity could lead to persistently higher prices than embodied in current futures curves. There had also been a drawdown in energy supply buffers during 2026 which could amplify price pressures. 4: In the September UK CPI inflation outturn of 3.5%, direct energy effects had contributed around 1 percentage point, most of which was driven by fuels. These direct energy contributions were projected to build further in the next few quarters but then fall back, reflecting base effects and conditioning assumptions for wholesale energy prices based on futures curves that were downward sloping. There had been little sign so far of indirect effects from higher energy prices on other consumer goods prices, and in particular food inflation had remained lower than expected earlier in the year. Members discussed whether this was a sign of either diminished, or simply delayed, indirect effects. Although many firms were already facing higher prices for oil and refined products, some had not yet seen large rises in gas or electricity prices owing to hedging or longer-term fixed-price contracts. Agency intelligence suggested that many firms were also absorbing higher costs partly through lower profit margins. 5: The outlook for indirect effects on inflation would depend on the duration of the energy shock, and the extent to which firms could bear down on other costs or rebuild their margins in a stronger demand environment. The Committee judged that, for the most part, firms’ buffers would only prove temporary and that these cost pressures could eventually pass through into higher consumer prices if the energy shock persisted. There was, however, a risk that firms’ resilience to the energy shock would not last, instead resulting in weaker demand and then limiting firms’ pricing power. 6: The latest near-term inflation projection by Bank staff, which was based on energy prices averaged over the 15 UK working days to 27 October, was for headline CPI inflation to reach around 4½% in 2027 Q1, around 1¼ percentage points higher than at the time of the July Report, and around 5% in 2027 Q2. 7: Members noted that there was still limited evidence to date of second-round effects in wage and price-setting, although such effects typically only emerged with a longer lag and few indicators could yet be expected to reflect the impact of recent increases in energy prices. Forward-looking indicators of wage and price expectations from the DMP survey and Agents’ intelligence had moved little since September, though households and firms’ attentiveness was judged to be high, and there was a risk that outturns for wage settlements would turn out higher than firms’ current expectations if they were faced by outturns for headline inflation in the new year that were stronger than they had previously anticipated. Since second-round effects were likely to be state-dependent and the outlook for headline inflation had risen materially, the Committee judged that the risk of material second-round effects emerging had risen further since September and could remain a risk for some time. 8: The Committee continued to monitor wider global cost pressures, such as those triggered by adverse weather events and demand for AI components, although the potential impact of these risks on UK inflation was likely to be much smaller than for the energy shock and was not judged to have increased significantly since September. Despite the energy shock and these non-energy cost pressures, global activity growth had proved more resilient than expected, although it was expected to fall back next year. 9: The Committee had been briefed on the Budget on 28 October. The projections and scenarios in the November Report were conditioned on announced Government policy. The new policy measures in the Budget were expected to have a downward impact of ¼ percentage points on CPI inflation by 2027 Q2 and a small impact on activity. In absolute terms, the stance of fiscal policy remained likely to detract from growth over the medium term. 10: The Committee discussed the recent path of domestic activity and its implications for inflationary pressures. Since September, there had been further evidence of the resilience of activity despite higher energy prices. Momentum had been provided by the impact of global growth on UK exports, and some positive impact from the deployment of artificial intelligence. The impact of artificial intelligence on the UK economy was uncertain but was likely to affect both demand and supply. There was also some evidence that consumer demand had held up so far despite the impact of higher energy prices on real incomes, although the most recent consumer confidence reading suggested that this might not be maintained. 11: There was uncertainty around the extent to which the recent strength in GDP growth might persist, but on balance members judged that it was likely to fall back somewhat in the coming quarters. The outlook for growth would be sensitive to the behaviour of households and firms in the face of rises in energy costs and tighter financial conditions. 12: The increase in growth had been associated with signs of a stabilisation of the margin of slack in the economy, although members continued to differ in their views on how wide that margin was in absolute terms. It was likely that some slack would persist given the headwinds facing demand from households and firms. It would also be important to judge whether the factors boosting productivity growth over the past two years would lead to an ongoing boost to potential growth in the economy and, more broadly, the extent to which future growth would reduce spare capacity in the economy. 13: The Committee discussed the extent to which the underlying disinflation process that had been underway for some time before the Middle East conflict had proceeded as expected. Many measures of underlying inflation were no longer falling, and were judged to be somewhat above rates consistent with meeting the inflation target in the medium term. For some members, the news on domestic activity and underlying inflation was a signal that monetary policy had not been as restrictive as previously judged. For other members, it was premature to draw too much signal from outturns over the past few months, given the volatility of short-term economic indicators, uncertainty about the impact of technological change, and the difficulty of interpreting measures of underlying inflation completely independently of the energy shock. 14: Forward market interest rates had remained elevated compared with pre-conflict levels, and had continued to feed through to rates faced by some households and firms. Benchmark two-year mortgage rates had risen by nearly 50 basis points since the beginning of September. According to the Bank’s latest Market Participants Survey, the median expected path for Bank Rate had increased since September, reaching 4% in November and 4.25% in February, but had remained below the UK short-term interest rate curve. 15: Most members judged that the stance of monetary policy was still restrictive, although this judgement was sensitive to the choice of measure of the monetary stance, for example the extent to which it reflected expected inflation. The stance of monetary policy would also be experienced differently by different households and firms depending on their exposure to higher energy prices, technological change and interest rates. Members also noted that growth rates of lending to businesses had remained strong, although new mortgage approvals for households had been falling. 16: The Committee considered the updated central projection and the two scenarios that were set out in the November Report. The central projection assumed that there would be greater second-round effects on wage and price-setting than in the July Report owing to higher energy prices. The adverse scenario explored the risk of persistently higher energy prices and an additional mechanism for larger second-round effects which might occur as a consequence. The weaker demand scenario assumed that the recent resilience of domestic growth would falter and that widening spare capacity in the economy would limit the scope for second-round effects to emerge. These scenarios would all require different monetary policy responses if any of them were to materialise. 17: Taken together, the Committee judged that the risk of stronger inflationary pressure had increased further since the September meeting. While most members continued to judge that there was still a margin of slack in the economy and that policy was still restrictive, it was less clear that this would impart sufficient disinflationary pressure to bring inflation back to target in a timely manner, given the further upward pressures on inflation which were anticipated and that had increased the forward-looking risks to inflation persistence. This could be especially important since households and firms appeared more attentive to outturns for headline inflation than in the past. While financial conditions had tightened materially compared with the start of the conflict, a rise in Bank Rate at this meeting would support the broader transmission of tighter financial conditions. 18: Given the significant uncertainty around the geopolitical situation and the impact of tighter financial conditions so far, the Committee would continue to keep the cumulative evidence on the propagation of the energy shock through the UK economy under close review, and judge whether the level of Bank Rate was imparting sufficient restrictiveness. Most importantly, the Committee would continue to monitor the prospects for second-round effects in price and wage-setting by considering the evolution of pay, pricing behaviour and slack via the available data and surveys, consistent with the framework set out in Box A in the November Report. The immediate policy decision 19: Eight members (Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Swati Dhingra, Megan Greene, Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill, Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor) preferred a 0.25 percentage point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. The duration and scale of the energy price increase had generated sufficient inflationary pressures in the pipeline to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. There was a range of views among these members about the extent to which the underlying disinflationary process prior to the conflict had continued, the degree of spare capacity in the economy, and the restrictiveness of the current monetary policy stance. These members agreed that, although evidence of second-round effects had been limited, the availability of evidence would increase over time, and would continue to need close monitoring, along with the implications of developments in energy prices for medium-term inflationary risks. 20: Catherine L Mann preferred a 0.5 percentage point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. From a risk management and credibility perspective, an activist approach was needed to prevent persistent inflationary dynamics becoming embedded as the economy reached thresholds that threatened to cause non-linear responses in price and wage-setting. 21: The Chair invited the Committee to vote on the proposition that: Bank Rate should be increased by 0.25 percentage points, to 4% . 22: Eight members (Andrew Bailey, Sarah Breeden, Swati Dhingra, Megan Greene, Clare Lombardelli, Huw Pill, Dave Ramsden and Alan Taylor) voted in favour of the proposition. Catherine L Mann voted against the proposition, preferring to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%. MPC members’ views 23: Members set out the rationale underpinning their individual votes on Bank Rate. Members are listed alphabetically under each vote grouping. References in parentheses relate to boxes in the November 2026 Monetary Policy Report. References to scenarios relate to those set out in Section 3 of the November Report. Votes to increase Bank rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 4%. Andrew Bailey : There has been a material further increase in energy prices. UK economic activity has strengthened and the labour market appears to be stabilising (Box C). Domestic services price inflation has flattened off. Meanwhile, indirect and second-round effects have not emerged yet (Box A). Firms are cutting costs and their margins are being compressed, while they are also benefiting from longer fixed-price energy contracts and cost hedging mechanisms. To varying degrees, these approaches can only be temporary. The central projection and weaker demand scenario require an alleviation of the factors that have pushed up energy prices to validate the slope of energy futures curves. Put simply, it requires real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East. Absent this, risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside. In view of the news, the case is clear for a 25-basis point rise now. Without news which softens the risks to inflationary pressures, I can see the argument for a further increase in rates and thereafter taking a more conditional approach, dependent on the evidence on energy prices and inflation dynamics. Recognising that some of the upward slope in the curve is explained by risk premia and not expected rates, the current level of restrictiveness is broadly appropriate. Sarah Breeden : Increased energy prices have further materially raised the near-term inflation outlook. Activity and the labour market have been more resilient than expected, but slack remains (Box C). Consistent with this and firm intelligence, little evidence has emerged so far of material second-round effects and indirect pass-through has been weaker than expected. While some measures of domestic inflation have flattened, I do not yet conclude that the earlier disinflation has stalled, given overlapping energy shocks and the seasonal pattern of wage negotiations. Slack will be leaning against the risk of material second-round effects (Box A). But with inflation expected to be above the threshold for non-linear effects, and little sign of a rapid or durable resolution to the conflict, the degree of inflationary pressure in the pipeline is now sufficient to warrant an increase in Bank Rate. The longer energy prices remain high the more likely persistent inflationary effects take hold, which would require further tightening in Bank Rate. But this will also depend on how energy prices propagate, especially given the risk that demand weakens. I will continue to assess the balance of risks at each meeting. For now, I judge the current restrictiveness of financial conditions as sufficient to balance these. Swati Dhingra : Even as underlying inflation normalised in line with peer countries, previous votes to maintain Bank Rate in restrictive territory guarded against immediate inflation risks from the unfolding energy shock. The scale and persistence of the rise in wholesale energy prices imply that households and businesses will continue to face higher energy costs in the near term. Broad-based price pressures remain subdued, however, and we cannot yet distinguish between delayed pass-through and weaker pass-through on the evidence available (Box A). Growth has been firmer than anticipated (Box C), partly reflecting an AI-driven sectoral and investment boost that presents two-sided risks to the inflation outlook. Set against this, the combined drag from energy prices and higher mortgage rates continues to weigh on real disposable incomes, limiting consumption growth and weakening activity in consumer-facing services. Raising Bank Rate by 25 basis points provides additional insurance against upside risks from stronger pass-through and firmer growth in demand. To support maintaining Bank Rate at a higher level for an extended period, I would need to see clear evidence of a recovery in firms’ pricing power and households’ purchasing power alongside signs of mutually reinforcing wage and price pressures. Megan Greene : Since September, we have had a more prolonged shock, a further leg up in energy prices and there is evidence of less benign initial conditions when the shock hit. Evidence of second-round effects has remained scant as expected, but the risks have clearly shifted to the upside. Underlying services inflation has been flat since spring and underlying wage growth is stuck around 3.5%, above target-consistent levels. GDP growth has surprised to the upside and aggregate credit volumes remain stronger than expected. Staff analysis shows we may have been marginally in a low inflation, loose labour market regime when the Iran conflict emerged, but we’ve since entered a high inflation, loose labour market regime. We project inflation will remain above the threshold in which expectations are more sensitive to outturns for most of the outlook period, likely buoying pay settlements in 2027 and 2028. I believe the output gap is smaller than we think and has likely peaked. We continue to face Knightian uncertainty, but a rate hike now is appropriate based on the central outlook rather than just risk management considerations. Additional hikes will likely be required going forward, though further out this will depend on pay, pricing behaviour and slack. Clare Lombardelli : The conflict has lasted longer than expected. This has kept oil, gas and refined product prices elevated, making the inflationary effects of the energy shock larger and more persistent. Cost pressures have remained elevated for sufficiently long that there is now a greater risk of second-round effects becoming embedded in price and wage-setting (Box A). Despite this, economic activity appears more resilient than previously expected (Box C). And recent data suggest that underlying disinflation may have stalled. There are some downside risks to the outlook for inflation, either from a more benign path for energy prices or a slowdown in economic activity. But overall I view the balance of risks to the inflation path as upside to our forecast given the ongoing energy price uncertainty and limited evidence of slack. Current circumstances warrant a 25-basis point increase in Bank Rate at this meeting. In the absence of evidence of weaker inflation pressures, there is likely to be a case for a further increase in rates in the near term. Beyond that, the path for rates is conditional on the interaction of the underlying economy, higher energy prices, the nature of their transmission and any further shocks. Huw Pill : Raising Bank Rate by 25 basis points at this meeting represents a significant step towards attaining the monetary policy stance needed to address current threats to price stability, including those stemming from uncertainty surrounding events in the Middle East and their influence over energy prices in the medium term. That uncertainty and its impact remains potentially considerable and of indeterminate duration. Nonetheless, of itself, a single 25-basis point hike is unlikely to be sufficient. Achieving the level of Bank Rate necessary to confront challenges and risks to lasting achievement of the 2% inflation target is likely to require more policy tightening, including in the near term. Looking into next year, monetary policy decisions should then become more dependent on evidence of inflation persistence and second-round effects, were it to emerge in the data flow. At each meeting, a broad-based interpretation of new data and surveys will support the extraction of the policy-relevant underlying signal from a range of indicators. Developments in domestic pay and pricing dynamics (Box A) deserve particular focus since they offer insight into the potential strength of second-round effects and, as such, inform the assessment of lasting threats to price stability. Dave Ramsden : The outlook for inflation has deteriorated, with higher energy prices following re-escalation of the conflict since July. I have also become somewhat less confident about the domestic disinflation process, the degree of slack, and how restrictive the policy stance has been to date. Activity has proved more resilient than expected (Box C), slack in the labour market is levelling off, and private sector wage growth has stopped declining. These less favourable starting conditions increase the risk of second-round effects (Box A). Indirect effects have been smaller and slower to build than anticipated in July, but looking ahead, are projected to be larger and more protracted. Risks around the inflation outlook have shifted further to the upside. Nevertheless, households and firms’ resilience could weaken, with adjustment occurring through employment losses or business failures rather than prices. A 25-basis point increase in Bank Rate is necessary now to ensure the appropriate degree of restrictiveness. I will continue to assess the evidence at each meeting, in particular how likely high energy prices are to feed through to other prices and the economy more broadly, by monitoring the evolution of pay, pricing behaviour, and slack. Alan Taylor : It is essential to communicate, and for markets to understand, that, as of now, this is not the start of a hiking cycle: policy isn’t on a pre-set, unconditional path. The risk is curve dislocation and unwarranted tightening in financial conditions. Rather, from an already restrictive position, this is a risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike. What has changed since July, and even September, is the magnitude of the energy disruption. A second, larger shock has roughly doubled the inflationary impulse; gas is beyond April’s worst scenario, while refined-product prices have risen sharply. The case for holding rested on avoiding such a shock and seeing no sign of second-round effects. The first condition has now failed. We lack evidence of second-round effects, but the larger shock raises the risk. That motivates insurance now. Further tightening, however, depends on continued energy price pressure (a function of stochastic geopolitics that we are ill-equipped to predict) as well as unfolding evidence of propagation into domestic wages, price-setting and expectations, particularly through the 2027 pay round. The next move could be up, down, or sideways. Telling data will arrive soon. Vote to increase Bank rate by 0.5 percentage points, to 4.25%. Catherine L Mann : My recent votes to increase Bank Rate by 25 basis points represented a ‘down payment’ to lean against second-round effects, reinforce credibility, and uphold ‘good policy’ (in the language of my Great Moderation speech). The challenge: projected CPI inflation reaches 4.9% by mid-2027 and would be some 25 basis points higher absent the measures announced at the latest Budget. This projection is conditioned on a significant decline in energy prices; similar futures curves earlier this year have not eventuated. My policy strategy importantly is informed by research, which points to non-linear inflation risks. Households are particularly attentive to energy and food price inflation, which may be reflected in 2027 wage demands. With CPI inflation at 3.5% in September, the economy has crossed the estimated statistical threshold into a high inflation-tight labour market regime where the asymmetric behavioural responses of households and firms support more robust second-round effects. A different research approach estimates that the economy may well have breached the policy credibility threshold, which worsens the policy trade-off. Moreover, a substantial inflation risk premium is in the UK yield curve, reflecting five years of above-target inflation, where it has averaged 4.7%. Therefore, from a risk management and credibility perspective, a 50-basis point hike in Bank Rate is ‘good policy’. Operational considerations 24: In line with the arrangements announced following the September MPC meeting, the stock of UK government bonds held for monetary policy purposes on 4 November was £362 billion. 25: The following members of the Committee were present: Andrew Bailey, Chair Sarah Breeden Swati Dhingra Megan Greene Clare Lombardelli Catherine L Mann Huw Pill Dave Ramsden Alan Taylor Daniel Gallagher was present as the Treasury representative. David Roberts was present on 28 October and 2 November, as an observer for the purpose of exercising oversight functions in his role as a member of the Bank’s Court of Directors. The Bank of England Act 1998 gives the Bank of England operational responsibility for setting monetary policy to meet the Government’s inflation target. Operational decisions are taken by the Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee. The minutes of the Committee meeting ending on 16 December will be published on 17 December 2026. title: Former FBI agent pleads guilty to Cryptocurrency theft
body: Press Release Former FBI agent pleads guilty to Cryptocurrency theft Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Virginia ALEXANDRIA, Va. – A former FBI agent from Ashburn pled guilty today to wire fraud and money laundering related to using his access to steal cryptocurrency. According to court documents, from 2017 through early 2025, Patrick Steven Yaroch, 37, worked at the FBI Boston Division on an investigative squad focused on an adversarial nation state. From February 2025 to July 31, 2026, Yaroch worked in the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, with access to FBI systems that contained cryptocurrency credentials that the FBI had collected as part of its investigations. Beginning no later than December 2024, Yaroch used his position to steal cryptocurrency from wallets controlled by the subjects of various other investigations or by adversarial nation state actors, and from at least one wallet the FBI created to use in an operation. Throughout his wire fraud scheme, Yaroch conducted approximately 100 fraudulent transfers using credentials related to 35 separate FBI investigations. He illicitly gained approximately $2,474,380.66 in fraudulent proceeds. Once Yaroch moved the stolen cryptocurrency, he would exchange it for a different type of cryptocurrency. Yaroch then laundered the cryptocurrency through additional financial transactions to obfuscate its source, nature, and ownership. Between Nov. 25, 2025, and Jan. 13, 2026, Yaroch transferred approximately $93,082 to one of his accounts, then transferred the funds between his other accounts from which he sent various payments to cover his debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans. In addition to paying off his debts, Yaroch intended to use the fraudulent proceeds to make other purchases, including financing a new life abroad. Yaroch asked ChatGPT how to maximize profit from investments and where to live in the European Union. Following ChatGPT’s suggestion of buying a vineyard in Portugal, on June 15, 2026, Yaroch provided a power-of-attorney to lawyers in Portugal to represent him before the Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority, to register him and obtain his tax identification number in Portugal, and to collect the password to access his finance portal. Yaroch then made arrangements to travel to Portugal in September 2026. As set forth in the agreed upon statement of facts, Yaroch’s actions compromised multiple FBI investigations related to both criminal groups and nation state adversaries.  His actions deprived FBI employees of their ability to carry out their functions to protect public safety and national security.  Yaroch’s actions also compromised FBI sources and methods used in foreign intelligence collection and criminal investigations. Yaroch is scheduled to be sentenced on March 4, 2027. He faces up to 20 years in prison. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, and Daniel S. Wierzbicki, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Washington Field Office’s Counterintelligence Division, made the announcement after U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted the plea. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Kathleen Robeson and Russell Carlberg are prosecuting the case. The National Security Cyber Section (NatSec Cyber) of the Justice Department’s National Security Division and the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General Mid-Atlantic Region provided significant assistance. Related court documents and information are located on the website of the District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia or on PACER by searching for Case No. 1:26-CR-208. Contact USAVAE.Press@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Fraud Public Corruption Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Office of the Inspector General USAO - Virginia, Eastern

title: Tigard Man Found Guilty of Federal Sex Trafficking Offense After Fleeing to Thailand
body: Press Release Tigard Man Found Guilty of Federal Sex Trafficking Offense After Fleeing to Thailand Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Oregon Tigard Man Found Guilty of Federal Sex Trafficking Offense After Fleeing to Thailand PORTLAND, Ore. — A federal jury has found a Tigard man guilty of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion after he attempted to profit from the commercial sexual exploitation of his girlfriend and later fled to Thailand to avoid prosecution, U.S. Attorney Scott E. Bradford announced today. Selva Delano Mudaliar , 40, was found guilty of sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion following a federal jury trial. According to evidence presented at trial, in December 2021, Mudaliar transported the victim from Portland, Oregon, to a hotel in Vancouver, Washington, where he attempted to arrange for her to engage in commercial sex acts with a customer in exchange for money. Prosecutors proved that Mudaliar fraudulently induced the victim to accompany him and used force, threats, and coercion in connection with the sex trafficking scheme. Trial evidence showed that after meeting a customer at a Portland nightclub, Mudaliar became interested in the customer after observing that he had substantial funds available in his bank account. Mudaliar directed the victim to introduce herself to the customer and later drove both individuals to a hotel in Vancouver, Washington. Once there, Mudaliar negotiated a deal under which the customer would pay $1,500 in exchange for sexual access to the victim. When the arrangement failed, Mudaliar became enraged and assaulted the victim. Evidence at trial established that Mudaliar repeatedly struck the victim in the face and head and strangled her until she lost consciousness. The victim suffered severe injuries that required emergency medical treatment and transfer to a Level 1 trauma center. Following the assault, the Washington County District Attorney's Office charged Mudaliar with multiple state offenses. Shortly before his scheduled state court trial in February 2024, Mudaliar fled the United States and traveled to Thailand. The FBI assisted in locating Mudaliar overseas, and he was arrested by Thai authorities. Mudaliar later consented to extradition and was returned to the United States to face the Washington County charges and additional federal charges. The charges in state court remain pending. “Sex trafficking is a violent crime that exploits vulnerable victims for financial gain,” said Scott E. Bradford, U.S. Attorney for the District of Oregon . “The defendant attempted to sell a woman for sex and then brutally assaulted her when his scheme failed. Today's verdict holds him accountable for that conduct and demonstrates our commitment to prosecuting those who use force, fraud, and coercion to exploit others.” Mudaliar faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 15 years in federal prison and a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 2, 2027. The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Tigard Police Department. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mira R. Chernick and William M. McLaren prosecuted the case. Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Human Trafficking Component USAO - Oregon

title: Repeat Drug Trafficker from Taylor County Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison for Methamphetamine Trafficking and Firearms Offenses
body: Press Release Repeat Drug Trafficker from Taylor County Sentenced to 15 Years in Federal Prison for Methamphetamine Trafficking and Firearms Offenses Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Kentucky BOWLING GREEN, KY – A Taylor County, Kentucky man was sentenced to 15 years in prison for methamphetamine trafficking and firearm offenses. U.S. Attorney Kyle G. Bumgarner of the Western District of Kentucky, Special Agent in Charge John Nokes of the ATF Louisville Field Division, and Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. of the Kentucky State Police, made the announcement. Brad L. Smith, 63, was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, for trafficking in over 2 kilograms of methamphetamine and possessing a handgun as a convicted felon. Smith was prohibited from possessing a firearm because he had previously been convicted of the following felony offenses. On May 19, 2020, in Taylor Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance, second offense, involving less than 2 grams of methamphetamine. On September 5, 2009, in Perry Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance. On September 8, 2009, in Perry Circuit Court, Smith was convicted of first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance (two counts), and second-degree trafficking in a controlled substance. In total, Smith had previously been convicted of 11 prior felony offenses and was considered an “armed career criminal” by statute. United States Attorney Kyle Bumgarner stated, “Brad Smith’s career as a drug trafficker is over. He will be in prison until his 80’s. Smith wasted his life committing felony offenses and harming his community as a drug dealer. I sincerely hope that others see Smith’s sentence 15-year sentence and decide to stop their destructive behavior.” ATF Special Agent in Charge John Nokes stated, “This sentence underscores the serious threat posed by repeat drug traffickers who combine the distribution of dangerous narcotics with illegal firearm possession. ATF will continue working alongside our federal, state, and local law enforcement partners to hold violent offenders accountable, disrupt drug trafficking operations, and protect our communities.” “Through strong partnerships and shared resources, the commonwealth was able to bring this individual to justice,” KSP Commissioner Phillip Burnett, Jr. said. “These partnerships send a clear message that those who bring illegal drugs into our communities will be held accountable.” There is no parole in the federal system. This case was investigated by the ATF Bowling Green Field Office and the Kentucky State Police. Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark J. Yurchisin II of the U.S. Attorney’s Bowling Green Branch Office prosecuted the case. This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. ### Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Operation Take Back America Component USAO - Kentucky, Western

title: Jury Finds Two Brothers Guilty of July 2020 Murder and Robbery Conspiracy
body: Press Release Jury Finds Two Brothers Guilty of July 2020 Murder and Robbery Conspiracy Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia USADC.Media@usdoj.gov Brothers Killed Victim in D.C. then Fled to Georgia WASHINGTON – Dijon Williams, 27, and Daivion Williams, 28, both from Georgia, were found guilty today for charges related to the murder of 30-year-old Nurudeen Thomas, in July 2020, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro. "These brothers, Dijon and Daivion Williams, traveled from Georgia to Washington, D.C., intending to rob their drug supplier, and the robbery ended in murder," said U.S. Attorney Pirro. "Although they fled back to Georgia after the killing, they could not evade justice. Today's guilty verdict demonstrates our commitment to holding violent offenders accountable, no matter where they run." A jury in D.C. Superior Court found both Dijon Williams and Daivion Williams guilty of one count each of first-degree murder while armed, conspiracy and attempted robbery. The Honorable Jason Park scheduled sentencing for January 22, 2027. According to the government’s evidence, Dijon Williams, a former Georgetown University football player, and his brother, Daivion Williams, conspired to rob their drug supplier, Nurudeen Thomas, of a large quantity of drugs. They drove from Georgia to Washington, D.C. to effectuate their plan. Shortly after arriving in D.C., on July 21, 2020, they drove to the 4100 block of 14th Street, Northwest, where they met Mr. Thomas, ostensibly to engage in a drug sale. Once there, they put their plan to rob him into action, during which Mr. Thomas was shot and killed. They then fled the District of Columbia for Georgia. Joining the announcement was Interim Chief Jeffery Carroll of the Metropolitan Police Department. This case was investigated by the Metropolitan Police Department and was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Yasmin Emrani and Daniel Bromwich. AUSA Rachel Forman investigated and indicted the cases. 2020 CF1 008306 (Dijon) 2020 CF1 008473 (Daivion) Contact USADC.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Firearms Offenses Violent Crime Component USAO - District of Columbia

title: Brothers Face Federal Charges in Retaliation Murder Case
body: Press Release Brothers Face Federal Charges in Retaliation Murder Case Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of New Mexico ALBUQUERQUE – Two men are facing federal charges after a series of violent assaults, one of which resulted in the death of a woman. According to court records, on August 30, 2024, Eloy Perea , 39, and his brother, Harold Perea, Jr. , 34, both enrolled members of the Navajo Nation, struck Jane Doe 1 with a vehicle and at some point, Jane Doe 1 was shot by Eloy . On October 7, 2024, Harold intentionally rammed a vehicle that Jane Doe 2 was standing next to and causing her to be pinned between the rammed vehicle and a vehicle parked next to it. Harold then exited his vehicle with a shotgun and discharged several rounds in Jane Doe 2’s vicinity without hitting her. On August 21, 2025, Harold assaulted Jane Doe 2 a second time with a motor vehicle, this time striking her directly. Harold and Eloy exited the vehicle armed with firearms. Harold struck Jane Doe 2 with the butt of the firearm and yelled at her for speaking to law enforcement about the previous assault. Eloy is charged with assault with two counts of using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence and one count each of second-degree murder, assault with a dangerous weapon and retaliation against a witness, victim or informant. He will remain in custody pending trial, which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Eloy faces no less than 17 years and up to life in prison. Harold is charged with assault with three counts of using and carrying a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence, two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon and one count each of second-degree murder and retaliation against a witness, victim or informant. He will remain in custody pending trial, which has not yet been scheduled. If convicted of the current charges, Harold faces no less than 27 years and up to life in prison. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Ryan Ellison and Special Agent in Charge Justin A. Garris of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office made the announcement today. The Gallup Resident Agency of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albuquerque Field Office investigated this case with assistance from the Navajo Nation Police Department and the Navajo Department of Criminal Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Seth Teleky and Jesse Pecoraro are prosecuting the case. An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Indian Country Law and Justice Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - New Mexico Press Release Number: 26-306

title: Law Enforcement Officials Gather To Discuss Partnerships, Collaboration, Preparedness
body: Press Release Law Enforcement Officials Gather To Discuss Partnerships, Collaboration, Preparedness Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov DENVER – Law enforcement officials from across Colorado gathered this week for the annual Colorado Law Enforcement Coordination Conference hosted by the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado. The event brings together agencies across local, state, and federal levels of government with the purpose of partnership development, collaboration, and preparedness. Over the two-day session, law enforcement officials spent time hearing from experts from across the justice system who spoke about topics including human trafficking, online radicalization of juveniles, violent crime, transnational criminal organizations, tracing illicit proceeds, and emerging tools and techniques. Another critical area of conversation involved state and federal collaboration during crisis response. The event’s keynote panel included U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly, Denver District Attorney John Walsh, and Boulder District Attorney Michael Dougherty – each of whom have unique professional experiences responding to and managing serious situations in the state. “It is both an honor and a critical opportunity for law enforcement officials from across Colorado to gather with the goal of developing partnerships, collaboration, and preparedness,” said United States Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly.  “Law enforcement is complex and critical work, and I am proud to stand with our partners at the local, state, and federal levels to advance justice and protect the people of Colorado.” “Colorado has a long history of cooperation between local, state and federal law enforcement," said Denver District Attorney John Walsh. "That cooperation, which continues today, has played a major role in significantly reducing crime in the state over the past few years.  This conference is a great opportunity for law enforcement agencies from across the state to make our partnership even stronger, and Colorado even safer.” “Collaboration and preparedness are critical to enhancing public safety which is a role we take very seriously,” said Boulder District Attorney Michael Dougherty.  “When federal, state, and local partners come together with shared purpose, we strengthen our ability to protect communities and respond to emerging challenges.  These discussions and partnerships reflect our collective commitment to working together to delivering meaningful results to the people we serve.” The Colorado Association of Chiefs of Police, the County Sheriffs of Colorado, the Colorado District Attorney’s Council, and the Colorado Fraternal Order of Police helped to make the event possible. Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: 40 Warrants Issued in Second Year of D.C. Sex Offender Enforcement Operation
body: Press Release 40 Warrants Issued in Second Year of D.C. Sex Offender Enforcement Operation Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Columbia USADC.Media@usdoj.gov 1,500+ compliance checks over two years as U.S. Attorney's Office and U.S.  Marshals Service vow continued enforcement after second-year sweep WASHINGTON – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, in partnership with the United States Marshals Service, reports a second year of city‑wide operations to verify that sex offenders residing in the District remain compliant with the law, announced U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro and United States Marshals Service (USMS) Director Gadyaces S. Serralta. The initiative , originally launched in October of last year, resulted in compliance checks on 883 sex offenders in 2025, with federal agents determining that 25 had failed to register. Nine of those individuals were classified as “Class A” offenders, meaning they had been convicted of extremely serious sexual assaults or had victimized multiple individuals. Between August and September of this year, federal agents conducted compliance checks on 694 sex offenders. Based on those compliance checks, arrest warrants have been issued for 40 sex offenders for failing to register. 13 of the 40 are “Class A” offenders. “My job as United States Attorney is to protect this community, especially our children, from repeat offenders who prey on the vulnerable,” said U.S. Attorney Pirro. “Over two years, we’ve conducted more than 1,500 compliance checks, including 694 in just the last two months. If you ignore the law, we will find you, arrest you, and prosecute you.” “Sex offender registration is a legal obligation, not a choice,” said U.S. Marshals Service Director Gadyaces S. Serralta. “Those who disregard the law should not expect to escape accountability. Working alongside the U.S. Attorney’s Office and our law enforcement partners, we will continue to investigate violations, locate noncompliant offenders, and execute arrest warrants. This is not a one-time crackdown. It is a sustained commitment to protecting our communities and ensuring that those who violate the law cannot evade its consequences”. The Supreme Court recognized decades ago that the “risk of recidivism posed by sex offenders is frightening and high.” Smith v. Doe , 538 U.S. 84, 103 (2003). The United States Marshals Service and The Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA) have been aggressively pursuing non-compliant offenders since August 24, 2025. The offenders are now being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Sex Offense and Domestic Violence and the Child Exploitation and Human Trafficking Sections. The operation identifies the sex offenders in the District who are required to register with CSOSA, uncovers and investigates offenders who are out of compliance, and arrests and aggressively prosecutes absconders. The operation is a high-priority project. The U.S. Attorney’s Office has devoted substantial prosecutorial resources to these two operations; USMS has committed 28 Deputy U.S. Marshals from across the country, and CSOSA has likewise participated fully. As of November 2, 2026, the Second operation has resulted in the following: Obtained 40 Superior Court Sex Offender Registration Act (SORA) arrest warrants (34 misdemeanor warrants and 6 felony warrants) 13 of these arrest warrants are for Class A offenders 1 of these arrest warrants is for an offender with 11 prior sex convictions Arrested and charged 17 sex offenders for SORA violations (12 on misdemeanor charges and 5 on felony charges) One offender was also referred to the Major Crimes Section for prosecution for possible ID Theft charges Indicted one sex offender for a felony violation of Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) Two sex offenders were also charged and convicted of Misdemeanor Failure to Register during the 2025 operation and are now charged again in the 2026 operation with Felony Failure to Register because they continued to be non-compliant (Tre Risper and Karl Gaddy, active Superior Court Cases pending for Felony FTR) Contact USADC.Media@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Violent Crime Components USAO - District of Columbia U.S. Marshals Service

title: Reward Offers Up to $50M for Information Leading to Arrests and/or Convictions of Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) Leaders Following Homeland Security Task Force Investigation
body: Press Release Reward Offers Up to $50M for Information Leading to Arrests and/or Convictions of Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) Leaders Following Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Note : Read the Superseding Indictment here. Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) leaders Yohan José Romero, also known as “Yohan Petrica,” 48; Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano, also known as “El Viejo,” 37; and Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez, also known as “Juancho,” 44, were previously charged in a 2025 six-count second superseding indictment in the Southern District of Texas, for conspiring to provide and providing material support to TdA. A nine-count third superseding indictment was later returned in July 2026 and unsealed this week. In those indictments, Mosquera Serrano is also charged with conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine and international cocaine distribution. “Since President Trump returned to office, the Department of Justice has charged more than 350 members and associates of Tren de Aragua, including Yohan Petrica, El Viejo, and Juancho,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Their criminal enterprise has spread fear, violence, and lawlessness, and we will not stop until those responsible are brought to justice. Anyone with information regarding the location of the three individuals listed in today’s superseding indictment should help save lives by notifying the FBI.” “These gang members are monsters, and we’ve indicted them as such,” said U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas. “I’m confident the enhanced bounties will incentivize these terrorists’ return to my district, where we will bring them to justice.” Mosquera Serrano is on the FBI’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives List. Jose Romero and Rivas Núñez are also fugitives. The Department of State’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL) is offering rewards under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program (TOCRP) of up to $50 million total for information leading to their arrests and/or convictions in any country. Yohan José Romero, also known as “Yohan Petrica” increased from up to $4 million to up to $20 million Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano, also known as “Giovanni” and “El Viejo” increased from up to $5 million to up to $15 million Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez , also known as “Juancho”: new offer of up to $15 million “By leveraging DEA's investigative expertise alongside our partners through the Homeland Security Task Force, we are bringing the full force of the U.S. government to bear against narco-terrorists that threaten our communities,” said Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Administrator Terrance Cole. “Today's announcement demonstrates what can be achieved through unprecedented coordination and intelligence sharing across federal law enforcement. Yohan José Romero, Mosquera Serrano, and Rivas Núñez have played key roles in directing and expanding Tren de Aragua's operations throughout the Western Hemisphere. TdA spreads violence, fear, and instability wherever it operates. Make no mistake - DEA will stop at nothing to identify, disrupt, and dismantle this criminal network.” “As Secretary Rubio has repeatedly stated, transnational criminal and terrorist organizations such as Tren de Aragua are the most urgent security threat in our hemisphere,” said Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Thomas G. DiNanno. “Today, we are offering rewards totaling up to $50 million under the Transnational Organized Crime Rewards Program for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions of the top three leaders of Tren de Aragua. The Trump Administration remains fully committed to eliminating narcoterrorist organizations in the region that traffic illicit drugs, commit violent acts, and cause harm to American communities.” If you have any information concerning these individuals, please contact the FBI via WhatsApp or Telegram at 281-787-9939. Those with information may also contact their local FBI office, nearest American Embassy or Consulate or can submit a tip online at tips.fbi.gov . The FBI and the DEA are jointly conducting the investigation with the assistance of the Houston Police Department, Harris County Sheriff’s Office, U.S. Marshals Service (USMS), Colombian National Police and the Colombian Attorney General’s Office (Fiscalía General de la Nación), with significant assistance from the Justice Department’s Office of Judicial Attaché in Bogota and Office of International Affairs. The case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Casey N. MacDonald and Anibal J. Alaniz for the Southern District of Texas along with Joint Task Force Vulcan’s (JTFV) Deputy Director David C. Smith and Trial Attorneys James Keller and Kelly McGann. TdA is a violent transnational criminal organization that originated as a prison gang in Venezuela in the mid-2000s. Since that time, TdA has expanded its criminal network throughout the Western Hemisphere and established a presence in the United States. TdA’s criminal activities range from drug trafficking and firearms trafficking to sex trafficking, kidnapping, robbery, theft, fraud, and extortion. TdA members also commit murder, assault, and other violent acts to advance the organization’s criminal activities. TdA has also developed an additional source of revenue stream by committing financial crimes that target financial institutions throughout the United States, including using ATM jackpotting to steal millions of dollars in cash. The investigation has revealed that the conspiracy has targeted or carried out ATM jackpotting attacks in 47 states, the District of Columbia, and several foreign nations. This case is part of JTFV. JTFV was created in 2019 to eradicate MS-13 and has now expanded to target TdA. JTFV is comprised of U.S. Attorney’s Offices across the country, including Southern and Eastern Districts of New York; Eastern and Western Districts of North Carolina; Western District of Virginia; Middle and Southern Districts of Florida; Eastern District of Texas; Western District of Oklahoma; Northern District of Indiana; District of Nevada; and the District of Arizona, as well as the Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys, and the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Criminal Division, and the Office of Judicial Attaché and DEA partners in Bogotá, Colombia. Additionally, the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), USMS, and the Federal Bureau of Prisons are essential law enforcement partners with JTFV. This prosecution is also part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF Houston comprises agents and officers from FBI; HSI; DEA; Texas Department of Public Safety; Houston Police Department; Harris County Sheriff's Office; ATF; USMS; U.S. Postal Inspection Service; Department of Transportation and IRS Criminal Investigation with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas leading the prosecution. A complaint and indictment are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Yohan José Romero a/k/a Yohan Petrica, 48; Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano a/k/a El Viejo, 37; and Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez a/k/a Juancho, 44, were previously charged in a six-count second superseding indictment returned in 2025. A nine-count third superseding indictment followed in July 2026. According to the allegations, all three face charges of conspiring to provide and providing material support to Tren de Aragua (TdA). title: Justice Department Says Federal Education Aid Cannot Be Tied to Unconstitutional Race-Based Criteria
body: Press Release Justice Department Says Federal Education Aid Cannot Be Tied to Unconstitutional Race-Based Criteria Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion clarifying the limits on the Department of Education’s authority to consider race when administering the Magnet Schools Assistance Program (MSAP). MSAP is a federal grant program designed to promote voluntary school desegregation and expand educational opportunities for students through competitive grants to school districts. The opinion reaffirms the federal government’s longstanding support for magnet schools while ensuring that federal assistance is not conditioned on unconstitutional race‑based criteria. “Today’s opinion reaffirms a foundational principle of our constitutional order: government programs must treat individuals as individuals, not as members of racial groups,” said Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser of the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel. “Although Congress has long recognized the value of magnet schools, the Equal Protection Clause limits how the federal government may lend them support. Only in exceptionally rare circumstances may funding decisions turn on a school’s racial composition.” “The Magnet School Assistance Program can continue to serve students across the country—but only if it is administered constitutionally,” said Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock, who signed the opinion. “Federal dollars must never be used to engineer unconstitutional racial balancing. Our Constitution is colorblind, and federal programs must reflect that.” The opinion explains that MSAP’s statutory and regulatory framework ties federal funding to race‑based concepts such as “minority‑group isolation” and the use of racial data to shape funding decisions. Because these criteria condition federal support on racial considerations, the opinion concludes that the program must be evaluated under the Constitution’s most rigorous standard: strict scrutiny. Under that standard, the Department of Education may approve MSAP grants only when an applicant demonstrates that its use of race is narrowly tailored to remedy a specific and identified instance of illegal discrimination. The opinion makes clear that grants based solely on goals such as increasing racial diversity, reducing racial isolation, or altering racial balance—untethered from the remediation of unlawful discrimination—cannot be approved. The Department of Justice will work closely with the Department of Education to ensure that MSAP awards fully comply with these constitutional requirements while continuing to support the mission of magnet schools: fostering academic excellence, innovation, and meaningful educational opportunities for students across the country. Read the full opinion here . Updated November 5, 2026 Component Office of Legal Counsel Press Release Number: 26-1326

title: Former Kokomo Police Department Officer Sentenced to 40 Years in Prison for Sexually Assaulting Minor, Lying to Investigators, and Destruction of Records
body: Press Release Former Kokomo Police Department Officer Sentenced to 40 Years in Prison for Sexually Assaulting Minor, Lying to Investigators, and Destruction of Records Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Sinmi Asomuyide, a former Kokomo, Indiana, police officer, was sentenced on Wednesday to 40 years in prison and three years supervised release for charges related to his on-duty sexual assault of a 14-year-old, and related obstruction. Asomuyide was previously convicted by a federal jury after a five-day trial in the Southern District of Indiana. “The Department of Justice takes civil rights abuses seriously, including those committed by the small minority of police officers that betray public trust,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “This defendant will be held accountable for the kidnapping and sexual abuse of a child. We hope the victim will be able to recover and prosper despite this horrific episode.” “This defendant exploited the badge in one of the worst ways imaginable,” said U.S. Attorney Tom Wheeler for the Southern District of Indiana. “What makes these crimes particularly disturbing is that he used the very tools, training, and authority entrusted to him as a police officer not only to assault a vulnerable child, but to try to conceal it. The evidence told a different story, and today's sentence sends a clear message that no one can use the authority of the badge as a shield from accountability.” “The very people entrusted with protecting children must never become the ones who victimize them. This defendant preyed on a 14-year-old girl and then attempted to cover up his crimes,” said Special Agent in Charge Timothy J. O’Malley of the FBI Indianapolis Field Office. “That kind of calculated abuse is unconscionable. The FBI remains committed to protecting children and relentlessly pursuing those who prey on them.” In particular, jurors found Sinmi Asomuyide, 33, guilty of willfully depriving the victim, who was then 14 years old, of her constitutional rights by sexually assaulting her. The jury found that the defendant’s conduct included kidnapping and abusive sexual contact of a child under the age of 16. Jurors also found Asomuyide guilty of lying to the Indiana State Police in an attempt to cover up the assault by denying having sexual contact with the victim, and lying about the presence of other corroborating evidence. Additionally, jurors found Asomuyide guilty of deleting a messaging application he had been using to communicate with the minor victim prior to the sexual assault in attempt to cover up the assault. The case was investigated by the FBI. Assistant U.S. Attorney Peter Blackett for the Southern District of Indiana, Civil Rights Division Trial Attorney Anita Channapati, and former Senior Sex Crimes Counsel Tara Allison prosecuted the case. Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Civil Rights Components Civil Rights Division Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Indiana, Southern Press Release Number: 26-1322

title: Attorney General Todd Blanche Honors 10 District of Hawaii Assistant U.S. Attorneys, Staff, and Agents at 2026 Director’s Awards
body: Press Release Attorney General Todd Blanche Honors 10 District of Hawaii Assistant U.S. Attorneys, Staff, and Agents at 2026 Director’s Awards Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Hawaii HONOLULU – United States Attorney Ken Sorenson announced that Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael D. Nammar, Assistant U.S. Attorney Aislinn K. Affinito, Victim Assistance Specialist Leilani Uganiza, Supervisory IT Specialist Cheryl Tagaca, and Supervisory Paralegal Specialist Kari Sherman, all of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Hawaii, as well as Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent Murray Acosta, IRS Criminal Investigation Special Agent Shaun Morita, Environmental Protection Agency Special Agent Jan Yukumoto, FBI Special Agent Thomas Palmer, and FBI Special Agent Joshua Parker were among 183 Department of Justice employees recognized by Attorney General Todd Blanche and Executive Office for U.S. Attorneys (EOUSA) Director Francey Hakes at the 2026 Director’s Awards Ceremony held October 28, 2026, in the Great Hall of the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building in Washington, D.C.  The awards recognize outstanding achievements by employees of the U.S. Attorney’s Offices. The team received the Director’s Award for Superior Performance by a Litigation Team for their role in the investigation and prosecution of the Miske Enterprise, led by Michael J. Miske, which was a violent criminal organization operating in Hawaii for decades.  Although not eligible for the Director’s Award, having since left the Department of Justice, the team also included former Assistant U.S. Attorneys Mark Inciong and KeAupuni Akina.  Inciong was the lead prosecutor who directed the investigation and prosecution of the Miske Enterprise and served as lead counsel at the trial of Michael J. Miske.  Inciong retired in March 2025 after nearly 27 years of service as a federal prosecutor. “I could not be prouder of the tireless work of the outstanding Assistant U.S. Attorneys, staff, and agents who dismantled the Miske Enterprise and brought Michael Miske’s reign of murder, felony assaults, kidnappings, intimidation, chemical attacks, drug trafficking, and fraud to an end,” said U.S. Attorney Ken Sorenson.  “Miske and his henchmen were a scourge upon the State of Hawaii, terrorizing our communities and openly profiting from violence, drug trafficking, and fraud.  In addition to those who received the Director’s Award, this achievement belongs to the many additional agents, staff members, and other prosecutors who assisted our team in this extraordinary prosecution, including those like lead Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Inciong, who have since left the Department of Justice or law enforcement.” Following an investigation lasting more than 10 years, the team presented a seven-month federal trial involving thousands of exhibits and hundreds of witnesses.  Its work addressed racketeering activities involving murder, kidnapping, murder-for-hire, drug trafficking, fraud, obstruction, and chemical weapons attacks.  The investigation and prosecutions resulted in the federal convictions of 20 members and associates, including Michael J. Miske, who was convicted at trial.  The team’s sustained preparation and coordination dismantled the enterprise and strengthened public safety in communities throughout Hawaii. The convictions were the result of an investigation conducted by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation, Homeland Security Investigations, the Criminal Investigation Division of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives, with assistance from the Honolulu Police Department, the Drug Enforcement Administration, the Coast Guard Investigative Service, the United States Marshals Service Fugitive Task Force, the Cybercrime Lab of the Department of Justice Criminal Division Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, the Hawaii Criminal Justice Data Center, the Honolulu Fire Department, the Hawaii National Guard, 93rd Civil Support Team, the Office of Investigations-Office of the Inspector General for the Social Security Administration, and the Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General. EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 94 United States Attorneys’ offices around the country.  For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao. Contact Aislinn Affinito Aislinn.Affinito@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Component USAO - Hawaii

title: Fayette County Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Car Loan Scheme and COVID-Related Fraud
body: Press Release Fayette County Man Sentenced to Federal Prison for Car Loan Scheme and COVID-Related Fraud Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Georgia ATLANTA - Hugh A. Brown, Jr. was sentenced to federal prison today for fraudulently obtaining roughly $1.25 million in pandemic relief and auto loans. “This defendant shamelessly fleeced federal taxpayers and financial institutions over half a decade through various loan fraud schemes,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “My office will continue to prosecute and seek prison time for anyone who abuses government relief programs.” “Submitting false information to obtain federal pandemic relief funds, using fraudulent documents and deliberate misrepresentations to secure loans from banks and credit unions, are serious offenses that undermine the integrity of our financial institutions and erode public trust,” said Acting Assistant Special Agent in Charge Patrick M. Palmer, IRS Criminal Investigation, Atlanta Field Office. “IRS Criminal Investigation remains steadfast in its commitment to identifying and investigating financial fraud. Working alongside our federal law enforcement partners and the U.S. Attorney’s Office, we will continue to protect taxpayers, safeguard the integrity of our financial system, and ensure that individuals who exploit these institutions for personal gain are held accountable under the law.” “The U.S. Postal Inspection Service sees firsthand through investigations how devastating fraud and deception can be on our communities. That’s why we commit, every day, to bring criminals that choose to undermine the integrity of our financial system and betray the trust of lenders to justice,” said Rodney M. Hopkins, Inspector in Charge of the Atlanta Division of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service. “The defendant in this case stole money earmarked to help people in a time of economic uncertainty and used it to increase their bank account. The Postal Inspection Service’s message and mission are clear: You commit fraud, exploit our financial systems, and do harm to our communities, we will find you and bring you to justice.” According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the indictment, and other information presented in court: In 2020, Brown applied for a Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loan by submitting false payroll information and fake IRS tax forms to a federally insured bank. As a result of the bogus application, Brown received a $162,500 PPP loan. In 2022, Brown fraudulently claimed Employee Retention Credits (ERCs), a refundable tax credit designed to encourage employers to continue to pay employees during COVID-19, on behalf of his company. After filing fraudulent tax returns, Brown received seven United States Treasury checks totaling $644,452.98 in ERCs and other credits. In addition, from at least February 2022 through February 2025, Brown obtained fraudulent bank and credit union loans worth nearly $450,000 by submitting fake documents, misrepresenting employment/income information, and providing fictitious vehicle details as loan collateral. Today, U.S. District Judge Victoria M. Calvert sentenced Hugh A. Brown, Jr., 35, of Fayetteville, Georgia, to two years, nine months in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release. Brown also was ordered to pay $1,244,243.81 in restitution to the Small Business Administration, the Internal Revenue Service, and financial institutions. On June 3, 2026, Brown pleaded guilty to bank fraud conspiracy and bank fraud. This case was investigated by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, the Internal Revenue Service, and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.  Valuable assistance was provided by Homeland Security Investigations. For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga . Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Fraud COVID-Related Fraud Financial Fraud Component USAO - Georgia, Northern
