title: Illegal Alien from Mexico Indicted for Attempting to Transport Minor from Colorado to Mexico, Producing Child Pornography
body: Press Release Illegal Alien from Mexico Indicted for Attempting to Transport Minor from Colorado to Mexico, Producing Child Pornography Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Texas EL PASO, Texas – A federal grand jury in El Paso returned an indictment on Wednesday charging an illegal alien from Mexico with five counts related to his alleged transportation of a minor for the purpose of engaging in illicit sexual conduct and production, possession and transportation of child sexual abuse materials, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas. According to court documents, Clemente Fernando Vazquez Serna, 34, was encountered on Oct. 11 aboard a Transborde bus that was selected for an outbound inspection at the Bridge of the Americas Port of Entry. A criminal complaint affidavit alleges that Vazquez Serna and a 14-year-old female both presented Mexican birth certificates. The two passengers were escorted off the bus for further inspection. It was then discovered that Vasquez Serna was engaged in a romantic relationship with the minor and that he was taking her to Mexico to live with him. Court documents further allege that an inspection of cell phones belonging to Vazquez Serna and the minor revealed multiple files of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) depicting the 14-year-old. Vazquez Serna was arrested and, on Oct. 16, he was ordered detained by U.S. Magistrate Judge Anne Berton. Vazquez Serna is now charged with transportation of a minor; production of visual depictions of minors engaging in sexually explicit conduct; transportation of a visual depiction involving the use of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct; attempt to transport a visual depiction involving the use of a minor engaging in sexually explicit conduct; and possession of a visual depiction involving the sexual exploitation of a minor. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Customs and Border Protection are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Scott Wisniewski is prosecuting the case. This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. An indictment is merely an allegation and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Contact USATXW.MediaInquiry@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Operation Take Back America Immigration Component USAO - Texas, Western

title: Leader of Multi-State Drug Trafficking Network Convicted After Federal Jury Trial
body: Press Release Leader of Multi-State Drug Trafficking Network Convicted After Federal Jury Trial Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Georgia ATLANTA – A federal jury convicted Roderick Battle, the leader of a nationwide drug trafficking organization, of multiple drug trafficking, money laundering, and firearms-related charges. “Despite a prior conviction for trafficking narcotics, Battle was undeterred, operating a prolific drug trafficking network that supplied large quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other narcotics throughout the country,” said U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg. “This conviction reaffirms the steadfast dedication of my office and our federal and state law enforcement partners in the Homeland Security Task Force to protect the public from individuals who poison our communities with deadly drugs.” “Roderick Battle led a sophisticated, multi-state drug trafficking operation that flooded communities across the country with dangerous narcotics, including fentanyl and methamphetamine,” said Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta. “This conviction is a testament to the strong partnerships and coordinated efforts of law enforcement to dismantle these criminal networks and hold those responsible accountable.” “Cases of this magnitude are not solved by one agency alone,” said Michael J. Connolly, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the DEA Atlanta Field Division. “This investigation demonstrates what can be accomplished when federal, state, and local law enforcement partners work together with a shared mission. As part of the Homeland Security Task Force, our collective efforts exposed a sophisticated drug trafficking and money laundering network, disrupted its operations, and secured a conviction against the individual responsible for leading it.” According to U.S. Attorney Hertzberg, the charges, and other information presented in court:  Between at least January 2021 and December 2024, Battle and his conspirators concealed drugs and drug proceeds in guitar amplifiers and transported the drugs nationwide using a stolen FedEx account that belonged to a sports memorabilia company. Additionally, Battle and his conspirators transported drugs hidden beneath vehicles on tow trucks. On May 6, 2023, the Pennsylvania State Police intercepted a package that contained six kilograms of cocaine shipped from Battle’s residence in southeast Atlanta. Four days later, federal and state law enforcement executed a search warrant at Battle’s home and seized large quantities of narcotics, including fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin, all packaged for distribution. Agents also located two firearms under Battle’s bed and approximately $76,000 in cash. Federal agents arrested Battle on a criminal complaint that day. While Battle was detained in the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service pending trial, he continued to facilitate the distribution of narcotics using a contraband cellular telephone. On November 3, 2026, a federal jury convicted Roderick Battle, 49, of Atlanta, Georgia, of conspiracy and possession with the intent to distribute fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, and heroin, as well as money laundering and firearms-related charges. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for March 2, 2027, before U.S. District Judge J.P. Boulee. Battle faces a mandatory minimum 20 years in prison. In determining the actual sentence, the Court will consider the United States Sentencing Guidelines, which are not binding but provide appropriate sentencing ranges for most offenders. This case is being investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Pennsylvania State Police, with valuable assistance provided by the Georgia State Patrol. Assistant United States Attorneys Dwayne A. Brown Jr., Brock Brockington, John DeGenova, and Patrick Cespedes are prosecuting the case. This prosecution is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of United States law enforcement towards identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. The Atlanta Wilhelm HSTF is comprised of agents and officers from ATF, CGIS, DEA, FBI, ICE-HSI, IRS-CI, DOL-OIG, DSS, USMS, USPIS, and USSS, as well as numerous state and local agencies, with the prosecution being led by the United States Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia. For further information please contact the U.S. Attorney’s Public Affairs Office at USAGAN.PressEmails@usdoj.gov or (404) 581-6185. The Internet address for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia is http://www.justice.gov/usao-ndga . title: CEO and VA Employee Sentenced for Paying and Receiving Illegal Health Care Kickbacks and Bribes
body: Press Release CEO and VA Employee Sentenced for Paying and Receiving Illegal Health Care Kickbacks and Bribes Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Two Florida men were sentenced today for their roles in a conspiracy to pay and receive illegal health care kickbacks. Laurent Cassagnol was sentenced to 6 months in prison, and Heriberto Rivera was sentenced to 13 months in prison. In addition to the prison terms, Cassagnol was ordered to forfeit $175,172, and Rivera was ordered to forfeit $515,542, which represented the proceeds that the defendants obtained from the offense. According to court documents, Cassagnol, 43, and Rivera, 43, both of Orlando, Florida, conspired to pay and receive illegal kickbacks and bribes to direct veterans and their families, who were patients of the VA Community Care Program (VACCP), to Rivera’s clinic, Family Integrative Medicine of Orlando, LLC (FIMO), for acupuncture, chiropractic adjustments, and other holistic medical services. Rivera, the CEO of FIMO, paid illegal kickbacks and bribes to Cassagnol, an Advanced Medical Support Assistant for VACCP, in exchange for Cassagnol using his position with the VA to steer VA patients to FIMO for medical services. Cassagnol was a vital point of contact between veterans and the VA health care system; his abuse of that role took advantage of veterans and their families who rely on the VA to obtain medical care. The actions of both defendants put profit before the needs of VA patients. As a result of the illegal kickbacks, over $14 million in fraudulent claims were submitted to the VA and VACCP, of which over $11 million was paid. The investigation was the result of a complaint made to the VA Office of the Inspector General (VA-OIG) fraud hotline. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; Special Agent in Charge Rodney E. Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office; and Acting Special Agent in Charge Josh Lollar of the VA-OIG Southeast Field Office made the announcement. FBI and VA-OIG investigated the case. Trial Attorneys Jody King and Angela Benoit of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section are prosecuting the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at https://www.justice.gov/fraud/health-care-fraud-section . Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Fraud Component National Fraud Enforcement Division Press Release Number: 26-1327

title: U.S. Attorney Charges New York State Police Sergeant With Sexually Exploiting Two Minors And Possessing Child Pornography
body: Press Release U.S. Attorney Charges New York State Police Sergeant With Sexually Exploiting Two Minors And Possessing Child Pornography Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of New York United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, Assistant Director in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (“FBI”), James C. Barnacle, Jr., and Superintendent of the New York State Police, Steven G. James, announced today the unsealing of a Complaint charging STEVEN CALDERON with sexual exploitation of children and possession of child sexual abuse material.  CALDERON was arrested this morning and presented this afternoon before Chief U.S. Magistrate Judge Judith C. McCarthy in White Plains federal court and detained. “Steven Calderon’s alleged crimes are all the more disturbing knowing he committed these alleged acts while serving as a law enforcement officer—a position entrusted with protecting the public including its most vulnerable members,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “The defendant’s alleged acts are a profound betrayal of the public trust and the oath he swore to uphold.” “Steven Calderon's alleged actions constitute a shocking breach of the public trust placed in law enforcement,” said FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle, Jr. “The FBI is committed to utilizing every available resource and tool to relentlessly pursue anyone who exploits a child.  This case should serve as a warning: no badge, title, or position will shield those who prey upon children and justice will find you.” “The allegations against Sergeant Calderon are deeply disturbing and stand in direct opposition to the oath every member of the New York State Police takes to protect and serve,” said New York State Police Superintendent Steven G. James. “Our responsibility to protect children and investigate allegations of abuse does not change when the accused wears our uniform. We remain committed to supporting the victims and working with the FBI, the U.S. Attorney’s Office, and our local partners to ensure a thorough investigation. The public deserves accountability, regardless of rank or position.” As alleged in the Complaint:(1) CALDERON has been a Sergeant with the New York State Police since in or about 2022.  On or about October 25, 2026, he was arrested and charged in the Town of Crawford with assault in the second degree and third degree. On or about October 25, 2026, New York State Police executed a search warrant at the Orange County residence of CALDERON, in connection with the assault investigation and recovered various electronic surveillance equipment and storage devices. The devices were found to contain thousands of sexually explicit images and videos of children, including prepubescent children, as well as numerous videos that appear to have been taken surreptitiously by CALDERON in a bathroom in CALDERON’s residence.  The review of these videos revealed that, on or about July 25, 2026, CALDERON surreptitiously recorded a 10-year-old child (“Victim-1”) undressing in a bathroom in order to capture sexually explicit images of Victim-1 and then edited the recording to create a short clip of Victim-1 in which she appears to be engaging in sexually explicit conduct. Further, on or about February 3, 2023, CALDERON surreptitiously video recorded a 9-year-old child (“Victim-2”) undressing in a bathroom in order to capture sexually explicit images of Victim-2 and created a sexually explicit screenshot of Victim-2 from the recording. There may be other victims.  If you have information to report, please contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (225-5324) or https://tips.fbi.gov . A photo of CALDERON is below. *                *                * CALDERON, 43, of the Town of Crawford, New York, is charged with two counts of sexual exploitation of a child, which each carry a maximum term of 30 years in prison and a mandatory minimum term of 15 years in prison.  He is also charged with one count of possessing child pornography, which carries a maximum term of 20 years in prison. The maximum potential sentences are prescribed by Congress and are provided here for informational purposes only, as any sentencing of the defendant will be determined by a judge. Mr. McDonald praised the efforts of the FBI, the Town of Crawford Police Department, the Orange County District Attorney’s Office, and the New York State Police in connection with this investigation. The prosecution is being handled by the Office’s White Plains Division.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys Samantha Briggs and Marcia S. Cohen are in charge of the prosecution. ^ As the introductory phrase signifies, the entirety of the text of the Complaint and the description of the Complaint set forth herein constitute only allegations, and every fact described should be treated as an allegation. Contact Nicholas Biase, Shelby Wratchford (212) 637-2600 Updated November 5, 2026 Attachment 26_mj_xxxx_-_u.s._v._calderon_-_complaint.pdf Component USAO - New York, Southern Press Release Number: 26-318

title: Southern District of Iowa Attorney Receives National Director’s Award for Excellence in Appellate Advocacy
body: Press Release Southern District of Iowa Attorney Receives National Director’s Award for Excellence in Appellate Advocacy Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of Iowa DES MOINES, Iowa – The Department of Justice has recognized Assistant United States Attorney Kyle Hanson of the Southern District of Iowa for his outstanding appellate advocacy. Hanson received a Director’s Award from the Executive Office for United States Attorneys (EOUSA) during an awards ceremony held on October 28, 2026, in Washington, D.C. AUSA Hanson was honored for Excellence as an Appellate Assistant United States Attorney, a prestigious award presented to only 12 attorneys from among the nation’s 93 United States Attorneys’ Offices. As the Southern District of Iowa’s Appellate Chief, Hanson prepares appellate briefs and presents oral arguments before the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. Hanson’s exemplary efforts have secured favorable results in significant cases involving a wide range of legal issues. Hanson also serves as an invaluable resource for the district’s trial attorneys facing complex and novel legal questions. “We are proud to work alongside AUSA Kyle Hanson in the Southern District of Iowa. Kyle provides exceptional appellate advocacy and rigorous legal analysis in every case. This national recognition reflects Kyle’s outstanding achievements over the past year and his ongoing dedication to the mission and values of the Department of Justice,” said United States Attorney David C. Waterman. Under the direction of the Deputy Attorney General, EOUSA provides oversight, general executive assistance, and direction to the 93 United States Attorneys’ Offices around the country. For more information on EOUSA and its mission, visit http://www.justice.gov/usao . title: Five Individuals Indicted for Firearms-Related Offenses
body: Press Release Five Individuals Indicted for Firearms-Related Offenses Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Nevada LAS VEGAS – The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Nevada announced that five individuals were indicted, and two more individuals made their initial appearances in court, all for crimes involving firearms. “The indictments handed down today represent a decisive strike against illegal gun violence,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada. “This office will not stand by while violent actors abuse firearms to terrorize our neighborhoods. If you unlawfully possess a firearm, if you traffic weapons, or if you use a gun to commit crimes in this district, federal law enforcement is coming for you. There will be no leniency. There will be no safe harbor.” A federal grand jury has indicted the following individuals. Lil Jarmarr Baker-Reed , of North Las Vegas, allegedly fired multiple rounds from a 9mm Ruger pistol at another individual. Some of those rounds hit a nearby restaurant. Baker-Reed has three prior felony convictions for burglary, grand larceny, and possession or transfer of a stolen vehicle. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. He is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. If convicted, Baker-Reed faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Kyle Fuller is prosecuting the case. Michael Kirk Brooks , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a 9mm P365 and possessed with intent to distribute methamphetamine. He has prior felony convictions for ownership or possession of a firearm by a prohibited person; battery resulting in substantial bodily harm constituting domestic violence; attempt of grand larceny; felon in possession of a firearm; and conspiracy to commit robbery, all in Clark County, Nevada. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. Brooks is charged with one count of possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, one count of possession of a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime, and one count of felon in possession of a firearm. If convicted, Brooks faces a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case. Jimmy Dean McFarland , of Las Vegas, allegedly robbed a store at gunpoint. McFarland has a prior felony conviction for robbery with the use of firearms. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. McFarland is charged with one count of interference with commerce by robbery, one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person, and one count of brandishing a firearm during and in relation to a crime of violence. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of life in prison. The FBI investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Melinda Brewer is prosecuting the case. A Las Vegas woman allegedly purchased a firearm for a Las Vegas man who is a prohibited person. Both are charged with one count of conspiracy to straw purchase firearms, false statement in acquisition of a firearm, aiding and abetting, and the woman is also charged with straw purchasing of firearms. If convicted, they each face a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Tina Snellings is prosecuting the case. Additionally, two men made their initial appearances in court on Wednesday for alleged violations of federal firearms laws. Dominic Flanagan , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a 9mm caliber pistol. He has prior felony convictions for battery by strangulation, attempted battery with a deadly weapon with substantial bodily harm, and armed robbery, all in Clark County, Nevada. He is prohibited by law from possessing a firearm. Flanagan is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. Jury trial is scheduled for January 4, 2027, before United States District Judge Cristina D. Silva. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The FBI investigated the case; and Assistant United States Attorney Melinda Brewer is prosecuting the case. Christiano Decarlo , of Las Vegas, allegedly possessed a .38 caliber firearm; a 12-gauge shotgun; a 410 bore firearm; and a 12-gauge shotgun. He has prior felony convictions for interfering with commerce by threat of violence and felon in possession of a firearm, both in Nevada. Decarlo is charged with one count of possession of a firearm by a prohibited person. Jury trial is scheduled for January 4, 2027, before United States District Judge Gloria M. Navarro. If convicted, he faces a maximum statutory penalty of 15 years in prison. The FBI investigated the case. The public may submit anonymous tips about gun crimes to ATF by calling 1-888-ATF-TIPS (1-888-283-8477) or by submitting a tip online at www.atf.gov/contact/atf-tips . An indictment merely contains accusations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. ### Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Drug Trafficking Firearms Offenses Component USAO - Nevada

title: Fayette County Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Federal Gun Crime
body: Press Release Fayette County Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Prison for Federal Gun Crime Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of West Virginia CHARLESTON, W.Va. – Eddie Daivon Morgan, also known as “Gutta,” 45, of Mount Hope, was sentenced today to 10 years in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release, for being a felon in possession of a firearm. According to court documents and statements made in court, on November 30, 2022, law enforcement officers had an active warrant for Morgan’s arrest on a malicious wounding charge when they observed him enter a vehicle in Fayette County. Officers conducted a traffic stop of the vehicle and found Morgan laying in the back seat of the vehicle. Officers seized a loaded Glock model 42 .380-caliber pistol and a loaded SCCY 9mm pistol from Morgan’s person. Federal law prohibits a person with a prior felony conviction from possessing a firearm or ammunition. Morgan knew he was prohibited from possessing a firearm because of his prior felony conviction for use of a communication facility to facilitate a drug trafficking offense in United States District Court for the Southern District of West Virginia on January 24, 2013. The warrant for Morgan’s arrest was issued after a November 18, 2022, confrontation between Morgan and another individual at a Fayette County residence. During the confrontation, a verbal altercation between Morgan and the other individual escalated when Morgan threatened to “shoot the place up.” Morgan later fired two rounds from a .380-caliber pistol, wounding the other individual in the arm. Morgan pleaded guilty to attempted second-degree murder, malicious assault, wanton endangerment involving a firearm, and use or presentation of a firearm during the commission of a felony in Fayette County Circuit Court on March 28, 2024. Morgan’s criminal history also includes prior convictions for second-degree manslaughter, second-degree assault, felony escape, wanton endangerment with a firearm, possession with intent to deliver a controlled substance within 1,000 feet of a school, battery, and domestic battery. United States Attorney Moore Capito made the announcement and commended the investigative work of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) and the Oak Hill Police Department. United States District Judge Irene C. Berger imposed the sentence. Assistant United States Attorney JC MacCallum prosecuted the case. This case is part of Operation Take Back America , a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. This case is also part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. A copy of this press release is located on the website of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of West Virginia. Related court documents and information can be found on PACER by searching for Case No. 2:23-cr-92. ### Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Operation Take Back America Project Safe Neighborhoods Firearms Offenses Component USAO - West Virginia, Southern

title: Castle Rock Man Sentenced to 450 Months In Prison After Pleading Guilty To Producing Child Sexual Abuse Material And Distribution
body: Press Release Castle Rock Man Sentenced to 450 Months In Prison After Pleading Guilty To Producing Child Sexual Abuse Material And Distribution Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Colorado DENVER – The United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Colorado announces that James Zachary Heath, 27, Castle Rock, was sentenced to 450 months in federal prison and a lifetime of supervised release after pleading guilty to one count of production of child pornography and one count of distribution of child pornography. According to the plea agreement and facts established at sentencing, the defendant came to the attention of law enforcement in July 2024 when a foreign law enforcement agency located an explicit video on the dark web of a man sexually abusing a toddler.  In September 2024, the foreign law enforcement agency found a longer compilation video that depicted the sexual abuse and exploitation of the minor and which ultimately led to the defendant being identified. “This lengthy prison sentence demonstrates how seriously the American justice system takes these horrendous crimes,” said United States Attorney Peter McNeilly.  “And I am glad this predator is out of our community for a very long time.” “Child sexual abuse material impacts not only the initial victims and their families, but it also feeds the abominable marketplace for the images and videos,” said FBI Denver Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski. “Child predators be on notice: The FBI and justice will find you. There is no place in our society for child exploitation.” The FBI Denver Field Division handled the investigation. Assistant United States Attorney Alecia L. Riewerts handled the prosecution. United States District Judge S. Kato Crews presided over the sentencing. This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the United States Attorney’s Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who sexually exploit children, and to identify and rescue victims.  For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit www.justice.gov/psc. For more information about Internet safety education, please visit www.justice.gov/psc and click on the "Resources" tab on the left of the page. Case Number: 1:24-cr-00309-SKC Contact USACO.PublicAffairs@usdoj.gov Updated November 5, 2026 Component USAO - Colorado

title: Federal Jury Convicts Dominican Republic Man of   Illegally Reentering the United States after having been Deported
body: Press Release Federal Jury Convicts Dominican Republic Man of   Illegally Reentering the United States after having been Deported Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Virgin Islands St. Thomas, USVI – U.S. Attorney Adam F. Sleeper announced today that a federal jury convicted Joan Manuel Tavarez Bueno, 34, of the Dominican Republic, for re-entry of a removed alien pursuant to 8 U.S.C. § 1326(a).  After a three-day trial, the defendant was convicted as charged. The defendant faces a statutory sentence of up to 24 months imprisonment. The Chief District Court Judge, Robert A. Molloy, will schedule a sentencing hearing to determine the sentence to be imposed. According to court documents and testimony presented at trial, on March 10, 2025, the defendant was a passenger in a vehicle that was stopped by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Special Agents during the course of an immigration investigation near Red Hook, St. Thomas. The defendant, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, was previously removed from the United States as an illegal alien from Miami, FL, on February 13, 2024. He then illegally re-entered the United States through St. John in November 2024 without first obtaining permission from the Secretary of Homeland Security. This case was investigated by HSI with the assistance of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorneys, Erik C. Tate, Kimberly Riley, and Criminal Chief Kyle Payne. Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Immigration Component USAO - Virgin Islands

The defendant faces a statutory sentence of up to 24 months imprisonment. The Chief District Court Judge, Robert A. Molloy, will schedule a sentencing hearing to determine the sentence to be imposed.

title: Illegal Alien from India Sentenced for Fraud Scheme Targeting Elderly Victims
body: Press Release Illegal Alien from India Sentenced for Fraud Scheme Targeting Elderly Victims Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maine Prakashkumar Prajapati defrauded eight victims in five states PORTLAND, Maine: An Indian national was sentenced yesterday in U.S. District Court in Portland for conspiring to commit wire fraud. Chief U.S. District Judge Lance E. Walker sentenced Prakashkumar Prajapati, 47, to nine years in prison and ordered him to pay $1,897,386 in restitution. Prajapati pleaded guilty on January 15, 2026. According to court records Prajapati conspired with others in a multi-state scheme to defraud at least eight victims in five states, including Maine. As part of the scheme, victims received telephone calls from individuals posing as government officials. These imposters instructed victims to withdraw cash and purchase gold to turn over to the government for safekeeping. The callers then arranged for victims to meet fake government agents to hand over the cash and gold. As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati directed his co-defendant Bharat Awasarmol to collect gold and cash from victims. Awasarmol was intercepted when FBI agents caught him accepting a package from a victim in Maine. The Maine victim had been instructed by an individual posing as an employee of the Federal Trade Commission to meet Awasarmol and provide him with gold bars. As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati and his coconspirators collected cash and gold from seven additional victims in New Hampshire, New York, New Jersey, and Virginia, all of whom had been deceived by individuals posing as government officials. As part of the conspiracy, Prajapati caused $1,897,386 in losses to the victims. Awasarmol pleaded guilty on December 9, 2025, and faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 on the wire fraud conspiracy charge and up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 on a false statement charge. Awasarmol is scheduled to be sentenced in January 2027. The FBI investigated the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (“Fraud Division”). The Fraud Division is investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice is committed to aggressively combating elder abuse, neglect, financial exploitation and fraud. Between July of 2025 and July of 2026, the Department pursued nearly 350 criminal and civil enforcement actions against 712 defendants either charged with stealing, or alleged to have stolen, over $4.8 billion from over 700,000 victims. The Department also returned millions of dollars to older victims and helped to prevent tens of millions of dollars in losses from older Americans. But enforcement alone is not enough. Preventing fraud and abuse in the first place is always the best outcome. For more information on elder fraud and abuse, visit the Department of Justice’s Elder Justice Initiative website at justice.gov/elderjustice. If you or someone you know has been the victim of elder fraud, please call the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 833-FRAUD-11. ### Contact Nicholas Scott, Assistant United States Attorney (Tel.: 207-780-3257) Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Fraud Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Maine

title: Missouri man sentenced for sexual meetup with FBI agent posing online as teen
body: Press Release Missouri man sentenced for sexual meetup with FBI agent posing online as teen Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Kansas KANSAS CITY, KAN. – A Missouri man was sentenced to seven years in prison for using the internet to arrange a sexual encounter with a minor without realizing he was actually communicating with an undercover Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agent. According to court documents, James D. Fishbaugh, 53, of Blue Springs, Missouri, pleaded guilty to one count of travel with intent to engage in illicit sexual conduct. In August 2025, Fishbaugh used a social media account to chat with an undercover FBI posing online as a minor living in Kansas. When the agent purported to be a 14-year-old girl, Fishbaugh responded by claiming he was 49. Fishbaugh then shifted the conversation to be sexual in nature. He asked “the girl” if she was a virgin and if she was “kinky.” Fishbaugh drove from his home in Missouri to a designated meeting place in Kansas, where agents arrested him and found condoms on his person.  Fishbaugh told officers that he believed he was talking to a 14-year-old girl and that he traveled to the residence to have sex with the minor. “Protecting children from sexual exploitation remains one of our highest priorities,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “The defendant continued pursuing what he believed was a sexual encounter with a 14-year-old child and took substantial steps to carry out that encounter. Thanks to the FBI’s proactive investigative work, he was stopped before any child could be victimized. Our office will continue working with our law enforcement partners to identify, investigate, and prosecute those who seek to exploit children.” The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Audrey McCormick prosecuted the case. Project Safe Childhood This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and CEOS, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to better locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . ### Updated November 5, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - Kansas

title: St. Louis Felon Who Fled from Police Sentenced to 110 Months in Prison
body: Press Release St. Louis Felon Who Fled from Police Sentenced to 110 Months in Prison Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Eastern District of Missouri ST. LOUIS – U.S. District Judge Joshua M. Divine on Thursday sentenced a convicted felon who was caught with drugs and a gun after fleeing from police to 110 months in prison. On August 26, 2025, the Missouri State Highway Patrol stopped Wendell Mosley, 36, in a Ford Taurus on U.S. Highway 67 in St. Francois County, Missouri. Mosley showed signs of deception and nervousness when asked about his reason for travelling. At one point, Mosley ran away from the trooper, hopped in his car and sped south on Highway 67. Mosley fled on foot after wrecking the car, discarding a bag before he was arrested. Troopers later found the bag, which contained a 9mm handgun and 232 capsules containing oxycodone. Mosley, now 36, pleaded guilty in August in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm and one count of possession with the intent to distribute oxycodone. The Missouri State Highway Patrol and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jolene Taaffe prosecuted the case. This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. Contact Robert Patrick, Public Affairs Officer, robert.patrick@usdoj.gov. Updated November 5, 2026 Topics Project Safe Neighborhoods Firearms Offenses Components Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) USAO - Missouri, Eastern

title: Federal judge sentences Wichita man to prison for setting fire to apartment
body: Press Release Federal judge sentences Wichita man to prison for setting fire to apartment Thursday, November 5, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Kansas WICHITA, KAN. – A Kansas man was sentenced to 77 months in prison for maliciously setting a fire that damaged an apartment building where families lived. According to court documents, Skyler D. Imel, 31, of Wichita, pleaded guilty to one count of arson. In March 2023, Imel intentionally damaged an apartment complex on West Central Avenue in Wichita by setting a fire inside the bedroom of a vacant unit.  Before starting the fire, Imel used a red Sharpie to write, “Sam apparment 2502 is geting killed” on the bedroom wall, and he disabled a smoke alarm. Imel attempted to set a second fire at apartment No. 2502 by throwing a Molotov Cocktail at the front entryway. That apartment was occupied at the time. “There were families living in the apartment complex so this incident could have easily turned into a horrific tragedy,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan A. Kriegshauser. “The fact that the defendant disabled the smoke detector indicates he wanted the fire to have time to spread before it was likely to be noticed, increasing the danger to the building’s residents.” The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives (ATF) and the Wichita Fire Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ola Odeyemi prosecuted the case. ### Updated November 5, 2026 Component USAO - Kansas

title: Isabel Schnabel: Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy
body:
Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Isabel Schnabel Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy Speech by Isabel Schnabel, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the ECB Conference on Money Markets 2026 Frankfurt am Main, 5 November 2026 The past seven years have been an extraordinary journey. [ 1 ] We have moved from a world in which inflation was persistently too low to one marked by recurrent inflationary shocks; from a historically accommodative monetary policy stance to the fastest tightening cycle in the history of the ECB; and from a deeply integrated global economy to one increasingly shaped by fragmentation and geopolitical tensions. As I reach the end of my journey here at the ECB, I would like to reflect on the lessons these experiences have taught me about the conduct of monetary policy in a world that has become less predictable. My remarks today are personal reflections on how the experience of recent years has shaped my thinking about monetary policy and what it may teach us about navigating the challenges ahead. There are four key takeaways. Takeaway one: preserve room for manoeuvre by avoiding commitments The first takeaway is that central banks should prioritise instruments that allow them to adjust monetary policy quickly as conditions change. We entered the pandemic after a long period in which inflation had been below our target (Slide 2, left-hand side). Globalisation, and the integration of China in particular, had structurally lowered the global cost of producing goods, putting downward pressure on inflation. At the same time, the global financial crisis and the sovereign debt crisis had weakened public and private balance sheets and left lasting scars on demand, weighing on economic activity and inflation. Over time, this experience gradually fostered the belief that these forces were permanent, leaving monetary policy primarily focused on bringing inflation back up to target. As a result, after chronically overpredicting inflation before the pandemic, we were slow to recognise that we had entered a new regime in which we would repeatedly underpredict it (Slide 2, right-hand side). Indeed, even as evidence of a more substantial and persistent rise in inflation was mounting, the initial reaction was one of relief: the economy finally seemed to be escaping the low-inflation environment. [ 2 ] But the rapid increase in the share of goods and services experiencing inflation above 2% signalled that price pressures were becoming increasingly broad-based (Slide 3). This exposed two key features of the inflation process that our analytical frameworks had not sufficiently accounted for. One was the steepening of the Phillips curve, which was in part a result of more frequent price changes as firms sought to protect their profit margins in the face of sharp cost increases (Slide 4). The other, related feature was the role of firms’ profits in inflation. Unlike the high-inflation period of the 1970s, when inflation was almost entirely driven by growth in unit labour costs, the post-pandemic inflation surge was to a significant extent driven by rising unit profits (Slide 5). [ 3 ] So, the pandemic was a structural break in many of the trends we had witnessed before. This included a shift in the global balance between savings and investment. Rising investment needs related to the green and digital transitions, alongside a changing geopolitical environment, have turned the savings glut of the past into a bond glut, as both private and public issuance have increased sharply. [ 4 ] This shift puts upward pressure not only on inflation but also on the natural rate of interest, r* (Slide 6, left-hand side). [ 5 ] None of these shocks or their consequences could have been predicted easily. The lesson is therefore that we should expect the unexpected – and avoid becoming too attached to a particular view of the world or a particular class of models. This has implications for the design and conduct of monetary policy. [ 6 ] We should be wary of commitments that depend too heavily on a particular economic environment or class of models, leaving little room to adjust when conditions change. Charles Goodhart – a distinguished scholar of monetary history who has seen the world change more than once – put it this way: “ The world changes, and if the world changes you need sufficient flexibility to change the way that you operate within that .” [ 7 ] In retrospect, forward guidance during the pandemic was too Odyssean. It tied our hands too closely to a world of persistently low inflation. The same applies to the choice of other policy instruments. Some instruments are inherently more agile than others. Policy rates can be adjusted swiftly at each meeting, whereas large-scale asset purchases continue to provide monetary accommodation long after the purchases themselves have ended (Slide 6, right-hand side). An instrument that is difficult to reverse is itself a form of commitment. That is also why we emphasise in our monetary policy strategy that our primary monetary policy instrument is the set of key policy rates. [ 8 ] This does not mean that asset purchases are never useful. [ 9 ] They are highly effective in stabilising financial markets that suddenly turn illiquid. And they remain a tool to counter deflationary pressures at the effective lower bound. One way to preserve flexibility is to separate instruments used to stabilise markets from those used to calibrate the monetary policy stance. [ 10 ] This can limit the scale of asset purchases and make them easier to unwind. The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) embodies this principle. It provides a dedicated tool to address unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that threaten the transmission of monetary policy, subject to clearly defined criteria. Takeaway two: what matters is how shocks affect the inflation outlook The second takeaway is that the appropriate monetary policy response to a shock primarily depends not on its nature, but on its implications for the projected inflation path. [ 11 ] Traditionally, the nature of the shock guided our thinking about how monetary policy should respond to price pressures. The standard prescription was that demand shocks called for an immediate response, while supply shocks could often be looked through, as the shock would either fade on its own or weaker growth would dampen emerging price pressures, reducing the need for monetary tightening. This distinction can be misleading, for two reasons. First, central banks rarely face one shock at a time. During the pandemic, supply chain disruptions, pent-up demand and unprecedented fiscal and monetary policy support interacted in ways that were difficult to disentangle (Slide 7, left-hand side). [ 12 ] Russia’s unjustified invasion of Ukraine added a major energy and food price shock to an already challenging environment. Such overlapping shocks can prolong the period of elevated inflation and make the “last mile” of disinflation particularly challenging. [ 13 ] Services inflation was still running above 3% before the start of the conflict in the Middle East, reflecting the drawn-out adjustment to the earlier inflation surge, including through staggered wage negotiations (Slide 7, right-hand side). Today, we again face overlapping shocks, from geopolitical tensions and rising energy prices to the rapid expansion of AI-related investment and large fiscal spending needs, including for defence. These developments affect demand, productive capacity, prices and financial conditions through different channels and over different horizons. Second, a sufficiently large and persistent adverse supply shock can push projected inflation above target, requiring a timely monetary policy response. What begins as a relative price adjustment can turn into a broader inflation problem through indirect price effects, wage dynamics and changes in inflation expectations. This is why we are closely monitoring these developments. In response to the latest energy shock, consumer inflation expectations over the medium to longer term have increased and gradually moved away from our 2% target (Slide 8). The lesson is therefore that monetary policy cannot be calibrated on the basis of simple classifications of shocks. What matters is how shocks affect the inflation outlook. This matters even more in a world in which adverse supply-side shocks are likely to become more frequent and persistent owing to geopolitical fragmentation and climate change. [ 14 ] The role of climate change for monetary policy has long been a source of contention. But the evidence is increasingly clear. More frequent floods, heatwaves and droughts lower agricultural yields, disrupt supply and damage infrastructure, all of which feed into price dynamics (Slide 9). [ 15 ] And “climateflation” is just one way in which climate change is becoming a challenge for price stability, bringing it squarely within our primary mandate. [ 16 ] So, for each shock, we need to assess its size and persistence, the state of the economy and the risk of inflation becoming entrenched in expectations and in price and wage-setting. The ECB’s response to the conflict in the Middle East reflects these lessons. ECB staff rapidly developed projection scenarios with varying assumptions about the indirect and second-round effects of the energy shock. Monetary policy, in turn, responded to the expected persistence of these inflationary pressures in a timely and forward-looking manner. As a result, we are now well positioned to address the current inflation challenge. Takeaway three: protect monetary dominance The third takeaway is that the ECB’s ability to fulfil its primary mandate relies on robust fiscal and regulatory frameworks that ensure monetary dominance. During the post-pandemic inflation surge, the ECB demonstrated its ability to tighten monetary policy forcefully, even though higher interest rates could have pushed the economy into recession or posed risks to fiscal and financial stability. The resilience of the banking sector was an essential condition for monetary policy to act as needed to restore price stability. This was largely thanks to the financial reforms introduced in the wake of the global financial crisis. Strong capital positions and healthy profitability allowed banks to absorb the rise in interest rates without coming under financial strain (Slide 10). Structural changes threaten monetary dominance Two developments, if left unchecked, could threaten monetary dominance in the future: first, structural changes in the financial sector, including the rise of non-bank finance; and second, the increase in public debt. [ 17 ] Over the past two decades, partly in response to tighter bank regulation, there has been a massive shift in the provision of financial services away from banks to non-bank financial intermediaries. Non-banks now hold financial assets on a par with those held by banks (Slide 11, left-hand side). [ 18 ] At the same time, euro area public debt as a share of GDP has increased by nearly 20 percentage points since the early 2000s, with large heterogeneity across member countries (Slide 11, right-hand side). This rise in part reflects the successive crises we have faced. Rising public debt is a global trend across advanced economies. The IMF projects government debt in the United States to rise to 145% of GDP in 2031, up from 124% last year. For China, it projects an increase to 122% over the same period, up from 99%. These two shifts interact in important ways. As central banks reduce the asset portfolios accumulated during years of monetary accommodation, a greater share of government debt must be absorbed by price-sensitive private investors. Hedge funds in particular are holding an increasing share of sovereign debt, often financed through repos, and they now play a key role in intermediating sovereign bond markets (Slide 12, left-hand side). As a result, monetary policy is transmitted more rapidly. [ 19 ] When policy tightens, higher interest rates will feed quickly into government financing costs through the higher funding costs of non-bank lenders. This dynamic is reinforced by governments shifting towards shorter debt maturities (Slide 12, right-hand side). At higher levels of public debt, however, non-linear effects are more likely to emerge. When volatility rises, falling collateral values, higher margin requirements or reduced access to funding can force leveraged investors to unwind their positions. The “dash for cash” episode in 2020 and the liability-driven investment (LDI) crisis in the United Kingdom in 2022 illustrated how such dynamics can destabilise sovereign bond markets, the bedrock of our financial system. To restore transmission, central banks may then be forced to stabilise markets to prevent a liquidity crisis from turning into a full-blown credit crisis, which would likely also spill over to the banking sector. [ 20 ] Such interventions can interfere with the central bank’s mandate and threaten monetary dominance. There are two lessons to be learned from this. Proper regulation reduces the risk of financial dominance First, a sound financial system reduces the risk of financial dominance. For this reason, governments should resist the current push towards deregulating the banking sector. [ 21 ] Many of the arguments put forward in favour of deregulation are flawed. Its benefits are doubtful and its potential costs are significant. Thanks to the reforms implemented following the global financial crisis, the banking system was an anchor of stability during recent shocks. Yet the shift of financial activity towards the less regulated non-bank sector has made the financial system more fragile. It also creates risks for banking sector stability: banks are closely interconnected with non-banks and increasingly rely on them as a source of funding, creating channels through which stress can spread across the financial system (Slide 13). Leverage, reliance on short-term funding and interconnectedness in core markets therefore require stronger oversight and a more effective macroprudential framework. Stronger regulation of non-banks would also bolster the case for considering their access to central bank facilities, which could further support systemic stability. Consolidation and growth reduce the risk of fiscal dominance Second, prudent fiscal policy reduces the risk of fiscal dominance. In the changed interest rate environment, it has become more difficult to put public finances back on a sustainable path. This challenge is well illustrated by the evolution of the differential between the effective interest rate paid on debt, r , and the economy’s growth rate, g . For years, r-g was negative (Slide 14, left-hand side). Such an environment allows governments to bring debt ratios down, even when running primary deficits. But the differential has now turned positive in many countries and is likely to rise further as governments refinance maturing debt at today’s higher interest rates. At the same time, potential growth in the euro area has been on a declining trend and is expected to weaken further (Slide 14, right-hand side). Population ageing is weighing on labour supply, while investment and productivity growth are unlikely to be strong enough to offset the resulting drag on potential growth. Efforts are therefore needed on both sides of the r-g differential. On the r side, a credible fiscal path helps contain both risk premia and interest rate expenditure. The best contribution the ECB can make is to keep the inflation risk premium low by ensuring that inflation expectations remain firmly anchored (Slide 15, left-hand side). On the g side, the euro area needs to regain competitiveness. [ 22 ] For a long time, productivity growth in the euro area has been weaker than in the United States (Slide 15, right-hand side). Achieving a lasting improvement requires progress on two fronts: strengthening Europe’s capacity to innovate and enabling the diffusion of new technologies across the economy. Both depend on scale. Boosting innovation requires an environment that allows promising ideas to grow into successful businesses on a European scale. Yet fragmented capital markets make it harder for firms to secure financing as they grow, while fragmented product markets limit the potential returns for investors. These obstacles reinforce each other: investors hesitate to finance companies that cannot scale up, while companies struggle to scale up without access to sufficient capital. The Single Market is critical to breaking this cycle. A product that can be sold across a market of more than 450 million Europeans offers a much greater growth opportunity than one that can be sold only in one country. Yet, despite decades of integration, barriers within the Single Market remain substantial. ECB estimates suggest that internal barriers are equivalent to tariffs of 96% for services and 67% for goods (Slide 16). A powerful step towards overcoming this fragmentation is a 28th regime: a unified European corporate framework that lowers barriers to cross-border activity, makes it easier to raise capital and attract talent, and allows innovative companies to scale up more quickly across the European Union. [ 23 ] The proposal currently under discussion could be an important step in that direction. A watered-down version, by contrast, would risk becoming another lost opportunity. But innovation alone is not enough. Productivity also depends on how effectively existing and new technologies are adopted throughout the economy. Here, too, scale matters. Smaller firms tend to be less productive, partly because they lack the resources to cover the fixed costs of adopting new technologies (Slide 17, left-hand side). This is particularly urgent as AI opens up new possibilities to transform production and raise productivity (Slide 17, right-hand side). Europe cannot afford to repeat the experience of the digital revolution of the 1990s and 2000s, when it was slow to adopt and exploit new technologies at scale. [ 24 ] The ECB is playing its part by introducing the digital euro and by harnessing distributed ledger technology (DLT) and tokenisation to future-proof Europe’s wholesale financial markets, reduce fragmentation and modernise the implementation of monetary policy. [ 25 ] These efforts will support strategic autonomy and help safeguard Europe against excessive reliance on foreign currency-denominated stablecoins, which could undermine monetary sovereignty and create risks for financial stability. [ 26 ] Takeaway four: implement monetary policy efficiently The fourth takeaway is that monetary policy should be implemented efficiently with a balance sheet that is no larger than necessary. In the wake of the global financial crisis, many central banks moved towards operating with abundant reserves. They did so not because this was necessarily their preferred way of implementing monetary policy, but as a consequence of large-scale asset purchases. By buying assets on a massive scale, central banks injected far more reserves into the system than banks needed to satisfy their liquidity demands. This came at a cost. Private market activity was displaced, asset prices were distorted and central banks, and thus ultimately taxpayers, were exposed to financial risks. [ 27 ] At one point, the scarcity of safe assets in the euro area was so acute that rates on some specialised repo transactions traded at a premium of more than 50 basis points above the ECB’s deposit facility rate (Slide 18, left-hand side). Abundant reserves also changed the liability structure of bank balance sheets. As reserves were injected into the system, banks issued more short-term, uninsured deposits. But these claims on liquidity did not decline in step with reserves when central banks subsequently reduced their balance sheets (Slide 18, right-hand side). [ 28 ] This created a ratchet effect. Banks became more dependent on central bank liquidity, potentially making the system more vulnerable in periods of stress. This experience highlights the limits of the Friedman rule in practice: supplying reserves abundantly is not without costs. There are two lessons from this. The first is that, as part of quantitative normalisation, we are winding down the portfolios accumulated under the asset purchase programme (APP) and the pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP). The monetary policy motivation for these portfolios no longer exists. In principle, we can reduce them all the way to zero, unless we were to return to the effective lower bound, in which case renewed purchases might become necessary to protect price stability. The second lesson is that banks are best placed to assess their own liquidity needs. The central bank should ensure that these needs can be met on appropriate terms, while encouraging banks to tap private funding markets before accessing central bank facilities. The ECB’s new operational framework reflects this insight. [ 29 ] Every week banks can request as much liquidity as they need through our standard refinancing operations at a fixed rate and against a broad set of collateral. As excess liquidity continues to decline, we expect banks to make increasing use of these operations. Accessing central bank refinancing operations will again become a normal part of banks’ liquidity management, without any stigma attached to it. [ 30 ] The recent standard refinancing operations covering the month and year-end were encouraging. They attracted significant demand from a broad set of banks. Over time, the take-up of our standard refinancing operations will give us valuable information about banks’ demand for reserves. In particular, if the amounts requested continue to rise and remain elevated, this will indicate that an increasing share of banks’ borrowing reflects persistent liquidity needs rather than temporary fluctuations. At that point, it would make sense to meet the more stable part of this demand through structural operations rather than requiring banks to roll over large amounts every week. Complementing our regular operations with structural liquidity-providing instruments, including longer-term refinancing operations and a structural securities portfolio, will provide banks with a more stable source of liquidity. In my reading, the current structure of the ECB’s balance sheet implies the following sequence in this transition. [ 31 ] As the sizeable legacy APP and PEPP portfolios will continue to provide liquidity for a long time, it is natural to begin by introducing structural longer-term refinancing operations. In addition, the Eurosystem holds assets for non-monetary policy purposes, which also contribute to the supply of reserves. Once the legacy portfolios have run off sufficiently, a structural securities portfolio will gradually be built. So, liquidity demand will ultimately be satisfied through a mix of instruments, also reflecting that part of bank’s liquidity needs is driven by autonomous factors beyond their control. But the fundamental principle will remain unchanged: the marginal unit of liquidity will be supplied through our standard refinancing operations in response to banks’ demand, rather than being injected at the central bank’s initiative. The advantage is that we do not need to estimate banks’ liquidity needs in advance or maintain an additional buffer in the face of uncertainty about the amount of liquidity the system requires. If calibrated appropriately, such a framework can achieve the best of both worlds: efficiently implementing monetary policy with fewer side effects, while ensuring that banks have the liquidity they need. Conclusion Let me conclude by bringing together the four takeaways from these reflections. First, preserving room for manoeuvre allows monetary policy to respond quickly when circumstances change in unexpected ways. Second, monetary policy should respond to the implications of shocks for the inflation outlook, not to their nature. Third, safeguarding monetary dominance allows central banks to act decisively when price stability is at risk. And finally, implementing monetary policy efficiently with a balance sheet that is no larger than necessary reduces side effects, preserves future policy space and fosters market activity. These four takeaways reflect what the past seven years have taught me about conducting monetary policy in a volatile world. The economic environment will keep changing. But the experience built over recent years leaves the ECB well equipped to navigate any stormy waters ahead, while remaining firmly focused on what ultimately matters: price stability. Thank you very much. I would like to warmly thank my Counsellors, Tobias Blattner and Johannes Gräb, for their extraordinary support and commitment.
