title: Piero Cipollone: Shaping the future of money
body:
Shaping the future of money Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date Piero Cipollone Member of the ECB's Executive Board SPEECH Shaping the future of money Keynote speech by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the eighth International Conference of Regional Card Schemes and Retail Financial Market Infrastructures Tirana, 5 November 2026 Money connects people and societies. But to do this, it must be trusted. It must allow people and businesses to transact safely and efficiently. And it must evolve with geopolitical and technological developments. For centuries, central banks have issued money and safeguarded its value. That mandate remains unchanged. But the environment in which money is used is being transformed. People are increasingly paying digitally. Tokenisation could reorganise the financial value chain. New solutions are being considered to enhance cross-border payments. And geopolitical fragmentation is making the resilience and governance of critical infrastructure ever more important. Central banks must therefore ensure that the money they issue remains fit for the future. This does not mean replacing the private sector or predicting which technology will prevail. It means providing a trusted public foundation for payments and finance on which private innovation can flourish. And it means preventing digitalisation from increasing fragmentation or creating new dependencies. This is why the Eurosystem has adopted a comprehensive payments strategy. [ 1 ] The strategy has four objectives: ensuring that central bank money can continue to settle retail and wholesale transactions as preferences and technologies evolve; strengthening Europe’s resilience and strategic autonomy; fostering an integrated, competitive and innovative payments ecosystem; and supporting the international role of the euro. In other words, we are seeking to comprehensively upgrade money and payments in Europe. The Western Balkans are also taking active policy steps to enhance and integrate payments in the region. Several countries, including Albania, have already joined the Single Euro Payments Area. And a clone of the Eurosystem’s fast payment system (TIPS), developed by Banca d’Italia, is already fully operational in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro and will soon be launched in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia. It allows real-time, low-cost domestic transactions in local currencies around the clock, every day of the year. This represents real, tangible progress that people will benefit from in their daily lives. But we must always think one step ahead. So today, I will discuss four key initiatives we are working on. We are modernising euro banknotes. We are developing a digital euro. We are making it possible to settle tokenised asset transactions in central bank money and creating the conditions for an integrated and innovative tokenised finance ecosystem. And we are interlinking fast payment systems to make cross-border payments faster and more efficient. These initiatives have a common goal: ensuring access to safe public money while creating space for private innovation and international cooperation. Modernising euro banknotes Let me begin with the most familiar form of central bank money: cash. In discussions about digitalisation, cash is sometimes talked about as a technology of the past. That is a mistake. In an age where cyber risks, hybrid threats and system outages make the headlines, cash remains the most resilient form of payment we have. More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation. People do not just see cash as a means of payment; they also view it as a store of value and a safeguard in periods of uncertainty. And it is one of the most tangible symbols of European unity. Moreover, cash is inclusive and simple to use, as it does not require a device or an intermediary. It protects privacy. And, most importantly, it gives people freedom of choice. That is why Europe is not choosing between cash and digital payments. We are investing in both. The Single Currency Package reflects this approach. [ 2 ] Alongside the proposed Regulation on the establishment of a digital euro, it includes a proposed Regulation on the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins. The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have adopted their respective positions, and the interinstitutional negotiations are under way. But protecting cash is not enough. We must also prepare it for the future. The next generation of euro banknotes will incorporate enhanced security features, have a smaller environmental impact and improve accessibility. We also want Europeans to feel that their banknotes reflect the cultural identity and natural environment they share. This summer, almost ten million people shared their views in a public survey on the ten shortlisted design proposals. Two-thirds of the responses came from people under the age of 35. [ 3 ] This remarkable level of participation shows that Europeans continue to care deeply about their banknotes. The ECB’s Governing Council expects to decide on the final design concept around the end of this year. The future euro banknotes should enter circulation gradually from the early 2030s, while existing banknotes will remain valid. So the future of public money will remain physical. But it must also be digital. Preparing a future-ready digital euro Today, central bank money is only available to the public as cash. But physical cash cannot be used online or for the ever-growing range of digital transactions. Europe also lacks a digital solution that can be used for everyday payments across the euro area. Digital payments remain fragmented along national lines and use cases. And we have a strategic dependency: 13 euro area countries rely entirely on non-European companies for in-store card payments. The digital euro would remedy this situation. It would be a digital form of cash issued by the Eurosystem, available and accepted throughout the euro area. It would complement banknotes and coins, not replace them. It could be used in shops, online and between individuals. It would work both online and offline. Basic use would be free for consumers. And we are designing it to provide high levels of security, privacy, accessibility and resilience. The offline functionality would allow payments to be made without an internet connection. It would also offer cash-like privacy, as the personal transaction details would be known only to the payer and payee. For online transactions, the Eurosystem would not know the individuals involved in the payment. The digital euro would therefore preserve people’s freedom to pay with central bank money as the economy becomes more digital. But it would do more than provide another payment option. It would create a common public infrastructure and acceptance layer for European payments. Payment service providers could build on that infrastructure and use the digital euro’s open standards to offer services throughout the euro area. The digital euro would help private European payment solutions expand beyond their current geographical and functional boundaries. It would lower investment costs and allow providers to focus investment on customer-facing innovation. And beyond the euro area, the digital euro standards and rulebook could provide a useful blueprint for countries that are considering developing a domestic scheme for digital payments. This would facilitate interoperability with the digital euro in the future. The objective of the digital euro is not to displace private payment solutions. On the contrary, it will provide a common foundation on which the private sector can compete, innovate and achieve European scale. Banks and other supervised payment service providers would remain the main point of contact for users. They would distribute the digital euro and provide customer services. The Eurosystem would not charge scheme or processing fees. This will generate savings for banks, merchants – especially small ones – and ultimately consumers. We are also designing safeguards to ensure that the digital euro functions as a means of payment rather than a form of investment. It would not be remunerated, and individual holdings would be limited. But this would not restrict transactions: a waterfall system with a linked bank account would ensure that amounts above the holding limit can be sent or received. Where the project stands The legislative process is advancing. The Council of the EU agreed its position in December 2025, the European Parliament adopted its position in July 2026 and the trilogue negotiations are now under way. The European Council has called for the negotiations to be concluded by the end of this year. Assuming the legislative process is concluded by the end of 2026, we aim to be ready for a potential first issuance in 2029. But technical preparations must advance in parallel. The digital euro pilot is planned to start in the second half of 2027 and will run for 12 months. We have selected 36 payment service providers from across the euro area following a call that attracted more than 50 applications. [ 4 ] Preparatory work is well under way. The objective is not simply to test technology. A payments system is an ecosystem comprising service providers, merchants, central banks, infrastructure operators and users. The pilot will allow the members of this ecosystem to test the design of the digital euro, learn from experience and identify improvements. On 15 September we launched a call inviting e-commerce and mobile-commerce merchants to take part in the pilot. The selected merchants will test customer payment journeys, assess integration with existing checkout systems and provide feedback on the user experience. [ 5 ] The digital euro is not merely a fix for existing shortcomings in the euro area payments landscape. It is a solution for the future. It will provide a platform to innovate and enhance the quality and breadth of payment services. New opportunities are arising. We want to make sure that European payment service providers are in the best position to seize them and gain a strong competitive edge. Against this backdrop, we recently launched a new wave of activities through the digital euro innovation platform, building on a first wave that involved around 70 market participants. [ 6 ] One workstream will experiment with integrated electronic receipts, payments involving multiple payers or recipients, conditional payments and new features offered through payment apps. A second workstream will look further ahead, exploring developments that could enhance the digital euro in future releases. This includes possible applications of artificial intelligence, such as AI agent-enabled payments or micropayments, and possible uses of a digital euro in interactions with public services, for example when paying for transportation, mobility and parking services. We cannot know precisely how Europeans will want to pay 20 years from now. But we can build a foundation that is open to innovation, robust enough to earn public trust and able to evolve with users’ needs. Pontes and Appia: supporting tokenised finance Our third initiative concerns digital finance. By allowing assets to be represented as digital files, tokenisation could change how they are issued, traded, settled, held and serviced. Today, these activities often take place across separate infrastructures and ledgers. Tokenisation could bring them into a shared digital environment, allowing smart contracts to automate processes and generating efficiency gains that could reduce costs and lower the barriers for smaller firms to access finance. But market participants have been clear that tokenised finance needs a safe settlement asset. Private instruments such as stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits can play useful roles. But central bank money provides risk-free final settlement and a common reference that private forms of money can be converted into at par. It ensures that one euro remains one euro, no matter its issuer, form or underlying technology. Pontes: an operational bridge The Eurosystem launched Pontes on 21 September. Pontes connects market distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms with the Eurosystem’s TARGET Services, enabling wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. It builds on the Eurosystem’s exploratory work in 2024, in which 64 participants conducted more than 50 trials and experiments and settled almost €1.6 billion in central bank money. That work demonstrated the feasibility of central bank money settlement for DLT-based transactions and confirmed strong market demand for a risk-free settlement asset. Pontes is now live with an initial group of market participants and DLT operators. On Monday, Pontes settled a €1 billion transaction in benchmark bonds successfully issued on DLT by the European Stability Mechanism. [ 7 ] Many other national and supernational institutions, including the World Bank, are preparing to issue on DLT and possibly settle in Pontes. Current Pontes services will be expanded gradually, with enhanced features, such as immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform and longer operating hours, being introduced as we move towards 24/7/365 availability in 2028. Pontes provides a dependable settlement foundation for tokenised securities and helps connect private tokenised settlement assets to central bank money. Appia: designing an integrated ecosystem With tokenisation, we have an opportunity to create an integrated market for digital assets from the outset, which would help address the fragmentation of Europe’s capital markets. But technology does not guarantee integration. It could instead produce incompatible platforms, closed networks and fragmented pools of assets and liquidity. For assets and services to interact across platforms, common standards are needed. Liquidity and collateral must be able to move. And the legal framework must provide clarity on issues such as ownership, settlement finality, custody and smart contracts. That is why we launched our Appia project. Appia addresses the architecture, standards and governance of a European tokenised financial ecosystem. It combines analysis, experimentation and public-private cooperation with the aim of delivering a blueprint in 2028. [ 8 ] The market is actively contributing to this work. The public consultation on the Appia roadmap received 127 responses, and 90% of respondents made at least one proposal to contribute. [ 9 ] Pontes and Appia are therefore two parts of one strategy. Pontes provides a bridge that makes it possible to settle DLT-based transactions in central bank money, while Appia is designing the digital finance ecosystem of tomorrow. Interlinking fast payment systems Our fourth initiative concerns cross-border payments. Domestic payments have become dramatically faster. Yet international payments often remain slow, expensive and opaque. High costs reduce the value of remittances. And long payment chains complicate trade, particularly for smaller businesses. Our approach is to connect the fast payment systems that central banks and the private sector have already built. This will help lower the cost of payments and make them faster. TIPS, the Eurosystem’s instant payment settlement service, settles payments in central bank money around the clock. It already supports the euro, the Swedish krona and the Danish krone, with the Norwegian krone and Icelandic króna set to join in the coming years. Its cross-currency service has been available since October 2025. In July the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Central Bank of Montenegro successfully launched a platform for the settlement of instant payments, which uses TIPS technology. The number of transactions is increasing each day: on Monday it was already close to 30,000 transactions per day. Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia are expected to join soon, bringing all countries participating in the initiative onto the platform. This will help to modernise payments in the region and support its integration. We are now working to connect TIPS with payment systems globally. Interlinking enables fast payment systems to communicate. People can continue using their existing bank and payment arrangements, while transfers reach beneficiaries connected to another jurisdiction’s system. This can shorten payment chains and reduce costs. It also respects monetary sovereignty because participating jurisdictions retain control of their currencies and domestic infrastructures. Interlinking therefore offers a practical model of international cooperation: strengthening connections without surrendering sovereignty. Work is advancing on a bilateral link with India’s Unified Payments Interface, the largest fast payment system in the world by transaction volume. We are also examining a potential connection to Nexus Global Payments, which will connect fast payment systems in South-East Asia, and exploring links with the instant payment systems of Switzerland and Brazil. Last week, the leaders of EU and Canada also indicated that they would support work towards connecting instant payment systems to facilitate faster, lower-cost and more seamless transactions across the two economies. [ 10 ] As for the Western Balkans, at least two tracks can be envisaged: the first and most straightforward is full integration in the EU. In that case the reference model would be Sweden and Denmark until the eventual adoption of euro. The alternative would be exploring possible interlinking with TIPS, once the business case justifies the investment. In any case, the TIPS clone should by its very nature already support integration, as payment services providers operating in both the euro area and the Western Balkans will be using two platforms that are technically very similar. This would make it easier for them to provide traditional correspondent banking services. Conclusion Let me conclude. The four initiatives I have presented today are different dimensions of the same transformation. We are making sure that central bank money remains fit for purpose as preferences, technologies and the geopolitical landscape evolve. Modernising banknotes ensures that public money remains tangible, inclusive and resilient. The digital euro would make public money available for digital payments and create a European infrastructure that private payment service providers can use as a platform for innovation. Pontes and Appia ensure that central bank money remains the settlement anchor as financial markets adopt tokenisation. And interlinking fast payment systems connects jurisdictions while respecting their monetary sovereignty. The future of money will not be defined by a single instrument or a single technology. It will involve physical and digital money, public and private solutions, and domestic and cross-border infrastructures. It will be shaped by the choices we make about trust, openness, resilience and sovereignty. These choices will determine whether Europe can once again be a cradle of monetary innovation. Our responsibility as central banks is to ensure that these elements form a coherent, trusted and resilient monetary system. We cannot merely observe the transformation of money from the sidelines. We have a duty to shape it in the public interest. Thank you. ECB (2026), The Eurosystem's comprehensive payments strategy . title: November 5, 2026 - FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to a New Treatment for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
body: FDA News Release FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to a New Treatment for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma For Immediate Release: November 05, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval to Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for the treatment of adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy. HNSCC is an aggressive, life-threatening disease for which there is a high unmet need for effective therapies. Rybrevant Faspro is not indicated as a treatment for patients with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma that is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV). Approval was based on trial results showing that more than double the percentage of patients responded to the drug compared to currently approved therapies. This is the first approval in 10 years of a drug for patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC who had received prior platinum-based chemotherapy. “Today’s approval represents a meaningful step forward for patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, a disease where treatment options have historically been limited and outcomes remain poor,” said Angelo De Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “This therapy offers patients and their physicians a new option with the potential to make a real difference in people’s lives.” The Accelerated Approval Program allows for earlier approval of drugs that treat serious conditions and fill an unmet medical need based on surrogate or intermediate endpoints. In this case, accelerated approval of Rybrevant Faspro was granted based on overall response rate and duration of response. Since it is not yet confirmed whether this will translate into a clinically meaningful benefit in long-term outcomes, the FDA has required confirmatory studies to verify and describe clinical benefit. In an open-label, multicenter clinical trial involving 102 patients with recurrent or metastatic HNSCC, Rybrevant Faspro had an overall response rate of 42%, meaning these patients saw their tumor either decrease in size or disappear. Of those patients who had a response, 56% had a response lasting six months or longer. Currently approved therapies are associated with an overall response rate of around 20% or less and poor outcomes. The prescribing information for use as a single agent includes warnings and precautions for hypersensitivity and administration-related reactions, interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis, dermatologic adverse reactions, ocular toxicity, and harm to an unborn baby. The FDA granted Rybrevant Faspro Breakthrough Therapy designation for this indication. The approval was granted to Janssen Biotech, Inc. Media: FDA Request for Comment 202-690-6343 Consumer: 888-INFO-FDA The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products. ###

title: Operation Economic Outcast Targets Global Maritime Fraud Network Supporting Iranian Regime
body: November 4, 2026 Network Circumvented Maritime Law to Enable Iran’s Shadow Fleet WASHINGTON —Today, as part of Operation Economic Outcast, the U.S. Department of the Treasury targeted the vast criminal network of India-based Suniel Kumar Sharma and his spouse, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid , who have supported Iran’s shadow fleet through a web maritime fraud. Their schemes have provided false flags and certifications to sanctioned vessels involved in transporting Iranian petroleum, including vessels operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies. “As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent .  “We know where you are, and we will sanction those who continue supporting the Iranian regime, whether by land, sea, or air.” False flags and fake maritime certifications allow vessels engaging in illicit activity to evade international regulations aimed at ensuring crew safety and safeguarding against environmental harm.  Falsely flagged vessels carry no valid protection and indemnity insurance, meaning that Iranian shadow fleet vessels operating under false flags could potentially cause billions of dollars in damages to the economies of the countries in whose territorial waters they operate. OFAC today also sanctioned Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc for its ongoing services in support of Iran’s aviation sector. Treasury has repeatedly warned that it will take action against those who continue to support Iran’s aviation industry, a key enabler of the regime’s destabilizing proliferation and terrorist activity. Concurrently with these designations, OFAC is issuing a new alert to industry to warn of the sanctions risks of dealing with potentially falsely flagged vessels, reemphasizing previous warnings from Treasury to the maritime industry to screen against unscrupulous actors such as Sharma and the vessels his network supports.  OFAC’s action also follows through on Treasury’s previous warning that any foreign firm or individual enabling sanctioned Iranian airlines—including through aircraft transfers, cargo services, or general sales agent support—will face serious consequences for supporting the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism.  The designations imposed today are being taken pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy. OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST IS ISOLATING THE IRANIAN REGIME Announced by Secretary Bessent on August 24, 2026 and dubbed Economic D-Day , Operation Economic Outcast is severing the remaining economic lifelines that sustain the Iranian regime.  Treasury has mapped the networks, facilitators, and financial channels that Iran uses to smuggle oil, evade sanctions, and fund terror.  Working with partners across the U.S. government, the European Union, United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds. Operation Economic Outcast significantly expanded sanctions risk for those who continue to choose to do business with Iran.  Treasury warned that any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the U.S. financial system. Operation Economic Outcast also expanded sanctions exposure for non-U.S. persons who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and will accelerate the pace of U.S. enforcement. More information on Operation Economic Outcast is available here . SHARMA CRIMINAL NETWORK For years, Suniel Kumar Sharma (Sharma) and his wife, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid (Shahid), have, through their base in Chandigarh, India, defrauded maritime regulatory administrations in multiple jurisdictions in order to establish false flagging authorities and maritime classification societies.  Purporting to represent nations from nearly every continent, from Guyana to Eswatini and Laos, Sharma and Shahid have allowed the Iranian shadow fleet, including those operating on behalf of the Iranian military and its proxies, to evade international restrictions on their operation. Sharma and Shahid’s operations began as early as 2014, when the couple sought to impersonate the flagging authority of the Caribbean nation of Dominica.  In 2023, Sharma established the Singapore-based Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. (Eswatini Maritime), which, despite being publicly disavowed by Eswatini authorities, continues to provide flagging services for vessels transporting Iranian petroleum, including the sanctioned vessel PING SHUN (IMO 9231901) , which at the time of its sanctioning had engaged in multiple shipments of Iranian oil. Many of Sharma and Shahid’s false flagging registries are not tied to registered companies, however.  In each case, the Sharma network purchases web domains, creating websites that claim to offer a variety of services on behalf of a country that has not authorized it to provide any of those services.  The services often include flagging, seafarer training and certification, and vessel classification, all of which are traditionally handled by legitimate organizations that hold vessels to strict international standards. Sharma’s network can be tied to multiple active websites that purport to belong to legitimate flagging registries.  Among these false representations are websites purporting to provide flagging services on behalf of Aruba, Guyana, Mali, Mozambique, Malawi, Sint Maarten, and Timor-Leste, among others.  Sanctioned shadow fleet vessels have since gravitated towards these registries despite widespread awareness that they are not endorsed by the relevant governments.  For example, on April 22, 2026, the U.S. Department of War seized the false Guyana-flagged MAJESTIC X, formerly known as the PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was carrying Iranian oil at the time of its boarding. Sharma and Shahid additionally manage a network of primarily India-based entities, some of which are used to establish fraudulent flagging registries.  Sharma is the managing director of India-based Oceaniek Technologies India , a company he has used to establish duplicitous flag registries, including those purporting to belong to Aruba, Nicaragua, and Sint Maarten.  Through these fraudulent registries Sharma has provided false flags to numerous sanctioned vessels that transport Iranian petroleum products, including LATTAFA (IMO 9245794), BINARY STAR (IMO 9380570) , and VERA (IMO 9304655) . As Sharma’s activities have garnered greater attention, Shahid has stepped in to manage—at least on paper—the pair’s business empire, which includes companies ranging from financial services businesses to media streaming platforms.  Following press coverage of his activities, Sharma has closed down multiple deceitful registries, including the Laos Ship Registry and Maritime Safety Administration, previously known as the International Maritime Safety Agency of Guyana, a company that served as a false flagging agency for Guyana and was likely intended to similarly impersonate the Laotian government. In addition to Shahid, Indian nationals Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh nominally serve as directors of Sharma’s businesses, including India-based Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited . Suniel Kumar Sharma is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy.  Jaspreet Preeti Shahid is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, Suniel Kumar Sharma. Eswatini Maritime Affairs and International Ship Registry PTE. Ltd. is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid. Oceaniek Technologies India is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Suniel Kumar Sharma. Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited is being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid.  Ashwani Kumar Dhiman and Ishwinder Singh are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Aryavart Ship Management Private Limited. In addition, the following India-based companies are being designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for being owned or controlled by, or having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, Jaspreet Preeti Shahid: Precept Trends Private Limited ; Polynesia Maritime Private Limited ; Alexarya Finserv Private Limited ; Alexarya Media and Entertainment Private Limited ; Viharaboating Private Limited ; and Aryavart Maritime and Educational Trust . GROUND HANDLING COMPANY SUPPORTING IRANIAN AIRLINES On August 24, 2026, Treasury issued determinations pursuant to E.O. 13902 against critical sectors––including aviation––that the Iranian regime uses to try to prop up its economy.  As Treasury has repeatedly highlighted, Iran uses its supposed “commercial” airlines, many of which are controlled by the regime and its military, to ferry fighters, ship weapons and sensitive technologies, and move gold and cash to its proxies.  Today, OFAC is taking action against a Türkiye-based ground handling company that continues to service sanctioned Iranian airlines, despite Treasury’s warnings of the sanctions risks associated with supporting Iran’s aviation sector. Türkiye-based Fugo Ground Services Inc provides ground handling and other services to several U.S.-designated Iranian airlines that continue to fly to Türkiye.  Fugo Ground Services Inc has direct service agreements with U.S.-sanctioned Iranian carriers including Iran Air Tour, Saha Airlines, Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Taban Airlines, and Ata Airlines Company, and began providing services to several of these carriers in the weeks after their September 8, 2026 designations . OFAC is designating Fugo Ground Services Inc pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the aviation sector of the Iranian economy. SANCTIONS IMPLICATIONS As a result of today’s action, all property and interests in property of the designated or blocked persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC.  In addition, any entities that are owned, directly or indirectly, individually or in the aggregate, 50 percent or more by one or more blocked persons are also blocked.  OFAC’s regulations generally prohibit all transactions, unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or exempt, by U.S. persons or within (or transiting) the United States that involve any property or interests in property of blocked persons. Violations of U.S. sanctions may result in the imposition of civil or criminal penalties on U.S. and foreign persons.  OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations on a strict liability basis. OFAC’s Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines provide more information regarding OFAC’s enforcement of U.S. economic sanctions.  The prohibitions include the making of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services by, to, or for the benefit of any designated or blocked person, or the receipt of any contribution or provision of funds, goods, or services from any such person.  Non-U.S. persons are also prohibited from causing U.S. persons to wittingly or unwittingly violate U.S. sanctions, as well as engaging in conduct that evades or conspires to violate U.S. sanctions.  Individuals located in the U.S. or abroad who provide information about sanctions violations to FinCEN’s whistleblower incentive program may be eligible for awards if the information they provide leads to a successful enforcement action that results in monetary penalties exceeding $1,000,000.  Financial institutions and other persons may risk exposure to sanctions for engaging in certain transactions or activities with designated or otherwise blocked persons, including the persons designated today.  This includes, in addition to blocking prohibitions, that OFAC can prohibit or impose strict conditions on opening or maintaining, in the United States, a correspondent account or a payable-through account of a foreign financial institution that knowingly conducts or facilitates any significant transaction on behalf of a person who is designated pursuant to the relevant authority. title: Summary of the RTGS CHAPS Industry Forum - 13 October 2026
body:
Summary of the RTGS CHAPS Industry Forum - 13 October 2026 | Bank of England – the UK's central bank Our use of cookies We use necessary cookies to make our site work. We’d also like to use some non-essential cookies (including third-party cookies) to help us improve the site. By clicking ‘Accept recommended settings’ on this banner, you accept our use of analytics cookies.   For more information on how these cookies work please see our Cookie policy . Accept recommended cookies Proceed with necessary cookies only Skip to main content Summary of the RTGS CHAPS Industry Forum - 13 October 2026 The second meeting of the RTGS CHAPS Industry Forum Published on  
        04 November 2026 Summary Date of meeting: 13 October 2026 Item 1: Introductions In the chair’s absence, the meeting was chaired by the Bank’s Head of Payment Delivery, who noted this was the second RTGS CHAPS industry forum. Minutes of the June meeting had been published. Item 2: Tokenisation workplan The Bank provided a brief update on its approach to tokenisation and the work underway across the Bank, HM Treasury and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). The Bank highlighted the potential for tokenisation to support greater efficiency through shared ledgers, enable new products and functionality, and potentially strengthen resilience. Work is underway considering the full lifecycle of tokenised assets, from issuance and use, through to payment and settlement. The Bank noted that feedback to its joint call for input alongside the FCA showed a desire from industry to move beyond piloting the approach towards live activity. A cross-authority roadmap is planned for Q4 which will set out the work underway to support this transition, including work to enable digital asset issuance, collateral use and innovative settlement in central bank money.  The RTGS initiatives covering extended settlement hours and synchronisation were highlighted as important contributors to this workplan. Item 3: Extended RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours The Bank provided an update on feedback received in response to its recently closed consultation on further extensions to RTGS and CHAPS settlement hours . Respondents had broadly supported the strategic direction and the use cases for longer settlement hours, though there was some difference of opinion on how this should be achieved. Notably responses indicated a preference for further weekday extensions before the addition of Sundays and bank holidays. The Bank has yet to reach conclusions on sequencing. The Bank noted the work around extended hours involved three principal drivers: innovation; cross-border payment enhancement; and liquidity and risk management. Members discussed a number of issues that will need answering as the design develops including liquidity, optional participation, operating costs, incident management, planned downtime and operational support. Key discussions focused on the appropriate approach to value-date rollover, including the relative merits of retaining the existing rollover (with CHAPS closing at 6pm) or aligning this more closely with the calendar day.  The Bank acknowledged that further work is needed on this. The Bank plans to publish a response to the extended hours consultation in early 2027. In response to a question, the Bank confirmed that work on implementing CHAPS opening from 1.30am is already underway and progressing well. Initial estimates suggest around 20% of CHAPS payments by volume will settle before 6am. Item 4: Synchronisation The Bank provided an update on its work to introduce synchronisation functionality into RTGS.  This would enable atomic settlement of external asset ledgers against sterling central bank money, conditional on all elements of a transaction settling together or not at all. Potential uses include both tokenised asset transactions and more traditional applications such as margin and collateral optimisation. The Bank noted the need for ecosystem readiness and the challenges of scaling services.  There was discussion of the practical arrangements needed to support a live service, including the role of synchronisation operators, participation, architecture, regulatory expectations and operating arrangements. The Bank is already working on many of these questions, and plans to publish relevant information in early 2027. The Bank is also arranging a showcase event in November 2026 including demonstrations from the prospective synchronisation operators testing in the synchro lab, showing how their propositions using the synchronisation functionality can deliver value. Item 5: Delay in standards releases The Bank outlined that, following Swift’s decision to delay the Swift Standards Release 2026 due to concerns about readiness for the removal of unstructured address fields, it too had delayed the November 2026 RTGS Standards Release. In the interests of both realising industry wide benefits from use of structured addresses, and to avoid being in this position again in future, the Bank wanted to understand early industry views on the possibility of mandating use of structured addresses via the CHAPS rulebook ahead of Swift (and CHAPS) formally retiring the unstructured address fields. Members expressed support for exploring this further though noted further engagement with industry would be needed.  All noted the work that had already been done to be ready for these changes, though noted, in particular, dependencies on customers to complete creditor address fields. There was broad support for mandating use of structured debtor addresses through rules, though continuing dependencies on improvements to the EISCD, the UK’s sort-code directory, were noted for intermediary address fields.  Interoperability with Swift channels was raised as a key concern, but this needed to be balanced with the need to make progress. Members also mentioned the need to take decisions on this promptly given budget cycles.  Members also flagged the work in Pay.UK on cross-border payments in FPS and noted the need for any wider implications on FPS to be understood. Item 6: Operational resilience The Bank discussed work on settlement contingency arrangements, including the challenges associated with processing payments when normal connectivity is unavailable such as during a Swift outage. The Bank noted that contingency arrangements need to consider the end-to-end payment journey, including how instructions are provided to the Bank and how confirmation of settlement is provided. The Bank set out the current arrangements, noting that these were small in scale and would only cover the most critical payments. Attendees noted that the Bank could also call a non-settlement day in the event of disruption. Members highlighted the limitations of manual processing and the benefits of automation in developing arrangements capable of operating at greater scale. There was also discussion of the balance between developing tactical contingency arrangements in the nearer term and a more strategic longer-term solution. The Bank will convene further discussions on this topic – both possible short-medium term improvements, but also longer-term arrangements. Item 7: Next steps The next Forum meeting is expected to take place in January. Close of meeting. Attendees Members: Richard Windram, Deputy Chair (Bank of England) Adrian Smyth, alternate (Natwest) Akshat Sharia (HSBC) Alex Loyden (JP Morgan) Ben Ashwell (Nationwide) Chloe Jenkins (Barclays) Douglas Peel (Goldman Sachs) Jason Roberts (Santander UK) Jon Rushton (Modulr) Jo Oxley (Government Banking Service) Mark Goree (Fnality) Martin Beed (Northern Trust) Naresh Aggarwal (Association of Corporate Treasurers) Peter Smith, alternate (Coventry Building Society) Stuart Bailey (Lloyds) Thair Hanif (Al Rayan Bank) Urs Spycher, alternate, (UBS) Other attendees: Michael D’Souza – Independent Member of RTGS CHAPS Board Noel Gordon – Senior Independent Member of the RTGS CHAPS Board Sharon Barber – Independent Member of RTGS CHAPS Board Bank of England standing attendees, secretariat and presenters for specific items Apologies: Beth Rudolf (Conveyancing Associations) Emma Hagen (Clearbank) Paul Miles (Euroclear UK & International) Simon Eacott (Natwest – alternate sent) Simon McConnell (Citibank) Vishal Majithia (Coventry Building Society– alternate sent) Convert this page to PDF Other news News // Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) 05 November 2026 Bank rate increased to 4% - November 2026... title: We're sharing our framework for building safer and more helpful AI for health.
body: We're sharing our framework for building safer and more helpful AI for health. Dr Sarah Montgomery-Taylor Clinical Evaluation Lead, Google for Health Nov 04, 2026 Many of us have turned to AI with a health question or received care from a doctor who’s using it. The adoption of technology for health is accelerating and impacts billions of people every day. But how can we assess if these tools are safe and helpful? In partnership with health experts Dr. Elizabeth McGlynn and Dr. Dana Gelb Safran , we published a whitepaper detailing an end-to-end evaluation approach to assess AI use cases for addressing people’s health needs. The framework evaluates models across three areas: accuracy, safety, and usefulness. It combines closed-question benchmarks, autoraters, and expert human review to assess common and high-risk health scenarios. We built and continue to utilize this framework to assess whether our models provide useful, accurate responses that promote safe interactions in health contexts. By sharing our methodology, we hope to promote transparency in how we approach this important area, and seek to support the entire health ecosystem — from developers to researchers to clinicians — in building AI tools people can trust.
