title: ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full year of 2026
body:
ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full year of 2026 Skip to: Skip to navigation Skip to content Skip to footer EN Български Čeština Dansk Deutsch Eλληνικά English Español Eesti keel Suomi Français Gaeilge Hrvatski Magyar Italiano Lietuvių Latviešu Malti Nederlands Polski Português Română Slovenčina Slovenščina Svenska Menu Search Menu ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Search Options Image Preview Sort by ANYTIME PAST MONTH PAST YEAR Suggestions Home Media Explainers Research & Publications Statistics Monetary Policy The €uro Payments & Markets Careers Suggestions Sort by Relevance Date PRESS RELEASE ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full
        year of 2026 4 November 2026 ECB wage tracker updated with wage agreements signed up to
            middle of October 2026; forward-looking horizon extended to end of September 2027 Headline ECB wage tracker at 2.7% in second half of 2026 and 2.8% in first half of 2027; it will decline to
            2.4% in third quarter of 2027 based on still-limited employee coverage ECB wage tracker excluding one-off payments increased from 2.6% in 2026 to 2.8% for first three quarters of
            2027 The European Central Bank (ECB) headline wage tracker, which covers active collective bargaining agreements with
        one-off payments smoothed over 12 months, indicates negotiated wage growth of 2.3% in 2026 (based on a coverage of 46.2% of employees in participating countries). The tracker stands at 2.7%
        for the second half of 2026 (based on a coverage of 45.6%) and 2.8% for the first half of 2027 (based on a
        coverage of 31.8%), and declines to 2.4% for the third quarter of 2027 (based on a still relatively low
        coverage of 23.3%). The relatively low ECB wage tracker in the first half of 2026 still reflects the downward
        mechanical impact of one-off payments that were initially paid in the second half of 2024 and not repeated in
        the following year. These effects dissipate fully in the second half of 2026. Compared with the September 2026 data release , the headline wage tracker was revised upwards
        slightly for the second half of 2026 and for the first half of 2027, by around 0.1 percentage points on average. The ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments stands at 2.4% for the
        third quarter of 2027, down from 2.7% for the first half of 2027 and for 2026 as a whole. The wage tracker excluding one-off payments moderates to 2.5% for the third
        quarter of 2027 from 2.9% for the first half of 2027 and stands at 2.6% on average for 2026, continuing to indicate a limited scope for
        one-off payments in recently signed collective bargaining agreements. Excluding one-offs, the ECB wage tracker
        averages 2.8% in the first three quarters of 2027, indicating a slightly higher permanent negotiated wage growth
        than registered for the full year of 2026. The headline ECB wage tracker is better suited to describing quarterly or monthly dynamics in negotiated wages as
        it smooths one-off payments over time. By contrast, the ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments is
        better suited to describing yearly dynamics in negotiated wages. The forward-looking horizon of the wage tracker has been extended up to the end of September 2027. As new
        agreements are signed and coverage of contracts reaching 2027 gradually increases, the forward-looking horizon
        of the wage tracker will be further extended to the full year of 2027 in the December 2026 data release. Employee coverage for 2026 stands at 46.2% but decreases significantly to
        31.8% in the first half of 2027 and to 23.3% in the third quarter of 2027. The employee coverage is still
        limited for the third quarter of 2027 and will steadily increase over time as more wage agreements are signed.
        The employee coverage for 2026 and the first half of 2027 is broadly similar to that recorded at the same time
        last year, as indicated in the November 2025 data release . See Chart 1 and Table 1 for further details. Overall, the ECB wage tracker may be subject to revision, and the forward-looking component should not be
        interpreted as a forecast, as it only captures information that is currently available for active collective
        bargaining agreements. Moreover, the ECB wage tracker does not perfectly track the indicator of negotiated wage
        growth, which is aggregated for the euro area based on country-level data on negotiated wage growth calculated
        by national sources (see Chart 1, left panel). Therefore, deviations from the indicator of negotiated wage
        growth are to be expected over time. For a more comprehensive assessment of wage developments in the euro area, please refer to the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area , which
        indicate a yearly growth rate of compensation per employee of 3.3% in 2026. The ECB publishes four wage tracker indicators for the aggregate of the nine participating euro area countries on
        the ECB Data Portal . The
        data release following the December 2026 meeting of the ECB Governing Council will exceptionally be published on
        18 December 2026. Chart 1 ECB wage tracker: forward-looking signals and revisions to the previous data release Indicators between January 2025 and September 2027 Revisions to previous data release (left-hand scale: yearly growth rates, percentages; right-hand
                                        scale: percentage share of employees) (percentage points) Sources: ECB calculations based on data provided by the Nationale Bank van België/Banque nationale
                    de Belgique, the Belgian Federal Public Service Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue, the Belgian
                    National Social Security Office, the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Bank of Greece, the Banco de España,
                    the Banque de France, the Banca d’Italia, the Dutch employers’ association AWVN, the
                    Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Suomen Pankki – Finlands Bank, the Confederation of Finnish
                    Industries, Statistics Finland and Eurostat. The indicator of negotiated wage growth is calculated
                    using data from the Belgian Federal Public Service Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue, the
                    Deutsche Bundesbank, the Spanish Ministry of Labour and Social Economy, the Banque de France, the
                    Italian National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT), Statistics Netherlands, Statistics Austria,
                    Statistics Finland, Haver Analytics and Eurostat. Notes: Dashed lines denote forward-looking information (which is not yet available for the
                    indicator of negotiated wage growth). The latest observations are for September 2027 for the ECB
                    wage tracker indicators (left panel), August 2026 for the indicator of negotiated wage growth (left
                    panel) and June 2027 for revisions to the previous data release (right panel). What do the four different indicators show? The headline ECB wage tracker is a tracker of negotiated wage growth that includes
            collectively agreed one-off payments, such as those related to inflation compensation, bonuses or back-dated
            pay, which are smoothed over 12 months. The ECB wage tracker excluding one-off payments reflects the extent of structural (or
            permanent) negotiated wage increases. The ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments is constructed using a methodology
            that, in terms of both data sources and statistical methodology, is conceptually similar to, but not
            necessarily the same as, that used for the ECB indicator of negotiated wage growth. The share of employees covered is the percentage of employees across the participating
            countries that are directly covered by ECB wage tracker data. This indicator provides information on the
            representativeness of the underlying (negotiated) wage growth signals obtained from the set of wage tracker
            indicators for the aggregate of the participating countries. Employee coverage differs across countries and
            within each country over time (more details can be found in Table 2). Table 1 ECB wage tracker summary (percentages) ECB wage tracker Coverage Headline indicator With unsmoothed one-off payments Excluding one-off payments Share of employees 2013-25 2.3 2.3 2.2 50.8 2026 2.3 2.7 2.6 46.2 Q1 2026 1.8 2.9 2.7 47.0 Q2 2026 1.9 2.4 2.4 46.6 July 2026 2.2 2.2 2.4 45.9 August 2026 2.7 3.2 2.7 45.9 September 2026 2.8 2.7 2.7 45.6 October 2026 2.8 2.8 2.8 45.5 November 2026 2.8 2.5 2.7 45.5 December 2026 2.8 2.7 2.7 45.0 Q1 2027 2.8 2.6 2.8 35.3 Q2 2027 2.8 2.9 2.9 28.3 Q3 2027 2.4 2.4 2.5 23.3 Sources: ECB calculations based on data provided by the Nationale Bank van België/Banque
                    nationale de Belgique, the Belgian Federal Public Service Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue,
                    the Belgian National Social Security Office, the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Bank of Greece, the Banco
                    de España, the Banque de France, the Banca d’Italia, the Dutch employers’ association AWVN, the
                    Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Suomen Pankki – Finlands Bank, the Confederation of Finnish
                    Industries, Statistics Finland and Eurostat. Notes: ECB wage tracker indicators reflect yearly
                    growth in negotiated wages as a percentage. Coverage is defined as the share of employees in
                    participating countries as a percentage. Rows with values in italics and bold refer to the
                    forward-looking aspect of the respective indicators. Data are subject to revision. Table 2 Employee coverage by country (share of employees in each country, percentages) Belgium Germany Greece Spain France Italy Netherlands Austria Finland Euro area 2013-25 38.7 42.8 18.5 61.3 52.5 51.5 63.9 75.5 65.9 50.8 2026 44.5 45.8 22.6 33.9 47.9 48.0 60.2 73.5 62.0 46.2 Q1 2026 44.4 46.0 23.0 35.9 49.3 48.3 60.8 75.7 62.6 47.0 Q2 2026 44.6 46.0 22.8 34.9 48.3 48.2 60.6 74.1 63.0 46.6 Q3 2026 44.6 45.8 22.3 32.5 47.2 48.2 59.8 73.0 61.8 45.8 Q4 2026 44.5 45.4 22.3 32.4 46.8 47.2 59.5 71.3 60.7 45.3 Q1 2027 44.5 41.8 14.4 16.4 26.2 44.8 46.9 43.5 60.3 35.3 Q2 2027 44.4 29.0 13.1 15.8 14.8 43.6 45.6 34.2 59.9 28.3 Q3 2027 44.3 25.1 13.1 14.5 1.3 42.4 38.3 29.7 59.1 23.3 Sources: ECB calculations based on data provided by the Nationale Bank van België/Banque
                    nationale de Belgique, the Belgian Federal Public Service Employment, Labour and Social Dialogue,
                    the Belgian National Social Security Office, the Deutsche Bundesbank, the Bank of Greece, the Banco
                    de España, the Banque de France, the Banca d’Italia, the Dutch employers’ association AWVN, the
                    Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Suomen Pankki – Finlands Bank, the Confederation of Finnish
                    Industries, Statistics Finland and Eurostat. Notes: The euro area aggregate comprises the nine
                    participating wage tracker countries. The coverage shows the relative strength of wage signals for
                    each country and the euro area. The historical average is calculated from January 2015 for Finland
                    and January 2016 for Greece. For the other countries, it is calculated from January 2013 to December
                    2025. Rows with values in italics and bold refer to the forward-looking aspect of the indicator.
                    Data are subject to revision. For media queries, please contact Benoit Deeg , tel.: +491721683704 Notes: The ECB wage tracker is the result of a Eurosystem partnership currently comprising the ECB and nine euro
            area national central banks: the Nationale Bank van België/Banque nationale de Belgique, the Deutsche
            Bundesbank, the Bank of Greece, the Banco de España, the Banque de France, the Banca d’Italia, De
            Nederlandsche Bank, the Oesterreichische Nationalbank and Suomen Pankki – Finlands Bank. It is based on a
            highly granular database of active collective bargaining agreements for Belgium, Germany, Greece, Spain,
            France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria and Finland. The wage tracker can be used to help assess wage
            pressures in the euro area. The wage tracker methodology uses a double aggregation approach. First, it aggregates the highly granular
            information on collective bargaining agreements and constructs the wage tracker indicators at the country
            level using information on the employee coverage within each country. Second, it uses this information to
            construct the aggregate for the euro area using time-varying weights based on the total compensation of
            employees among the participating countries. Given that the forward-looking nature of the tracker is dependent on the underlying collective bargaining
            agreements database, the wage signals should always be considered conditional on the information available
            at any given point in time and thus subject to revision. This is particularly relevant at the turn of the
            year, as many agreements are signed or renewed in the first quarter in some countries. title: READOUT: Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s Meeting with Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco
body: November 2, 2026 WASHINGTON – Today, Secretary Bessent met with Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, congratulated him on his appointment, and discussed developments in Venezuela and opportunities to advance the Trump Administration’s three-phase approach of stabilization, recovery, and transition. Secretary Bessent underscored the Trump Administration’s commitment to supporting Venezuela’s economic recovery and revitalizing its critical sectors, including boosting energy production and reconnecting the Venezuelan financial sector, with the goals of restoring confidence, attracting investment, and laying the groundwork for a more prosperous Venezuela. ###

title: Treasury Announces Marketable Borrowing Estimates
body: November 2, 2026 Sources and Uses Table WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of the Treasury today announced its current estimates of privately-held net marketable borrowing for the October–December 2026 and January–March 2027 quarters. During the October–December 2026 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $618 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-December cash balance of $850 billion. The borrowing estimate is $10 billion lower than announced in August 2026, primarily due to the higher-than-assumed beginning of quarter cash balance, partially offset by lower projected net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed beginning-of-quarter cash balance, the current quarter borrowing estimate is $24 billion higher than announced in August. During the January–March 2027 quarter, Treasury expects to borrow $800 billion in privately-held net marketable debt, assuming an end-of-March cash balance of $1.000 trillion. During the July–September 2026 quarter, Treasury borrowed $742 billion in privately-held net marketable debt and ended the quarter with a cash balance of $984 billion. In August 2026, Treasury estimated borrowing of $739 billion and assumed an end-of-September cash balance of $950 billion. The $4 billion in higher privately-held net marketable borrowing resulted primarily from the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, offset by higher net cash flows. Excluding the higher-than-assumed end-of-quarter cash balance, actual borrowing was $30 billion lower than announced in August. Additional financing details relating to Treasury’s Quarterly Refunding will be released at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. ### 1. Privately-held net marketable borrowing excludes rollovers (auction “add-ons”) of Treasury securities held in the SOMA but includes financing required due to SOMA redemptions. Secondary market purchases of Treasury securities by SOMA do not directly change privately-held net marketable borrowing but, all else equal, when the securities mature and assuming the Federal Reserve does not redeem any maturing securities, would increase the amount of cash raised for a given privately-held auction size by increasing the SOMA “add-on” amount. Additionally, buybacks are not expected to significantly affect privately-held net marketable borrowing as new issuance replaces securities that are bought back. 2. title: Economy Statement for the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee
body: November 2, 2026 Introduction The economy under the Trump Administration is strong, supported by robust business investment in equipment and intellectual property products, as well as solid household consumption growth. Business fixed investment (BFI) rose by over 10% at an annual rate over the first three quarters of 2026, driven by investments in new equipment and intellectual property. Since December 2025, the private sector has added 634,000 net new jobs across a broadening range of industries. The unemployment rate and initial unemployment claims remain low, and real weekly wages have grown since the President’s inauguration. Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) The economy in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q26) grew at the fastest pace in the last four quarters. According to the advance estimate, real GDP grew by 3.4% at an annual rate, accelerating sharply from the 2.2% advance in 2Q26. Core demand in the private sector remained unusually strong, with private domestic final purchases (PDFP) – the combination of PCE, BFI, and residential investment – rising 4.9% at an annual rate, the strongest pace in over five years and following a 4.6% gain in 2Q. Apart from outsized growth of PDFP in the recovery from the short pandemic recession, these were the first back-to-back gains above 4.5% since 2014. The robust PDFP growth in 2Q and 3Q26 suggests a marked boost in the economy’s already-solid capacity for self-sustaining growth in future quarters. BFI grew by 12.7% at an annual rate in 3Q26 – after the very rapid paces of 9.0% in 2Q and 9.9% in 1Q26 – and alone contributed 1.8 percentage points to GDP growth. The third quarter’s rate was the fastest in 15 years, outside of wide swings seen during the pandemic. Equipment investment surged by 20.9% at an annual rate, the third consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, bringing the annualized rate thus far in 2026 to 16.6%.  While super intelligence-related (SI-related) investments contributed to record levels of equipment capital expenditure through the first three quarters, capital expenditure growth was broad-based in 3Q26. Industrial equipment investment rose at an annual rate of 24.7%, following 27.0% annualized growth in 2Q26. Investment in intellectual property products expanded by 8.4% at an annual rate, reflecting businesses’ continued high levels of investment in software, as well as research and development. Structures investment turned strongly positive in 3Q26, rising 5.4% at an annual rate, after inching up 0.1% in the previous quarter. Structures investment in 3Q26 was the strongest since 4Q23, and this quarter marked the first back-to-back quarterly gains in structures investment in three years. Spending on data centers accelerated to a triple-digit pace in 3Q26. Persistently strong personal consumption expenditures (PCE), which account for roughly two-thirds of the U.S. economy, remained the largest contributor to GDP growth. PCE grew by 3.8% at an annual rate in 3Q26, matching the 2Q pace and adding 2.5 percentage points to real GDP growth. Consumer spending on services accelerated in 3Q26 (led by both health care services and food services and accommodations), while goods spending remained solid (led by prescription drugs). Residential investment declined by 3.3% at an annual rate, reversing a 2.8% increase in 2Q.  The decrease in residential investment shaved 0.1 percentage points from growth.  Spending on single-family structures and brokers’ commissions (the latter related to existing home sales) both declined, more than offsetting a slight increase in multifamily structures investment. Of the remaining components of GDP, the trade deficit widened, posing a larger drag on growth. Exports of goods and services declined, led by petroleum and related products—though exports of intellectual property services increased at a double-digit rate. Meanwhile, imports surged, largely due to non-automotive capital goods. These imports are enabling U.S. businesses to meet the increased demand arising from a boom in capital expenditures. On balance, net exports subtracted 3.3 percentage points from GDP growth. By contrast, the change in private inventories and total government spending both added to economic growth. The federal contribution to growth surged, reflecting more national defense expenditures as well as less drawdown in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Meanwhile, state and local government expenditures were essentially flat. Public spending and the change in private inventories added a combined 2.5 percentage points to real GDP growth in 3Q26. Labor Markets Job growth remained consistent with breakeven employment in 3Q26, and other measures of labor markets remained healthy (see Table 2 – Labor Market Indicators). Private-sector employment growth and the unemployment rate indicate a full-employment economy—one that has steady job growth with neither rising unemployment nor inflationary pressures from wages. The prime-age (ages 25 to 54) labor force participation rate (LFPR) remained at a high level despite a slight decline in the overall LFPR. Job openings were relatively stable in both absolute terms and relative to the number of unemployed persons. Preliminary 4Q26 readings indicate that unemployment claims through mid-October stand near multi-decade lows. Net new payrolls averaged 51,000 per month in 3Q26. Year to date, establishments have added an average of 68,000 jobs per month in 2026. The private sector continues to lead job growth, and payroll job creation has begun to broaden across various sectors. In 3Q26, average job growth in the private sector was 54,000 per month, slowing from 79,000 per month in 2Q26. For the first time since early 2023, health and education services accounted for less than half of private-sector job growth and manufacturers, wholesale traders, and transportation and warehousing firms saw solid net employment growth. Government payrolls declined slightly in 3Q26, shedding an average of 4,000 jobs per month that was largely due to local governments. Total federal payrolls continued to hold at about 2.68 million workers, down from 3.01 million in January 2025. The unemployment rate declined further in 3Q26 to an average of 4.1%—down from averages of 4.3% in the first half of the year. This is well in line with mainstream estimates of the noncyclical unemployment rate—that is, consistent with stable inflation and steady economic growth. Wage growth remained solid in the third quarter: over the year through September 2026, nominal average hourly earnings (AHE) for all employees were up 3.0%, and average weekly earnings were up 3.6% over this period. The difference between AHE and AWE growth reflects a small increase in average weekly work hours. The Employment Cost Index (ECI) for all private workers, which controls for compositional changes and includes employee benefits, rose 3.4% over the year ending in September 2026.  This was a tick faster than Q2’s pace, reflecting stable wage growth and slightly faster increase in employee benefits. Labor force participation declined slightly in 3Q26, partly reflecting ongoing demographic pressures. The overall LFPR slipped to an average of 61.6% in 3Q26 from 61.7% in 2Q26. Although the LFPR among prime-age workers ticked down in 3Q26 to 83.5%, it remained 0.4 percentage points above the previous business cycle peak in January 2020. Participation remains particularly resilient among prime-age men: the LFPR for this group averaged 89.3% in 3Q26, just 0.1 percentage point shy of the previous business cycle peak. Monthly job openings averaged 7.2 million in July and August (latest data available), down 0.2 million from 2Q but up from 6.9 million per month in 4Q25 and 1Q26. The ratio of job openings to unemployed persons averaged 1.0 per month in July and August. Other indicators reflect labor markets’ ongoing health and stability. The layoff rate remains stable and near historical lows and the hires rate has remained stable since mid-2024. Initial unemployment claims trended down in 3Q26 and remained exceptionally low by historical standards through mid-October. Business applications reached a record high of more than 576,000 in July and remained high through Q3, indicating potential increases in new firm births and associated opportunities for American entrepreneurs. Inflation Headline CPI rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September 2026, picking up from the 3.0% annual CPI inflation rate through September 2025. Energy inflation drove roughly 40% of the increase. Average headline inflation ticked up to 0.4% per month in 3Q26 from 0.2% in 2Q26 (see Table 3 – Inflation Indicators). Energy price inflation accelerated in 3Q26. CPI inflation for energy goods and services averaged 1.9% per month in 3Q26, up from the monthly average of 0.6% in 2Q26 but well below the 3.2% monthly average in 1Q26. Food price inflation averaged 0.1% per month in 3Q, down from 0.3% in 2Q, as pressures in the food-at-home category – including beef and coffee prices – receded. Over the 12 months through September, food price inflation was 2.5%, 0.6 percentage points below its year-earlier rate. Twelve-month core CPI inflation, which excludes the volatile components of food and energy, stood at 2.6% as of September, slowing from the 3.0% rate through September 2025. On a monthly average basis, core inflation ticked up to 0.3% in 3Q26 after averaging 0.2% per month in the first and second quarters. Monthly core goods prices increased 0.2% on average in 3Q26, after declining by 0.1% per month in 2Q26. About half of the swing was attributable to new and used motor vehicles, which had flipped from a deflationary to an inflationary force beginning in 2Q. Nonetheless, on a twelve-month basis, core goods inflation was 0.7% through September 2026, the slowest rate since June 2025. Rent of housing inflation decelerated to 0.3% per month in 3Q26, down from 0.4% in 2Q26. Rent of housing inflation was 3.2% over the year through September, well below the 3.7% year-earlier rate and slightly below the pre-pandemic average of 3.3%. Inflation for rent of housing services (rent of primary residence and owners’ equivalent rent) has eased since 2024. After slowing by half in 2Q26, inflation for non-housing core services averaged 0.4% per month in 3Q26. Most of the acceleration of non-housing core services was due to a pickup in transportation services. Over the year through September 2026, non-housing core services inflation was 3.1%, slowing slightly from the 3.2% year-earlier rate. The PCE price index has notable differences in weights and methodologies versus the CPI. Over the past 20 years, twelve-month CPI inflation has exceeded PCE inflation by about 0.35 percentage points on average. Over the year through September 2026, headline PCE inflation was 3.6%, above the 2.8% pace over the year through September 2025. The Federal Reserve’s target for headline PCE inflation is 2%. Risks to the Outlook Looking ahead to the next few quarters, the outlook for the U.S. economy is favorable and economists view the risk of a recession as low. According to The Wall Street Journal’s survey of economists in October, the average probability of a recession in the next 12 months was just 24%, little changed from 25% in the July survey. The survey also indicated an improved near-term outlook. Projected real GDP growth in 2026 was revised up by 0.3 percentage points to 2.4%, and the expected unemployment rate in December 2026 was revised down to 4.2%. Compared with the July survey, respondents projected slightly higher headline inflation, lower core inflation, and higher interest rates. Energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty: Geopolitical uncertainty remains a risk to the medium-term inflation outlook. Energy prices are among the most volatile categories of inflation and reflect this uncertainty. Indeed, the energy goods and services CPI fell 1.5% in July but rebounded 2.1% in August and 5.2% in September. The timing, duration, and magnitude of energy price swings contribute to the risk of increased inflation in other goods and services – such as food (through fertilizer and fuel for farming equipment) and airfares – adding uncertainty to the medium-term inflation outlook. Importantly, the Trump Administration’s policies have made the U.S. economy more resilient to fluctuations in global oil prices. This resilience is due to a wide range of policies enacted, including deregulatory actions that have increased production and exports of oil and gas, and strategic actions abroad that have resulted in increased demand for U.S. crude and increased supply to the U.S. outside of the Middle East. Average domestic crude oil production in 2025 rose by 350,000 barrels per day relative to the 2024 average, and production and exports have risen further in 2026 as U.S. producers continue to build out U.S. infrastructure. The United States is increasingly the world’s largest producer of petroleum products and natural gas, and it is a net exporter of both. Business fixed investment and the manufacturing outlook: Recent data suggest that the economy is in the early stages of a policy-driven capital-expenditure boom. Since the passage of the Administration’s signature tax bill (the Working Families Tax Cuts), real BFI has risen by a cumulative 9.4% through 3Q26.  Provisions in the tax law – such as full expensing of research and development, 100% bonus depreciation for business equipment investments, and restoring deductibility of interest expenses for capital-intensive manufacturers – have contributed to this rapid business investment growth. Indeed, business equipment investment alone has added 0.8 percentage points to GDP growth over the past four quarters, while spending on intellectual property products has contributed 0.5 percentage points. The tax law also included a temporary provision for full depreciation deduction for the costs of new, nonresidential manufacturing facilities. Although real investment in factories and manufacturing structures has declined since mid-2024, the manufacturing outlook appears favorable. Jobs related to the construction of nonresidential buildings have grown by 116,000 since September 2025, presaging future manufacturing sector growth as new facilities are completed and products are deployed. In addition, firms that manufacture durable goods have increased their payrolls by 101,000 so far this year. Job openings in durable goods manufacturing grew by 93,000, and layoffs and discharges fell by 7,000. This capital expenditures boom bodes well for future economic growth. Capital expenditures correlate with productivity growth, which is a strategic pillar of the Administration’s economic agenda: productivity growth helps drive stronger economic growth and, as a positive supply-side development, is usually disinflationary while increasing wage growth. Interest rates: At the end of 2025, the yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 4.18%. As of October 30, it was 76 basis points higher. Several factors may have contributed to this increase, including optimism around U.S. growth expectations alongside higher demand for capital from investments related to SI. Since last year, economists’ forecasts have improved: the Blue Chip consensus for real GDP growth five years ahead has increased from 1.9% in the October 2025 report to 2.1% in the October 2026 report. Improved growth prospects can lead to higher interest rates as the returns from business investment rise. Increased demand for credit to finance capital investment also correlates with higher interest rates. The risk to the economic outlook is that higher borrowing costs could worsen the federal debt trajectory. However, U.S. fiscal sustainability does not appear to be a significant driver of the year-to-date increase in interest rates. Rate increases have been a global phenomenon even among countries with lower debt-to-GDP ratios. Super intelligence (SI): Investment in super intelligence has been a significant driver of economic growth in recent quarters. In the first three quarters of 2026, SI-driven investment (BFI in software, computers and hardware, and data center structures relative to pre-large language models trend) accounted for nearly 30% of GDP growth. In the long run, firms’ continued investment in super intelligence is likely to lead to efficiency gains, particularly in service-sector industries where productivity growth has been slower. However, the timeline and magnitude of productivity gains are uncertain, as is the ultimate effect on the composition of labor markets. If the integration of super intelligence acts as a standard technology improvement, productivity growth could return to historical norms after a period of above-trend growth. On the other hand, super intelligence could prove transformational and permanently upshift the path of productivity as it enables workers to build skills and human capital faster than in the past. Labor markets: While labor markets are in balance, labor data indicate an environment of lower job churn than in the past, which could leave the economy with less slack to absorb a negative shock. So far this year, the median private-sector hires rate has been 3.6%, compared to a median of 4.2% in 2019. By contrast, rates of layoffs and discharges for the private sector have remained near historical lows, with the layoffs rate at just 1.2% in August. The lower turnover environment, while indicating that labor markets are in balance, also suggests a large shock could shift markets out of balance as hiring may not be able to offset an increase in the layoffs and discharges rates. Conclusion The U.S. economy remains resilient, and the outlook is favorable. Historically high capital expenditures and steady household consumption growth have increased the economy’s capacity for self-sustaining growth. In the labor market, the unemployment rate and layoffs are low, wages are increasing, and new business applications hit an all-time high. Although energy markets have affected headline inflation, the U.S. economy is resilient to fluctuations in the supply of oil from the Strait of Hormuz, and energy prices should recede following the cessation of conflict in Iran. The Trump Administration has successfully stewarded major fiscal legislation to prevent a historic tax increase and lower the cost of capital, which has increased return expectations in the market. Since its passage in July 2025, we have seen significant business equipment investment, including industrial equipment. Indeed, current macroeconomic conditions bode well for increasing economic growth as the private sector leads. A net 22% of small businesses report plans to make capital outlays over the next six months, and the Business Roundtable reports that its index of CEO expectations of capital expenditures is now at its highest level since early 2022. Announced investments in U.S. manufacturing, production, and innovation total trillions of dollars, reflecting global confidence in the United States as a destination for investment. This capital expenditure boom is made possible by the Administration’s policies allowing full expensing of equipment and R&D, tariffs and reshoring incentives, and deregulation. The combined policies of the Trump Administration, both enacted and planned, provide a solid foundation for economic growth and will bring prosperity to all Americans. title: November 2, 2026 - FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality
body: FDA News Release FDA Provides Clarity to Support Cell and Gene Therapy Development and Quality FDA issues final guidance for cell and gene therapy manufacturers, recommends building potency assurance into every stage of a therapy’s lifecycle — from early development through patient delivery For Immediate Release: November 02, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today issued final guidance for manufacturers of cellular and gene therapy (CGT) products to implement a comprehensive, science- and risk-based plan for making sure their products meet potency standards. The guidance provides FDA’s recommendations for a Potency Assurance Strategy, which guides manufacturers to test and verify — before a product reaches a patient — that every batch meets a defined standard of potency to do what the product is supposed to do therapeutically. The Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products final guidance replaces FDA's 2011 potency testing guidance for CGT products and applies to treatments for serious and often life-threatening conditions. By law, manufacturers are expected to verify that their products work as intended, from the time of approval through post-approval monitoring. This final guidance provides FDA’s current thinking and recommendations on how manufacturers can meet that requirement. "Patients who receive cellular and gene therapies are often battling serious or life-threatening conditions, such as cancers and rare diseases, and they deserve the assurance that the product administered to them will perform as intended," said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research . "This guidance reflects the FDA's commitment to ensuring America remains the best place in the world to innovate — and that innovation is matched by the highest standards of product quality and patient safety." The guidance provides flexible, risk-based recommendations for manufacturers on how to integrate potency considerations at every stage of development and commercialization — from early-phase investigational new drug (IND) submissions through biologics license application (BLA) approval and continued post-market verification. Key topics include controls for variability in raw materials, testing during manufacturing, and lab tests that confirm each batch is biologically active in a way that matches its intended therapeutic effect. The guidance also addresses specialized considerations for products with short shelf lives, viral vector gene therapies, and patient-specific therapies. By giving manufacturers a clear, predictable roadmap, this guidance supports faster access to safe and effective therapies for patients who often have no other treatment options — many of whom receive products made individually for a single person. In doing so, it advances the FDA's public health pillars: protecting patients through rigorous quality standards, promoting innovation by providing regulatory clarity, and reinforcing the integrity of the supply chain for some of the most complex medical products in existence. The FDA will host a webinar on December 10, 2026, to help stakeholders understand and implement the guidance. title: October 30, 2026 - FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First Plasmid DNA-based Immunotherapy for Adults with Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis Groundbreaking therapy provides additional treatment option that fights the disease at its source, not only its symptoms For Immediate Release: October 30, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for Voceryq (doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid-gxfd) for treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), a rare disease caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) that leads to the formation of small, wart-like growths in the patient’s airways. This approval, the first for a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy in the U.S., offers patients a new therapeutic option that targets the root cause of RRP and has been shown to reduce the burden of surgical intervention, representing an important step forward for a patient population with limited treatment options. “Adults living with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis often face an exhausting and relentless cycle of repeated surgeries, managing their disease, but never truly escaping it. Today’s approval represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough: a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body’s own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP,” said Karim Mikhail, B. Pharm., M.S., Director of the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) . “For patients, that could mean fewer surgeries, fewer disruptions, and more time living their lives on their own terms. The FDA is proud to help bring that possibility within reach.” The agency based this accelerated approval on clinical trial data showing Voceryq helps reduce the frequency of surgical procedures required to remove growths in adult patients with RRP — an intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The accelerated approval pathway allows the FDA to approve drugs or biologics for serious or life-threatening conditions based on an effect on a surrogate or intermediate clinical endpoint reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The manufacturer must conduct post-approval clinical trials to verify and describe Voceryq’s clinical benefit. RRP is a rare, chronic disease in which wart-like growths caused by HPV types 6 and/or 11 form in the airways, most often around the larynx (voice box), particularly the vocal cords. These growths, called papillomas, can cause symptoms like hoarseness, chronic cough, and voice changes, and in severe cases can spread to other parts of the respiratory tract, causing difficulty breathing. While surgery can remove the growths, there is no cure, and the virus persists in the tissue even after the growths are removed, so patients often need repeated procedures over many years. In some cases, RRP carries a risk of becoming cancerous over time. Voceryq is a recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that delivers two plasmids (small pieces of DNA originally derived from bacteria) into the body’s cells, one of which contains the genetic instructions for specific HPV proteins and the other an immune response-enhancing molecule called IL-12. The therapy is designed to stimulate the immune system to respond to and attack cells infected by the specific types of HPV that cause RRP (types 6 and 11).  Voceryq is administered via intramuscular (IM) injection using the CELLECTRA 5PSP Device, which delivers the dose and facilitates electroporation, a technique which uses brief electrical pulses to temporarily and reversibly create pores in the cell membranes to enable the delivery of Voceryq into the body’s cells. The safety and effectiveness of Voceryq was evaluated in an open-label multicenter clinical trial in 32 adults diagnosed with RRP. Eligible patients had two or more surgeries to remove laryngotracheal papillomas in the 12 months prior to Voceryq treatment, including a scheduled surgery at trial entry. Seven (27%) out of 26 patients who had at least three baseline surgeries did not require any surgery intervention during the first year after treatment. The most commonly reported adverse reactions to Voceryq were injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension (high blood pressure), nausea, and dizziness. Adverse effects associated with the electroporation technique may include brief muscle contractions or tetany, temporary bleeding at the administration site, anxiety, vasovagal reactions including lightheadedness and dizziness, transient changes in creatine phosphokinase, erythema (skin redness) at the injection site, and pain at the injection site. The FDA granted Voceryq Breakthrough and Orphan Drug designations. The FDA granted accelerated approval of Voceryq to Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. title: Report on U.S. Portfolio Holdings of Foreign Securities at Year-End 2025
body: October 30, 2026 Washington – Fial data from an annual survey of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 were released today and posted on the Treasury web site at https://home.treasury.gov/data/treasury-international-capital-tic-system/tic-forms-instructions/us-claims-on-foreigners-from-holdings-of-foreign-securities .  Preliminary data were released and posted on the Treasury web site on August 31, 2025. The survey was undertaken jointly by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. A complementary survey measuring foreign portfolio holdings of U.S. securities also occurs annually.  Data from the most recent such survey, for securities held at end-June 2026, are currently being processed.  Preliminary results are expected to be reported on February 26, 2027. Overall Results This survey measured the value of U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities at year-end 2025 as approximately $19.3 trillion, with $15.2 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.6 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities (original term-to-maturity in excess of one year), and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The previous such survey, conducted as of year-end 2024, measured U.S. holdings of approximately $15.8 trillion, with $12.1 trillion held in foreign equity, $3.3 trillion held in foreign long-term debt securities, and $0.4 trillion held in foreign short-term debt securities.  The increase in U.S. holdings of foreign securities in 2025 was mainly in equity (see Table 1). U.S. portfolio holdings of foreign securities by country at the end of 2025 were the largest for the Cayman Islands ($3.1 trillion), followed by the United Kingdom ($2.0 trillion), Canada ($1.9 trillion), and Japan ($1.5 trillion) (see Table 2). October 22, 2026 - FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches New Program to Advance Neuroscience Medical Product Development Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus to coordinate agency action on brain and nervous system conditions, with inaugural focus on Alzheimer's prevention For Immediate Release: October 22, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today announced the launch of the Neuroscience Advancement and Innovation Nexus (NAIN) , a new agency program aligned with the Trump Administration’s efforts to accelerate medical innovation and deliver breakthrough treatments. NAIN is designed to advance the science, tools, and regulatory approaches needed to support the development of medical products for conditions affecting the brain and nervous system. NAIN’s inaugural initiative, the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator , will focus on advancing medical products that help delay or prevent Alzheimer's disease. Both efforts support the National Alzheimer’s Project Act (NAPA), the federal government's comprehensive roadmap for coordinated action on Alzheimer's and related dementias. "The launch of NAIN reflects FDA's commitment — in support of the Trump Administration’s drive to transform health care innovation — to making sure our regulatory science and cross-center collaboration keep pace with the rapid advances happening in neuroscience," said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. "Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, we are bringing the full breadth of FDA's expertise to bear on one of the most urgent public health challenges of our time.” Developing medical products for neuroscience indications is associated with complex scientific and clinical challenges, including limited understanding of underlying biology, variable disease presentation, and difficulties in demonstrating meaningful clinical benefit, particularly for conditions that develop over many years. Advances in biomarkers, digital health technologies, and other medical product development tools, however, offer important opportunities to address these challenges. NAIN will bring together scientific and regulatory expertise from the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and Center for Devices and Radiological Health to address scientific and regulatory questions that benefit from coordinated consideration across drugs, biologics, and devices. NAIN will encompass conditions that affect the brain and nervous system broadly, including neurologic and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders, and pain. NAIN will also support robust engagement with patients, industry, academia and other stakeholders to advance these efforts. As its first initiative, NAIN is launching the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator . This inaugural initiative will draw on perspectives from across the FDA and engage patients and caregivers, researchers, industry, public-private partnerships and other government agencies. The initiative will explore innovative approaches to advancing clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease prevention and early-intervention drug development with emphasis on trial populations, stage-appropriate endpoints, and evidentiary approaches for demonstrating prevention or delay of cognitive decline due to Alzheimer’s disease. The FDA has long been committed to supporting the development of safe and effective medical products that address diseases and conditions of the brain and nervous system. Through NAIN and the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, the agency is taking a proactive, coordinated approach to accelerating progress, bringing together its scientific and regulatory expertise, engaging the broader research and development community, and working in concert with federal partners to meet the scale of this public health challenge. title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software
body: FDA News Release FDA Issues Final Guidance on Prescription Drug Apps and Software New policy clarifies when app content requires FDA review and how drug-connected software must be described on medication labels For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today released final guidance establishing a clear framework for how drug companies can develop, distribute, and label apps used alongside their prescription medicines. The guidance ends longstanding uncertainty by providing recommendations about when app content is subject to FDA submission requirements, when an app should be mentioned on a drug’s official label, and what companies should submit to the agency. “Mobile apps are playing a growing role in how patients manage their medications and health conditions,” said Captain Chris Wheeler, Pharm.D., Director of the Division of Medical Policy Programs within FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “This guidance helps ensure that the information these tools provide is accurate, evidence-based, and clearly communicated to both patients and their providers.” The guidance addresses three key questions for industry: when app content is treated as FDA-required labeling versus promotional labeling, when an app should be referenced in a drug’s official prescribing information, and what companies should submit to FDA when they distribute app content to users. The guidance identifies two categories of companion software: Apps connected to a medical device (such as an app paired with an asthma inhaler) generally should be described on the drug’s official prescribing label, given the central role the software plays in how the medicine is used. Standalone apps (such as symptom trackers, dose reminders, or health coaching tools) should appear on the prescribing label if the company can show the app is essential for safe and effective use or can demonstrate a meaningful clinical benefit. In most cases, content a companion app displays to users will be treated as promotional material, consistent with how the FDA handles other drug advertising. “This guidance reflects FDA’s commitment to responsible, risk-proportionate oversight of digital health, an area that is a key priority for the agency and is evolving rapidly and holds significant promise for improving patient care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “By aligning our approach across drug and device centers, we are giving developers a clear and consistent pathway to bring safe, effective digital health technologies to patients.” “Companion apps are quickly moving beyond simple dose reminders toward tools that adapt to each patient,” said Jared Seehafer, M.S., FDA Deputy Commissioner for Technology . “Finalizing this guidance gives drug companies and their technology partners a stable foundation to build on as these technologies advance and helps ensure patients and providers can trust the information they receive.” This guidance also reflects the FDA’s ongoing commitment to modernizing its regulatory framework to keep pace with rapidly evolving digital health technologies. By providing clear, practical recommendations for both drug-connected software and standalone software, the agency aims to reduce unnecessary uncertainty for developers and manufacturers while preserving the safety and effectiveness standards that patients and healthcare providers rely on. The final guidance is available here . title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration yesterday approved the first generic of Climara Pro (estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system, 0.045 mg per day/0.015 mg), a transdermal hormone therapy patch for women with an intact uterus applied once a week. The approval aligns with FDA’s Public Health Pillar : Increasing Access to Affordable Medicines & Medical Products. “Menopause is a universal experience for women, and it can greatly affect a person’s quality of life. This approval makes effective treatment more accessible,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Approvals like this reflect FDA’s ongoing commitment to expanding American patient access to safe, affordable, high-quality medications.” The generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system is therapeutically equivalent to Climara Pro, which is indicated for use in women with an intact uterus for: Treatment of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause Prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system contain both estrogen and progestogen in a single patch; this differs from estrogen-only patches commonly used in menopause treatment. Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are specifically approved for women with an intact uterus, as the progestogen component is included to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with estrogen use alone. “Once-weekly dosing can make a real difference in how patients manage their care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “A patch offers a convenient alternative to daily oral medications, which may help patients stay on track with their treatment.” Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are contraindicated in patients with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; breast cancer or a history of breast cancer; estrogen-dependent neoplasia; active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE) or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease or a history of these conditions; known anaphylactic reaction or angioedema or hypersensitivity to estradiol and levonorgestrel; hepatic impairment or disease; and protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders. The most common adverse reactions (greater than or equal to 5%) are: application site reaction, vaginal bleeding, breast pain, upper respiratory infection, back pain, depression, pain, headache and flu syndrome. In the U.S., nine out of 10 prescriptions filled are for generic drugs. Increasing the availability of generic drugs helps to create competition in the marketplace, which then helps to make treatment more affordable and increases access to healthcare for more patients. Learn more about the FDA Drug Competition Action Plan . Climara Pro is a registered trademark of Bayer. The FDA approved Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA) Inc.’s Estradiol and Levonorgestrel Transdermal System. Please contact the manufacturer for information about the medicine’s availability. title: October 20, 2026 - FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment New treatment may allow some patients to maintain viral control after stopping all hepatitis B therapy For Immediate Release: October 20, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research . “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements. Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review . The approval was granted to GSK plc. October 19, 2026 - FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery
body: FDA News Release FDA Approves Immunotherapy That May Allow Certain Patients with Rectal Cancer to Avoid Chemotherapy, Radiation and Surgery For Immediate Release: October 19, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today granted accelerated approval for a new use of the immunotherapy Jemperli (dostarlimab-gxly) that may allow some patients with locally advanced rectal cancer to avoid common treatments that can have a lasting impact on their daily life. Patients with locally advanced rectal cancer often receive chemotherapy and radiation prior to surgery, which can affect bowel, urinary, and sexual function, as well as fertility. Surgery also carries risks of serious, sometimes life-threatening complications, including poor healing and leaks where the bowel is reconnected, and in some patients, permanent colostomy. “The FDA is committed to closing the gap between scientific progress and patient access, and that commitment has to show up not just in policy, but in the pace of our work,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “American patients deserve timely access to innovative treatments, and the Trump Administration is making that a reality. Completing this review nearly 4 months ahead of schedule means some patients who might otherwise be preparing for surgery, radiation or chemotherapy may now have a different conversation with their doctor.” Today’s approval is for Jemperli used alone in adults with previously untreated stage II or stage III locally advanced rectal cancer. At these stages, the cancer has grown into nearby tissue or reached nearby lymph nodes but has not spread to distant organs. To be eligible, patients’ tumors must be mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H), as determined by an FDA-authorized test. Published estimates suggest that approximately 3% of locally advanced rectal cancers are dMMR or MSI-H. Both terms describe a defect in the way cancer cells correct errors when copying their DNA. Normally, a built-in repair system catches and fixes these mistakes. When the system does not work properly, errors accumulate and create proteins the immune system can recognize, making these tumors particularly vulnerable to immunotherapy. Jemperli works by blocking a signal that cancer cells use to shield themselves from the immune system. Specifically, it targets a protein called PD-1 on immune cells. “Standard treatment for rectal cancer has major life-changing effects. For certain types of rectal cancer, this approval represents a groundbreaking option that avoids surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. This represents a significant benefit for patients and their families,” said Angelo de Claro, M.D., director of the FDA’s Oncology Center of Excellence . “The FDA is acting on emerging evidence to bring new approaches to patients sooner, while requiring further studies to confirm that these treatments provide lasting benefits.” The FDA based its decision on interim results from AZUR-1 ( NCT05723562 ), a phase 2 study evaluating Jemperli alone in 154 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. In the study, patients received up to nine doses of Jemperli, given every 3 weeks over 6 months. After a median follow-up of more than 2 years — meaning at least half of patients had been monitored for that long — almost three-fourths of patients had not needed surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Longer follow-up is needed to understand the duration of response and how often the cancer returns. An earlier study at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center ( NCT04165772 ) evaluated Jemperli alone in 50 patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. None of the patients had detectable signs of cancer after Jemperli treatment, and nearly all patients (93%) maintained that cancer-free status for at least 12 months. Of the 27 patients followed for at least 3 years, only one had their cancer return, and it recurred in the same area. Jemperli can cause the immune system to attack healthy organs and tissues. These reactions can be severe or fatal. The most common side effects, reported in at least 15% of patients treated for this type of rectal cancer, were fatigue, rash, diarrhea and itching. The FDA granted Priority Review to the application and Breakthrough Therapy designation to Jemperli for the treatment of dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer. This action marks the 11th approval of a drug reviewed under the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher pilot program , which aims to help accelerate the review of therapies that address national public health priorities. Because this is an accelerated approval based on interim trial results, the sponsor must continue following patients to show these responses create lasting clinical benefit. The approval was granted to GSK. October 14, 2026 - FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development
body: FDA News Release FDA Launches the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to Develop a Holistic, Fit-For-Purpose Framework for Rare Disease Drug Development Effort begins by Soliciting Public Feedback For Immediate Release: October 14, 2026 The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a division within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), today announced the Rare Disease Framework Initiative to reimagine the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. As outlined in a new white paper , the Initiative will develop an optimized, fit-for-purpose framework that reflects the realities of rare disease drug development by considering the nuances of each disease, patient needs, product type and the evidence that can be realistically generated in small patient populations. To solicit feedback on the Rare Disease Framework Initiative from patients and disease advocates, industry, and others, the FDA will host an October 28 meeting at the FDA’s White Oak campus. The meeting will be facilitated by the Reagan-Udall Foundation for the FDA. “Americans with rare diseases cannot afford a regulatory system that treats every condition the same,” said HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “Under President Trump, FDA is rethinking rare disease drug development by putting patients at the center and matching regulatory requirements to the realities of small patient populations. We will remove unnecessary barriers, embrace cutting-edge science, and accelerate promising treatments while upholding FDA’s rigorous standards.” “Patients and families living with rare diseases have few or no approved treatment options, and the burden of uncertainty can extend across every part of their lives,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “As we learn more about rare diseases and better understand the breadth of suffering they cause, we must ensure that America’s regulatory system remains at the forefront — prepared to respond to emerging science, anticipate the needs of patients and families, and help bring safe and effective therapies to those who need them. The FDA will fight hard for patients by building a more consistent, predictable, and innovative approach to rare disease drug development while maintaining the rigorous standards Americans expect from the FDA.” The FDA has long used regulatory flexibility and developed targeted programs to support innovation in the development of drugs and biologics for rare diseases. These efforts have led to meaningful advances for patients and families. Nevertheless, with only 5% or so of rare conditions having an FDA-approved treatment, the FDA agrees with patients, drug developers, and providers that more must be done to speed the development of safe and effective treatments for rare diseases. In developing the framework, the FDA is committed to the following: Providing greater clarity, consistency, and predictability in regulatory decision-making through tailored guidance and transparent communication. Embedding the patient’s voice both early, and at clearly defined milestones, in the drug development and review process. Further leveraging external expertise to support customization of regulatory review. Building shared resources, robust training, and institutional knowledge on rare disease drug development and review. Applying risk-based approaches, particularly to chemistry, manufacturing, and controls review and pre-approval inspections. Championing the use of cutting-edge science, novel methods and innovative statistical approaches in rare disease drug development. The Initiative is led by the FDA’s Rare Disease Innovation Hub, partnering with the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, and the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Patients with rare diseases and their families deserve a regulatory process that addresses the uniqueness of each of their conditions while maintaining the FDA’s rigorous standards,” said the Hub’s Director, Amy Comstock Rick, J.D. “A bold vision to reimagine the framework for rare disease drug development that builds on key learnings and milestones is necessary to meet this moment. This new framework will enhance consistency and predictability for both sponsors and for patients.” Further opportunities to provide input will follow the public meeting, including sector-specific roundtables, Requests for Information, and internal FDA feedback sessions. This feedback will inform the detailed development of a new framework, which might include potential new or revised guidance, revisions to regulations, staff training, and organizational changes.
